#9956. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

#9955. Two apps one process

So what if you can handle thousands of concurrent users per core? Even the front page of HN gets you what? 100 concurrent users on a good day?

Exactly! Most successful apps have like what 10 or 20 concurrent users at any given time? This is basically academic for most projects. What does performance give you other than knowing that your app won't need to scale past a single server? Pointless!

Well what if you could run multiple apps in one process?

Isn't that the same as a bunch of apps behind a reverse proxy?

No. It's not. Separate processes have to compete for OS resources, have their own thread pools, schedulers, heap, GC, caches and so on. Each process needs to be sized relative to the other apps running on the system.

But, in a single process you can size the process for the machine and then run an arbitrary number of apps in that process. If the apps share a process, they can share all sorts of things: a single JVM, GC, caches, buffers, http server, HTTPS certificate management, batching, game loop etc. You'd eliminate thread contention between apps. This lets you scale further with less resources!

Performance lets you run as many apps as you want in that one process.

Disclaimer: all my writing and code is handcrafted by me. By the end of this you may wish it wasn't.

If you have multiple JVMs you duplicate a bunch of fixed costs:

If you have multiple HTTP servers you duplicate:

If you have multiple framework engines you duplicate:

All of this adds up to more memory, more threads and more contention. If you own all your app and don't need the isolation a processes give you, then it can be a big performance win to have one JVM, one http server, and one framework engine.

X * n where X is you fixed cost for the above and n is your number of apps. If all of the above takes 500MB, then four apps is an extra 1.5GB.

Indeed. If you think about it an app at it's simplest is a domain, a database and some routes.

But, my reverse proxy handles HTTPS certs and stuff! Where is your god now?

Yes certs are a pain. But Clave: Automatic HTTPS certificate management and renewal via ACME, implemented in pure Clojure with minimal dependencies exists. I use it with aleph. But, it also works with jetty and it's simple to extend to other servers.

To bundle our apps we import them as dependencies into a separate project who's only purpose is to configure and start the server.

So adding a new app is as simple as importing it and adding it to the list of apps:

We can then build this project as an uberjar and scp it to the server.

Well this is nice and all, but whenever you deploy an app, you restart the process. DOWNTIME! UNACCEPTABLE!

Here's a gif of me deploying the jar to production:

If a deploy is indistinguishable from network blip did the app really go down?

That's it. We've reduced the overhead and cost of deploying a new app to zero.

#9954. Attackers backdoor trusted AWS integrations to steal secrets

Wiz researchers uncovered the secret-stealing supply-chain attack

Unknown attackers used compromised identity and access management (IAM) credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account to access customer AWS environments, stealing secrets and other sensitive data from S3 buckets.

Qubole is a cloud data processing platform that uses cross-account IAM roles to manage compute and access storage in customers' AWS environments without requiring customers to provide long-lived AWS access keys. The supply-chain attack abused this third-party, cross-account trust relationship.

Google’s cloud-security shop Wiz declined to tell us how many organizations were affected, but called it a “broad, opportunistic supply chain campaign” that hit “multiple” customer environments.

“Because many organizations left trust policies active even after deprecating the platform, the attacker was able to successfully assume integration roles, enumerate cloud resources, harvest secrets, and siphon data,” the researchers told The Register in an emailed response to questions.

Neither AWS nor Qubole responded to The Register's inquiries.

Wiz, working with Google's Mandiant incident responders after AI data security company Sentra flagged suspicious activity, traced the malicious activity back to October 14, when credentials associated with Qubole's AWS account were used to call the sts:AssumeRole API to obtain temporary credentials for customer-managed integration roles.

The calls originated from Qubole AWS account 805246085872, and used IAM user ID AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS, Wiz analysts Zack Morrow, Sean Johnstone, and Benjamin Read said in a Monday blog about the supply chain attack. “Across the affected environments, Wiz CIRT has not observed this IAM user in any activity other than that associated with this threat actor,” the trio wrote.

This activity continued on October 15, and on October 18, the digital intruders began using a second IAM user from the same account.

Once inside customers’ environments, the crooks began probing a ton of AWS services and stealing credentials, keys, and other secrets stored across Lambda, Secrets Manager, and SSM Parameter Store.

The miscreants also used TruffleHog to test AWS credentials belonging to victim organizations, discover their Microsoft Entra ID secrets, and request OAuth tokens using Okta client credentials also uncovered while snooping around the AWS environments.

Abusing the integration roles also allowed the criminals to steal data from customers’ S3 storage, although it seems they were largely opportunistic attackers, in some cases downloading entire buckets, as opposed to state-sponsored spies looking for specific data.

The threat hunters haven’t attributed the supply chain attack to any particular group, and say they don’t have any insight into how the miscreants are using the stolen data.

While investigating this incident, Wiz spotted a separate campaign between October 8 and October 11 that also used customer-owned AWS access keys for Qubole integrations. While a “small number” of these also resulted in the intruders compromising victim organizations’ AWS environments, Wiz said it can’t definitively connect the two sets of malicious activity.

Organizations that have integrated with Qubole should rotate credentials - although rotating a credential does not end temporary sessions that were already issued.

Customers should also review CloudTrail from October 1 onward, looking for AssumeRole events where userIdentity.accountId matches Qubole's AWS account ID, 805246085872, particularly those originating from non-AWS IP addresses.

“For every role session you find, review all subsequent activity from that session, especially Secrets Manager, SSM Parameter Store, Lambda and S3,” the researchers wrote. “If the threat actor assumed an integration role, rotate every secret, parameter and Lambda environment variable the role could read, and revoke active sessions for the role.”®

#9953. The race to secure record-like information for domains

It’s sort of surprising, but we’re still figuring out how to secure simple, record-like information for domain names in an application-accessible way.

Think about it. How would you bind the following to a domain name?

Since we’re talking about domain names, lets start with DNS. The classic solution adds configuration as TXT records:

Notice that we use an underscored subdomain label to make it clear we aren’t talking about a hostname. The protocol name is then repeated to make it abundantly clear this record is related to the protocol.

As is, we can’t claim this solution is secure. DNS-based network interference is trivial and widespread. The best practice for securing DNS records is DNSSEC, which uses cryptographic signing.

I’m not going to debate the security properties of DNSSEC in this post. There are strong opinions on both sides and the most helpful answer likely depends on the context in which you work. For the sake of this blog post I’ll wave my hands and call this “secure enough” to side-step the issue. In any case, the rest of the post doesn’t depend on a favorable or unfavorable assessment of the security properties of DNSSEC.

Even the strongest supporters of DNSSEC need to face the reality that DNSSEC isn’t widely adopted.

There’s no single answer that quantifies DNSSEC adoption. At Fox Loop Software I collect adoption metrics for various Internet protocols; we just released the first dashboard. Our approach highlights that adoption rates vary widely depending on which cohort you measure. For example, here are the adoption rates of DNSSEC signed MX records among second-level domain names that accept email:

From the perspective of an application developer, it is not reasonable to expect that a customer domain name will support DNSSEC. Until this changes, application developers must use alternate solutions if they need security.

If my application is web-based then there’s a pretty obvious solution as I already have an HTTPS secured endpoint. I can use the HTTPS .well-known approach (RFC 8615).

These records are secured by HTTPS. The developer experience is excellent: adding a record could be as easy as dropping a file in a web server directory. Fetching records is a simple HTTP GET request.

But not everything is a web-based application. Can we extend this solution to other protocols?

Email is a very old protocol, predating not only TLS but the entire Internet as well. Over time all sorts of additions have been bolted on to modernize and maintain the protocol. Many of these additions added new DNS TXT records, such as SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. These records can be secured by DNSSEC but do not require it, so tampering of these records is unmitigated or otherwise tolerated.

Let’s look past these examples to a problem that clearly requires a secure record.

Email has an awkward problem, which is how hostnames are managed. When a message transfer agent (MTA) relays an email it needs to discover the destination MTA. This is solved using an MX record, which specifies the target MTA’s domain name. I’ve measured that around 80% of domains host their email on a different domain name, often using providers like Google or Microsoft.

When sending an email, the MTA will discover a chain from the user’s email address to the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate, like this:

The sending MTA now needs to decide if it trusts the connection. Unfortunately, smtp.provider.com, as seen in the TLS certificate, does not match example.com, as provided in the email address. The only link between the two domain names is an MX record, which typically unsigned and therefor insecure. Without trustworthy information, certificate validation cannot succeed and the sending MTA must skip validation.

Lack of certificate validation means that receiving MTAs can use a self-signed, expired, or even a certificate with the wrong name; the sending MTA does not care. This approach is known as “opportunistic encryption” and it provides strong protection against passive eavesdropping. But without a way to validate the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate, active attacks remained unmitigated.

Email cannot enforce authenticated MTA-to-MTA transit encryption until this hostname mis-match problem is solved in a secure way.

Many email security conversations focus on end-to-end encryption. It is a great solution to many of the security problems facing email, but it doesn’t fully address the problem being discussed here.

Message relaying requires the MTA to know the recipient’s email address. This is known as “envelope information” and it cannot be end-to-end encrypted. Methods like PGP encryption can not and do not protect this information, as they only encrypt the message body.

The only way to protect this information from network-level attackers is to ensure the message is delivered to the correct MTA, which requires authenticated transit encryption.

When I first encountered this issue I was surprised as there is no analogous problem on the web. The issue relates to the semantic difference between a CNAME and an MX record. A CNAME record pointing at a web hosting provider’s server is a matter of identity and that server can get a TLS certificate to prove it. An MX record does not permit the target email server to get a corresponding TLS certificate.

A web browser is able to compare the name in the TLS certificate with the name shown in the address bar and can expect these to strictly match. An MTA doesn’t compare the name in the TLS certificate with the domain name in the “to” address as a mismatch is typically expected.

Further, email is sent asynchronously so there are no humans involved in MTA-to-MTA communications. While web browsers can show a certificate warning message to allow users to make their own security decisions, an MTA is all on its own. Email providers often tout support for transit encryption but the lack of certificate validation makes email traveling between MTAs about as secure as a user browsing the web while always clicking through invalid certificate warnings.

Interestingly, email has adopted two solutions to this problem: a DNSSEC-based approach and an HTTPS .well-known approach. This give us a unique opportunity to compare these approaches head-to-head as they attempt to solve the same problem.

The DNSSEC approach is SMTP DNS-based Authentication of Named Entities (DANE) (RFC 7672), which was standardized in 2015. DANE requires DNSSEC signing in both the customer and email provider’s DNS zones for the protection to have full effect.

DANE adds the TLSA DNS record. Here’s an example:

This record indicates that the MTA-to-MTA connection can use authenticated encryption. Specifically, this record indicates that the receiving MTA should provide a TLS certificate with a public key digest of “6111A…”. Validating this pinned certificate does not depend on the certificate authority (CA) system.

SMTP DANE signals that it should be possible to cryptographically validate the chain from the domain name in the email address to the domain name on the receiving MTA’s TLS certificate.

One key benefit of DNSSEC, which we’ll revisit, is that blocking of a signed record can be distinguished from a non-existent policy. When the TLSA record does not exist, the authoritative DNS server should provide a signed proof of non-existence (NSEC). This acts as a fail safe: if DNSSEC is enabled and the sender cannot determine the DANE policy, then the sender can conclude that it is not safe to send the message as network interference may be present.

Email providers realized that slow adoption of DNSSEC was delaying authenticated transit encryption between MTAs. They looked at what other tools were available and found inspiration from the HTTPS .well-known approach. Standardized in 2018, SMTP MTA Strict Transport Security (MTA-STS) (RFC 8461) provides an HTTPS-based solution.

Notice that the mta-sts subdomain is used instead of the bare domain. This best practice stems from the need to isolate security policies from whatever website lives at the bare domain; often a marketing website which may not have a security posture suitable for cross-protocol policies like MTA-STS. To distinguish any pre-existing use of the mta-sts subdomain the “_mta-sts” TXT record must also be set.

Finally, policy caching was added as a partial mitigation of intermittent network interference.

Like DANE, MTA-STS signals that the sender should strictly authenticate TLS. The MX record is duplicated in the MTA-STS policy, relying on HTTPS to secure the link. MTA-STS requires the receiving MTA to have a TLS certificate issued by a well-trusted CA.

An MTA-STS policy document is fairly unchanging, making it well-suited for inexpensive, widely available, and highly scalable static web hosting. Many domain owners implement MTA-STS by adding the subdomain to an existing web server, as a virtual host, although it turns out this isn’t always a good idea.

The TLS certificate renewal process is an obvious point of failure for MTA-STS. When a user-facing website goes down users complain, support tickets are filed, and the certificates are quickly renewed. The MTA-STS policy server fails open when it’s certificate expires. Senders will fall back to using opportunistic encryption and users won’t notice any disruption. As such an expired TLS certificate on an MTA-STS policy server can go unnoticed. To address this lack of visibility, TLS Reporting (RFC 8460) was created, which allows email servers to share deliverability reports with each other.

Another problem, which I think is an even larger issue, are web servers that block email servers from accessing their MTA-STS policy. You’ve probably noticed a sharp rise in bots, scrapers, and other unwanted automated traffic impacting the web. In the rush to protect web servers from these ills many sites inadvertently blocked access to their MTA-STS policy. An email server fetching an MTA-STS policy can look a lot like unwanted traffic: it’s automated and its coming from data center IP ranges. Misapplying security policies intended to protect user-facing websites from unwanted bot traffic degrades API-like interfaces.

One unique benefit of SMTP DANE is that the policy cannot be blocked without the sender noticing. An MTA-STS policy server can be blocked just like any other web server and this blocking cannot easily be distinguish from a non-existent policy.

While MTA-STS caching can protect against intermittent network-level blocking of the policy server, the first email sent to a domain is always vulnerable due to an empty cache. The effectiveness of MTA-STS in preventing an on-path attacker from intercepting email is questionable if the same on-path attacker can block the sender from discovering the MTA-STS policy.

By these measures, DANE seems like the stronger option.

DANE’s reliance on DNSSEC signing is its major weakness. Measurements show that 0.9-1.2% of domain names that receive email have DANE support, which doesn’t provide much practical protection yet. Worse, large providers like gmail.com lack DNSSEC support, so the per-user impact may be larger. Unless DNSSEC adoption can grow among large email providers, DANE can only be a partial solution. In contrast, HTTPS is very widely adopted making MTA-STS familiar to practitioners, even with these challenges.

The web has blazed a path that MTA-STS can likely follow. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) (RFC 6769) is essentially MTA-STS for the web (or visa-versa). HSTS is similarly vulnerable when the cache is empty. Web browsers mitigate this issue using a preload list, which ships in the browser. Out-of-the-box, the web browser knows that popular websites, like wikipedia.com, strictly use HTTPS. While there are challenges with HSTS, like the size of the list, this may have marginal impact for a server-side technology like email.

I think MTA-STS can copy this solution. There are unknowns, like who would build an MTA-STS preload list, why we trust them to do so, and the exact semantics needed for a domain to be added. In any case, I think we should wait on increased MTA-STS adoption before we take those next steps.

The adoption rates of MTA-STS and SMTP DANE tell an important story about how application protocols can secure domain information in practice. The fact that email has both a DNSSEC and an HTTPS approach gives us a way to spectate.

Current measurements show that MTA-STS has overtaken DANE among the top-ranked domain names.

Given the importance of protecting messages, including envelope information which cannot be end-to-end encrypted, these results are disappointing.

Prior work shows that TLS downgrade attacks on email are widespread. With the slow adoption of email security protocols since that study, the situation is unlikely to have improved. We can and should do better.

MTA-STS isn’t the only protocol that works this way.

OpenPGP Web Key Directory (WKD) (draft-koch-openpgp-webkey-service-22) uses an HTTPS .well-known approach to secure PGP key distribution, facilitating end-to-end encryption of message bodies.

The WKD “advanced method”, seen above, follows the best practice of using a protocol-specific subdomain.

The analogous DNSSEC-based approach is OPENPGPKEY (RFC 7929).

Other protocols like Mail AutoConfig (draft-ietf-mailmaint-autoconfig-07) simplify the process of setting up an email client and similar applications.

Again we see this protocol follow the security best practice of using a protocol-specific subdomain.

There are over 100 registered .well-known URIs, showing the popularity of this approach. Many of these tolerate lower security properties and use the bare domain name instead of a protocol-specific subdomain.

While I’ve thus far framed the discussion as a competition, DNSSEC and HTTPS .well-known are actually complementary. We don’t need one approach to defeat the other: we’ll see ecosystem improvements as both solutions are adopted, side-by-side. HTTPS .well-known can offload large policy documents and allow rapid experimentation, avoiding the size limits of UDP packets and the slow process of adding new DNS record types. DNSSEC can sign the CAA record, providing improved security during TLS certificate issuance.

DANE could even replace the CAs entirely, a topic of renewed interest after the recent eMudhra mishap. After all, we wouldn’t need the CAs if we had a secure DNS.

I see complementary nature of DNSSEC and HTTPS .well-known emphasized in another draft, Domain Authority (DA): A DNS-Designated Service Endpoint for Domain Information (draft-swaminathan-da-00), which seeks to standardize the use of HTTPS to add capabilities to domain names beyond what DNS can natively support. While I think the current draft is too ambitious in scope, it provides a great summary of the benefits an HTTPS-based policy retrieval layer can provide beyond DNS.

Unfortunately, we still have an insecure DNS. But progress in the domain name ecosystem is not blocked by DNS. MTA-STS shows that an HTTPS approach is immediately usable.

#9952. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#9950. France blames Iran for supermarket hack meltdowns

The 'first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory'

France has turned up the heat on Iran over destructive cyberattacks targeting refrigeration controllers at more than 700 grocery stores in October, spoiling food and sparking fires. The country vowed to take action using “all available means of response.”

The supermarket attacks, which affected Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour, and Intermarché groups, started at least 15 fires and caused food losses in the tens of millions of euros, according to a Monday report by France’s Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4).

The C4 includes the National Cybersecurity Agency of France, the Directorate General for External Security, the Directorate General for Internal Security, the Directorate General for Armament, and the Cyber Defence Command.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, thus constituting the first cyber offensive campaign carried out purely for the purpose of sabotage on national territory,” France’s Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

Both the report and the statement attributed the refrigeration controller hacks to the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ (IRGC) Shahid Kaveh cyber unit. The Shahid Kaveh unit, which French national security officials say is led by Reza Salarvand and Mahdi Lashgarian, is better known by its hacktivist personas, including CyberAv3ngers.

This is the same crew suspected of involvement in the July attacks that targeted more than 100 internet-exposed water systems in America. While the US government hasn’t attributed the intrusions to any country or group, private-sector security analysts blamed Iran, and specifically CyberAv3ngers.

The IRGC-affiliated hacking crew has been breaking into industrial controllers for years, and in 2023, American national security and law enforcement agencies attributed a series of cyberattacks against "multiple" US water facilities to CyberAv3ngers.

“The Iranian cyber threat against French interests is not new,” according to the Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs. “Iran has already carried out several destabilizing acts against us, notably targeting the weekly magazine Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and the organization of the Paris Olympic Games in 2024.”

Since at least June 2024, the Shahid Kaveh unit has had the ability to scan, access, and control industrial control equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens, and Rockwell, the French government said in its report. It pins the refrigeration controller hacks on this particular Iranian crew for a couple of reasons.

First: the infrastructure used to carry out the October supermarket attacks was also used during this timeframe to conduct reconnaissance on Schneider Electric equipment, zeroing in on small- and medium-sized energy and water production units. “The techniques used during these actions are known to have been used by the Shahid Kaveh unit since at least April 2026,” the report says.

It also notes that investigators found “traces of Farsi use” in the attack infrastructure. Plus, Iranian media outlet CyberbanNews, which is reportedly linked to the Shahid Kaveh unit, publicized the incidents that occurred late on October 11 and into October 12 extremely quickly: “as early as October 13.”

In early November, similar cyberattacks on commercial refrigerators and freezers were reported across Europe, with grocery stores in Belgium, Ireland, Luxembourg, and Sweden reporting widespread food losses after miscreants spiked temperatures to as high as 122°F (50°C).

Last week, the US federal government urged owners and operators to take security measures to prevent these types of attacks from spreading to America.

The French government, for its part, said that it would “use all available means of response, including within the European Union and alongside its European and international partners, to anticipate, prevent, deter and respond to destabilizing and destructive actions targeting it in cyberspace.”

This includes proposing additional EU sanctions against Iranian entities and individuals involved. France also vowed to express “its strongest condemnation of these cyberattacks” to the Iranian ambassador.

However, the country didn’t rule out responding with more than just harsh words: “France reserves the right to take any additional measures, public and non-public, deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to these cyberattacks.” ®

#9949. Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

So on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that shows up in the token bill.

Consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

Delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:

On the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

Where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:

Figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.)

Both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

The ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

DeepSeek-V3.2 — by difficulty (baseline → +memory): the two systems start from different no-memory baselines (79.8 vs 72.0 TGC overall) because of the prompt-template difference above.

#9947. Anthropic's super bug-finding Mythos model is going into Cisco and IBM products

Enterprise security tools will offer its capabilities without handing customers the model itself

Anthropic has started extending access to its bug-finding Mythos model by allowing Cisco and IBM to make it part of their security products.

Cisco announced its integration today at an event in Melbourne, Australia, where it revealed that the red teaming tools in its AI Defense suite, which looks for weaknesses and inappropriate activity in AI models, agents, and applications they power, will be able to call Mythos to test customers’ setups.

“At a very high level, AI Defense has the ability to look at models and break them,” said Jeff Schultz, Cisco’s senior vice president for portfolio strategy and marketing. He said the tool is now “super-charged by Mythos” and will identify more danger that AI Defense will then address.

AI Defense already uses AI-powered red teaming to find flaws. Mythos will become another option. Cisco will make it available under users’ existing licenses, without additional cost.

Natalie Mead, Anthropic’s head of applied AI for the Asia-Pacific, said the company has a long queue of buyers who want to use Mythos, and working with Cisco will make it easier to satisfy that demand.

Anthropic initially made Mythos available under "Project Glasswing," a program that gave vetted organizations access to the model to test their codebases, but has since expanded access through other controlled programs, an arrangement that makes considerable sense because in the wrong hands Mythos could help attackers exploit software flaws.

The Cisco deal exposes the functionality of Mythos to end-users, without letting them use the model itself.

The Register asked Mead if Anthropic has similar deals with other third parties and she demurred. That may be because a few hours after Cisco told us about its use of Mythos, IBM announced that it will also integrate Anthropic’s model into a product – namely its Concert tool, which uses AI to scan applications for risks and weaknesses.

IBM says it will use Mythos “to uncover weaknesses traditional scanners miss, determine which pose real risk and generate fixes for developer approval.”

We have asked Anthropic if these integrations represent a decision to open Mythos to more users in more ways. We will update this story if we receive a substantial response.

Also on Monday, Anthropic introduced version 5.2 of Mythos and Fable, which the company says generate outputs up to 30 percent faster than version 5.1 yet cost less: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Users can choose to run both models in “fast mode,” which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times, and doubles prices to $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Anthropic says it “ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes.”

After those tests, the company concluded “high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures.

“Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.”

The latter is a telling admission, given Anthropic believes Chinese AI labs use distillation to effectively clone its models without doing expensive training work. ®

#9946. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#9945. A C++ Quicksort Faster Than std::sort

blqsort is a very fast quicksort algorithm. I am not aware of any other general-purpose comparison-based sorting algorithm that is faster on random data. Only specialized SIMD-based algorithms are generally faster when dealing with small primitive data types.

The main ideas are branchless partitioning, sorting networks for small partitions and robust pivot selection.

The implementation is available on GitHub under the MIT license. There is also a C version of it, including multithreaded versions, each as a single header file.

The following benchmarks show the execution times for sorting 50 million random doubles using different sorting implementations. The measurements were taken on an Apple M1 system using Clang and on an Intel i5-9300H Linux system using GCC, both compiled with the -O3 option.

For a fair comparison, the single-threaded version of blqs was used here. On the M1, the multithreaded versions are roughly another factor of 3 faster. In terms of runtime, the C versions differ only very little from the C++ version.

Execution times for sorting 50 million of these structs with random id values.

struct entry { int id; int value; bool operator<(const entry& other) const { return id < other.id; } }; struct entry data[SIZE]; blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE);

Already sorted and reverse-sorted inputs are detected and handled efficiently. Inputs with many duplicate keys are optimized as well.

The execution times, unless otherwise specified, apply to an Apple M1 system.

#include #include #include constexpr int SIZE = 50000000; double data[SIZE]; double time() { static auto time0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); auto t = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); std::chrono::duration diff = t - time0; return diff.count(); } void sortq(double ar[], int len) { if (len < 2) return; double piv = ar[0]; int mid = 0; for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) { if (ar[i] < piv) { mid += 1; std::swap(ar[mid], ar[i]); } } std::swap(ar[mid], ar[0]); sortq(ar + mid + 1, len - mid - 1); sortq(ar, mid); } int main() { double t0; printf("Sorting %d million doubles\n", SIZE / 1000000); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = rand() / 1024.0; t0 = time(); sortq(data, SIZE); printf("sortq: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); } c++ -O1 main.cpp && ./a.out Sorting 50 million doubles sortq: 4.61s If you sort the sorted data again, all elements in the partition are greater than or equal to the pivot element. The second partition becomes only one element smaller each time, and the function is called recursively millions of times, which leads to a stack overflow after a few hours.

You can prevent this with tail call elimination. That is, the first recursive call remains, while the second is replaced by a loop iteration. You now need to ensure that the smaller partition is called recursively. So swap them if necessary.

void sortq(double* ar, int len) { while (len >= 2) { double piv = ar[0]; int mid = 0; for (int i = 1; i < len; i++) { if (ar[i] < piv) { mid += 1; std::swap(ar[mid], ar[i]); } } std::swap(ar[mid], ar[0]); double* ar2 = ar + mid + 1; int len2 = len - mid - 1; len = mid; if (len2 > len) { std::swap(len, len2); std::swap(ar, ar2); } sortq(ar2, len2); } } Now the program no longer crashes, but it will take a few days to finish. Because of this unfavorable partitioning, the worst-case scenario of O(N²) has become a reality. However, insertion sort would not make it any faster either.

Let’s just use the middle element as the pivot - then the problem of sorting already sorted data will be gone.

. while (len >= 2) { std::swap(ar[len / 2], ar[0]); double piv = ar[0]; . The only remaining risk is that someone intentionally sends specially crafted data to trigger this behavior. To eliminate this threat, the pivot point should be selected randomly.

This implementation is sufficient for many purposes and is also reasonably fast. By the way, “Lomuto” partitioning is used here. “Hoare” partitioning performs fewer comparisons and swaps, but on modern CPUs its cache behavior can be less favorable.

But why write your own implementation when std::sort exists?

. #include . . t0 = time(); std::sort(data, data + SIZE); printf("std::sort: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); . std::sort: 1.31s That’s on ARM Mac - on a x86 system, std::sort is only about 10% faster.

How can you make a quicksort run faster than std::sort?

For partitions with up to about 20 elements, insertion sort is faster than quicksort. But there is something even faster for small partitions: sorting networks. Each partition size is handled in its own program branch. For a partition size of two, the two elements are simply compared and swapped if necessary. However, as the number of elements increases, the logic becomes increasingly complex.

inline void sort2(double& a, double& b) { if (a < b) std::swap(a, b); } inline void sort3(double& a, double& b, double& c) { sort2(a, b); sort2(b, c); sort2(a, b); } inline void sort4(double& a, double& b, double& c, double& d) { sort2(a, b); sort2(c, d); sort2(a, c); sort2(b, d); sort2(b, c); } inline void sort5(double& a, double& b, double& c, double& d, double& e) { sort2(b, c); sort2(d, e); sort2(b, d); sort2(a, c); sort2(a, d); sort2(c, e); sort2(a, b); sort2(c, d); sort2(b, c); } . while (len >= 6) { . . } if (len == 5) sort5(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2], ar[3], ar[4]); else if (len == 4) sort4(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2], ar[3]); else if (len == 3) sort3(ar[0], ar[1], ar[2]); else if (len == 2) sort2(ar[0], ar[1]); }

Let’s consider a simple task: Iterate through an array and copy all numbers less than 500 into a new array. A straightforward implementation in C looks like this:

smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { if (numbers[i] < 500) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += 1; } } If the numbers are randomly distributed, the result of the if condition becomes unpredictable for the branch predictor. This results in a high misprediction rate, which severely impacts performance because the processor must constantly flush its pipeline and restart execution.

We can avoid this problem by using a branchless approach:

smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += (numbers[i] < 500); } Although this version introduces an unconditional write operation (writing to memory even if the condition is not met), the associated overhead is generally much lower than the performance loss resulting from a branch misprediction.

Branchless does not mean that there are no jumps at all. The term refers only to the comparison, which is difficult to predict. Obviously, the loop jump remains, but that is not a problem because it is easily predictable - it is skipped only once.

To get meaningful results, we run both routines for 1000 iterations using 100,000 random numbers.

#include #include #include #define SIZE 100000 int numbers[SIZE]; int small_numbers[SIZE]; int smlen; double ts(void) { static double t0; struct timeval tv; gettimeofday(&tv, NULL); double h = t0; t0 = tv.tv_sec + tv.tv_usec / 1000000.0; return t0 - h; } void init(void) { srand(1); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) numbers[i] = rand() % 1000; ts(); } void small_if(void) { smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) { if (numbers[i] < 500) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += 1; } } } void small_bl(void) { smlen = 0; for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) { small_numbers[smlen] = numbers[i]; smlen += (numbers[i] < 500); } } int main(void) { init(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) small_if(); printf("Time if: %.3f\n", ts()); init(); for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) small_bl(); printf("Time bl: %.3f\n", ts()); } Benchmark results were obtained on an Apple M1 with -O1 optimization. On this benchmark, -O3 did not yield additional speedup, only larger generated code.

Time if: 0.345 Time bl: 0.036 Assembly Analysis

Using objdump -d, we can see the difference in how the CPU processes these loops.

With the if version, the compiler generates a conditional branch b.gt.

ldr w13, [x10], #0x4 ; load numbers[i] cmp w13, #0x1f3 ; compare with 499 (0x1f3) b.gt 0x100000678 ; branch if greater (The bottleneck) str w13, [x12, w8, sxtw #2] ; store value in small_numbers[j] add w8, w8, #0x1 ; j += 1 With the branchless version the compiler uses the cinc (conditional increment) instruction.

ldr w13, [x10], #0x4 ; load numbers[i] str w13, [x12, w8, uxtw #2] ; unconditional store to small_numbers[j] cmp w13, #0x1f4 ; compare with 500 cinc w8, w8, lt ; conditional increment (No branch) In this version, there is no jump based on the data. The control flow is perfectly linear, allowing the CPU to use its full pipeline width.

Why doesn’t the compiler optimize the if case automatically?

The compiler doesn’t know the nature of your data. If only a small fraction of numbers were less than 500, the branch version might actually be faster because the predictor would almost always be right.

The branchless version performs a write operation (str) every single time. The compiler cannot safely assume that it is permitted to write to memory if a write operation in the original source code was intended to occur only under a specific condition - for example, to avoid writing past the end of an allocated buffer.

Since quicksort essentially works by dividing the data into large and small numbers, it should be possible to speed it up using this technique.

So, as described above, we can make the partitioning step branchless. (comp is the comparison function):

int h = comp(*left, piv); *lwr = *rwr = *left++; lwr += h; rwr -= !h; We can also make sort2 - the basic operation for the sorting network - branchless:

inline static void sort2(double& a, double& b) { double x = a; double y = b; bool m = x < y; a = m ? x : y; b = m ? y : x; } Here’s how it works (in short) :

First, about 250 elements are copied from one page into an auxiliary buffer to make room for subsequent operations. We then alternately copy a block to the left and to the right, without using any branches.

The pivot element is also carefully selected. Several medians are determined from various elements of the partition, and the final median is then calculated from these medians. This results in a much more even distribution of the data. Some randomness is added to the pivot selection process to prevent inputs from consistently triggering worst-case behavior.

If the distribution is still very uneven, however, the algorithm switches to heap sort for these partitions as a precaution. Uneven distribution often occurs when there are many identical elements; in this case, they are identified and grouped together.

In addition, the code includes the sorting networks, which are used for partition sizes up to 16.

And with a for (int i = 16; i--;) { ... } loop, the compiler unrolls the loop, generating 16 copies of the loop body.

This version consists of a single C++ header file that can be easily included. It can sort any data type, and the comparison function can be supplied by the user, just like with std::sort.

#ifndef BLQS_H #define BLQS_H #include #include #include #include #include #ifndef BLQS_RAND #define BLQS_RAND #include static thread_local uint64_t blqs_seed; static inline unsigned blqs_rand(void) { if (!blqs_seed) { std::random_device rd; blqs_seed = ((uintptr_t)&blqs_seed) ^ (((uint64_t)rd() << 32) | (uint64_t)rd()); if (!blqs_seed) blqs_seed = 1; } uint64_t x = blqs_seed; x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17; blqs_seed = x; return (unsigned)x; } #endif namespace blqs { constexpr int SMALLPART = 1024; constexpr int SWSZ = 512; constexpr int UNROLL = 16; template static inline void sort2(T& a, T& b, Compare comp) { T x = a; T y = b; bool m = comp(x, y); a = m ? x : y; b = m ? y : x; } template static inline void sort3(T& a, T& b, T& c, Compare comp) { sort2(a, b, comp); sort2(b, c, comp); sort2(a, b, comp); } template static inline void sort4(T& a, T& b, T& c, T& d, Compare comp) { sort2(a, b, comp); sort2(c, d, comp); sort2(a, c, comp); sort2(b, d, comp); sort2(b, c, comp); } template static inline void sort5(T& a, T& b, T& c, T& d, T& e, Compare comp) { sort2(b, c, comp); sort2(d, e, comp); sort2(b, d, comp); sort2(a, c, comp); sort2(a, d, comp); sort2(c, e, comp); sort2(a, b, comp); sort2(c, d, comp); sort2(b, c, comp); } template static inline void sort6(T& a, T& b, T& c, T& d, T& e, T& f, Compare comp) { sort2(a, b, comp); sort2(c, d, comp); sort2(e, f, comp); sort2(a, c, comp); sort2(b, d, comp); sort2(e, f, comp); sort2(a, e, comp); sort2(b, f, comp); sort2(c, e, comp); sort2(d, f, comp); sort2(b, c, comp); sort2(d, e, comp); #include #include #include #include "blqs.h" constexpr int SIZE = 50000000; double data[SIZE]; double time() { static auto time0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); auto t = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now(); std::chrono::duration diff = t - time0; return diff.count(); } int main() { double t0; printf("Sorting %d million doubles\n", SIZE / 1000000); for (int i = 0; i < SIZE; i++) data[i] = rand() / 1024.0; t0 = time(); blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE); printf("blqs::sort: %.2fs\n", time() - t0); } c++ -O3 test.cpp && ./a.out Sorting 50 million doubles blqs::sort: 0.95s std::sort took 1.33. And on x86 systems, it’s now three times as fast as std::sort

Interestingly, this idiomatic C notation is compiled into very efficient, branchless code on ARM-based Macs using the csel command: if (comp(x, piv)) *lwr++ = x; else *rwr-- = x; Surprisingly, this doesn’t work with the more explicit version:

if (comp(x, piv)) { *lwr = x; lwr++; } else { *rwr = x; rwr--; } One would actually expect that the compiler would treat these two variants as equivalent. Many people don’t trust AI to generate good code. Perhaps we shouldn’t blindly trust the compiler either.

This code is generated (on ARM Macs) - but only in the compact if version:

; x9 = current element pointer ; x0 = left destination (grows forwards) ; x20 = right destination (grows backwards); d8 = pivot ; x8 = 8 (positive increment) ; x10 = -8 (negative increment) loop: ldr d0, [x9], #8 fcmp d0, d8 ; compare value against pivot csel x11, x0, x20, mi ; target is left (x0) or right (x20) str d0, [x11] ; store value to the selected destination csel x12, x8, xzr, mi ; left_step is 8 or 0 csel x13, xzr, x10, mi ; right_step is 0 or -8 add x0, x0, x12 ; left += left_step add x20, x20, x13 ; right += right_step b.ls loop So, branchless without that double store.

On x86, it works similarly with Clang. But not with GCC, and not with the longer if version either. It is also slower than the explicit, branchless version.

blqs_seed = ((uintptr_t)&blqs_seed) ^ (((uint64_t)rd() << 32) | (uint64_t)rd()); if (!blqs_seed) blqs_seed = 1; } uint64_t x = blqs_seed; x ^= x << 13; x ^= x >> 7; x ^= x << 17; blqs_seed = x; return (unsigned)x; Sorting 50 million doubles blqs::sort: 0.67s

You only need to include blqs.h, and it can be used just as easily as std::sort.

For the C++ multithreaded variant, which uses C++ threads, include blqs_thr.h instead of blqs.h. The function call remains the same.

In practice, we often need to sort custom data structures. This is where SIMD libraries like Google Highway - while very fast for simple numbers - become difficult to use.

Using std::sort or blqsort gives you much more flexibility.

#include "blqs.h" struct entry { int id; int value; bool operator<(const entry& other) const { return id < other.id; } }; struct entry data[SIZE]; blqs::sort(data, data + SIZE); Depending on the compiler and platform, either the if version or the explicit branchless version is used.

For types with higher copy costs that are not is_trivially_copyable (such as strings), the buffer-based branchless approach becomes less efficient. In such cases, a BlockQuicksort (Edelkamp and Weiß) variant is used instead. This processes only the element indices in a branchless manner. This requires C++17 or later.

c++ -O3 -std=c++17 test_double.cpp && ./a.out
