#9926. How Much Memory Does Your Agent Actually Need?

In our previous post, we compared ALTK-Evolve with ACE and showed that how you deliver an agent's self-distilled guidelines — a few retrieved per task vs. the whole set injected — drives both accuracy and cost. This post steps back to the question that comes before it: how much should you give it?

Equipping an agent with agentic memory sounds simple: distill lessons from its past work, put them back in context, and more experience should mean better performance. It doesn't always work that way. When we scaled the evaluation to eight models — from a 30B dense model to frontier proprietary systems — one finding stood out:

Agentic memory is not a feature you switch on. It's a dose you calibrate to the model.

ALTK-Evolve lets an agent learn from its own past trajectories: distilling reusable guidelines and injecting them back at inference time, with no weight updates and no human annotation.

The right dose differs by model tier: strong models with headroom want the full guideline set, weaker models do best with a compact core plus per-task retrieval, and saturated models show no measurable gain.

Curated retrieval can be both the most accurate and the cheapest option: gpt-oss-120b gained +16.1pp task completion at only +5% tokens — and prompt caching keeps even the full guideline set affordable in production.

Not every model benefits from the same amount of memory. Across eight models spanning the capability spectrum, we saw three recurring patterns:

Strong models with headroom want the full guideline set — every guideline, including rare edge-case lessons. They have the capacity to absorb and apply all of it. DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B MoE) climbed +9.5 percentage points in task completion when given its full self-mined guideline set.

Smaller or weaker models get drowned by a large guideline set. For these, a tight, high-confidence core plus a handful of task-relevant guidelines retrieved per task works best. gpt-oss-120b (117B MoE) gained +16.1pp with this selective approach — while the full guideline set gained less and cost ~50% more tokens.

Already-saturated models show no measurable gain. We call this the saturated pattern — the label describes what we observed, not a proven cause. The model may already have been near its ceiling on these tasks, the guidelines may not have addressed its remaining failures, or it may not have applied the guidance effectively. GLM-5 (745B MoE) sat here in our runs.

What puts a model into one pattern rather than another isn't simply parameter count. Benchmark headroom, context-window size, architecture, guideline quality, and task distribution all appear to shape where a model lands, and separating those factors is ongoing work. The practical takeaway holds either way: the right dose of memory depends on the model, and we can calibrate it.

"Memory" here doesn't mean replaying a past transcript. It means a guideline set — strategies that worked, mistakes to avoid, and edge cases — distilled from the agent's own prior trajectories. The loop is straightforward:

The agent attempts tasks and produces trajectories.

ALTK-Evolve extracts behavioral guidelines from both its successful and unsuccessful runs.

It consolidates those guidelines into a reusable set.

At inference time, the agent receives either the full guideline set or a task-relevant selection of it.

No model weights are updated. The learning loop changes the guidance available to the agent, not the underlying model — which is exactly why it's cheap to adopt and portable across the eight models we tested.

We evaluated on AppWorld — 585 multi-step tasks (168 test_normal + 417 test_challenge) across 9 simulated apps (calendars, messaging, payments, and so on). Tasks are scored two ways: whether the agent fully completes each task (TGC — Task Goal Completion) and whether every variant of a scenario passes (SGC — Scenario Goal Completion, a stricter, all-or-nothing bar). Full definitions are in the appendix.

Because the confusing part of any memory study is what's actually in the context window, we define the configurations up front.

Both memory configurations draw from the same guideline set, mined once (via the loop above) from AppWorld's training split only. What changes between them is only how that one set is delivered — the full guideline set injects all of it every step, while curated retrieval delivers a selected subset — never how the guidelines were produced, and no test-split data ever goes into building it.

The number of guidelines a model mines depends on its own capability, so we report configurations by strategy — "full guideline set" vs. "curated retrieval" — rather than by raw counts, which aren't comparable across models.

Representative models from the eight-model sweep, measured by task completion (TGC) on test_normal:

Figure 1. Representative models in the three observed patterns. Bars show TGC on AppWorld test_normal for baseline vs. the best-memory configuration; the x-axis begins at 40% to make differences visible. TGC alone understates the larger SGC gains — see the SGC columns in the table below.

The figure plots TGC to keep it readable; the table adds the stricter SGC metric, where the gains are often larger:

Reading the SGC column, the stricter metric usually moves more than TGC — DeepSeek's SGC jumps +16.1pp against a +9.5pp TGC gain — because good guidelines especially help an agent clear every variant of a scenario, not just the average case. And the effect doesn't disappear at the top of the range: GPT-5.5 and Opus, both near the ceiling on TGC, still gain +7.2 and +7.1pp SGC respectively. Memory keeps paying off as long as a model has a remaining failure mode to target.

A practical concern: injecting a full guideline set inflates every ReAct step's input, because the guidelines are re-sent each turn. Here's what we observed:

Table 1. Average token use per task, accumulated across agent steps, measured against the no-memory baseline.

Curated retrieval keeps cost near baseline. For weaker models, where selection wins on accuracy, it also wins on cost — the best of both worlds (+16.1pp TGC at only +5% tokens for gpt-oss-120b). Better performance here does not require more inference cost.

Memory doesn't blow up the reasoning loop. DeepSeek runs about the same number of ReAct steps with memory as without (≈18–19 on average), so the added cost is input-token inflation, not longer trajectories.

The real efficiency lever in production is prompt caching: the static portion of the guideline set is identical across steps and can be cached, cutting effective cost substantially. Cache-aware prompt design — keeping the shared guideline-set prefix stable so it stays cacheable — is worth engineering for. We also hypothesize that context-window size plays a role: models with larger windows may absorb the full guideline set more effectively, while smaller-context models benefit more from retrieval that keeps injected content compact. We have not yet run controlled experiments isolating this factor.

The lesson isn't to give an agent everything it has learned. It's to give it the amount of experience it can actually use.

For weak models, that means a compact core plus a few task-specific lessons — which, conveniently, is also the cheapest option.

For strong models with headroom, it means preserving the full guideline set, kept affordable in production via prompt caching.

For saturated models, it means spending no extra context until their remaining failure modes are better understood.

The gains are real across the board — automatic, leakage-free, and requiring no human annotation — but only when the dose fits the model.

This is a starting point, not the finish line:

A learned selector. Our current retrieval ranks guidelines by cosine similarity, which we've shown doesn't perfectly predict which guidelines help a given task. A selector trained on outcome signal is the natural next step.

Memory for very weak models. Below a minimum capability baseline, self-distillation lacks signal. Teacher-distilled memory for very weak models is a separate problem we're exploring.

Beyond AppWorld. These results are validated on AppWorld — a rigorous multi-step benchmark, but a single one. Broader agent benchmarks and real-world deployments are in progress.

Isolating context window. As above, we want controlled experiments that separate context-window size from raw capability.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

AppWorld tasks are graded by two metrics, both reported as percentages (higher is better):

TGC — Task Goal Completion. The share of individual tasks the agent completes fully and correctly. This is the headline "did it get the job done" number.

SGC — Scenario Goal Completion. A stricter, all-or-nothing metric. Each scenario bundles several variants of the same task (the same request with different data, phrasing, or edge conditions). SGC counts a scenario as passing only if the agent succeeds on every variant. It measures reliability — an agent that solves a task most of the time but fails on one variant scores on TGC but not on SGC.

Really interesting take on agentic memory. The idea that memory needs to be calibrated to the model rather than simply accumulated is especially useful for production systems. Selective retrieval also seems like a practical way to improve reliability without unnecessarily increasing context and inference costs. It makes a strong case for thoughtful custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions, where memory, performance, and cost all need to be designed together. https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

#9925. Google DeepMind melds humans and AI agents to vet Signal's secure messaging techniques

Post-quantum handshake and Triple Ratchet get a formal security check

Google DeepMind researchers have completed a formal verification of Signal's messaging security, marking what they claim is the first time AI has helped devise a proof that links protocol-level security guarantees to a widely used cryptographic implementation.

They did so using AlphaProof Code, a multi-agent framework for formal software specification and verification. AlphaProof Code relies on a human-guided agent that writes a Lean specification, assesses machine code semantics, and crafts an agent-authored proof that the Lean kernel checks against the specification.

In this instance, AlphaProof Code verified Signal’s post-quantum PQXDH handshake and Triple Ratchet, thereby validating the design of libsignal's forward secrecy, authentication, post-compromise security, and handshake secrecy.

In so doing, the Google/DeepMind team – Swarat Chaudhuri, Andrew Ferraiuolo, Anton Kovsharov, Tej Chajed, Sam Schlesinger, Karn Seth, Jonathan Katz, Charles Sutton, and Pushmeet Kohli – has taken a step toward a challenge the Beneficial AI Foundation issued in April to formally verify the Signal protocol and Signal app with Lean.

The AlphaProof Code process involves working with various models to turn Signal's security goals into a human-reviewed mathematical specification. Based on this spec, the researchers assigned Gemini Carbon agents to generate Lean code proving the correctness of the libsignal implementation. After the agents generated 6.5 million lines of Lean code, they undertook an auditing pass and flagged bits that required human review.

The result is theoretical in that it assumes perfect cryptography and doesn't guarantee the computational secrecy of bytes. But it's still a meaningful assertion of correctness.

"It's a system that is fundamentally built for human AI collaboration," said Swarat Chaudhuri, research scientist at Google DeepMind and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin, in an interview with The Register.

Traditionally, said Chaudhuri, you start proving theorems with well-defined problems formulated by a mathematician that get submitted to an AI agent for proof. In this case, the researchers had to figure out what to prove.

"In formal methods, we always had this belief that verification is the hard bit," he said. "There's thirty or forty years of work on how to scale up verification. Now we are able to do that. So now the question is what are we verifying? … That process is fundamentally human-in-the-loop, but we devised a process of trying to scale it up to the extent possible with AI."

As Chaudhuri and his colleagues note in their research paper, "AlphaProof Code: Verifying Signal’s Security at the Machine-Code Level," formal verification used to require heroic efforts. Formally verifying the seL4 microkernel took 20 person-years, while developing the verified CompCert C compiler took six years.

AlphaProof Code, they believe, can drastically reduce the cost of formal verification, though their Signal work still took four weeks for a team of five people and "quite a few tokens."

"The dream is definitely to scale this up," said Chaudhuri. "So you know there's been this rise in offensive AI capabilities, right? There are a lot of insecure systems around the world, and they're going to be exploited.

"So what we really need to do is to apply this kind of technology to code at large all over the world and figure out what is it that you want to guard against? How do you write those properties, how do we specify those properties? That's going to be super important, but we have to figure that out."

Pointing to a related DeepMind project, AlphaProof Nexus, which is focused on mathematics, Chaudhuri said the next step is to apply this technology during the software design process – not just to cryptographic protocols but code in general.

"We really believe that the next frontier is not going to be proof but specification in this kind of research," he said. "And so that's why we took on this domain where that was actually a hard problem. And I think that we have some really good insights now about how to go about this, although not the last word by any means." ®

#9924. Up to 3.2x Faster Inference with LFM2.5-DSpark

Today, we release DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models from our LFM2.5 family: LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, LFM2.5-2.6B, and LFM2.5-8B-A1B. These add a speculative decoding path that trades a minimal memory increase for a large decoding speedup without changing output quality:

The decode phase in LLM inference is traditionally memory-bound. Most latency comes from streaming weights from DRAM into SRAM, not from intense computation. Speculative decoding addresses this by using a lightweight draft model to produce candidate tokens, then having the target model verify them all in a single forward pass, sharing the cost of loading the weights across all tokens we verify.

Over the years, multiple approaches of speculation have been proposed, with the most prominent being EAGLE-3, DFlash, and, most recently, DSpark, which combines three components:

We follow the DSpark recipe with a larger and more diverse data mix covering SFT, chat, code, and function-calling data. Based on our ablations, the first versions of the draft models are simplified attention-only draft models, with 5 layers and a block of 9. For each draft model, we ran 15 epochs on the entire dataset and selected the epoch with the highest acceptance rate rather than the lowest loss.

The resulting draft models are relatively small, with each around ~300M parameters.

Under greedy decoding, a draft token is only accepted if it matches the target model’s distribution. On rejection, the target model's own token takes its place. The emitted sequence is therefore identical to baseline greedy by construction, so benchmark accuracy (pass@1 or exact match) is unchanged.

Our DSpark draft models for LFM2.5 ship with day-one support for llama.cpp (implementation builds on top of the official codebase, which we run with experimental metal kernels) and **SGLang (**implementation builds on the official SGLang implementation of DSpark).

We measure on-device throughput with llama.cpp and Metal on an M4 Max MacBook Pro using FP16 GGUF weights and up to 256 output tokens. We measure GPU throughput with SGLang on a single H100 80 GB in BF16. Both configurations use a DSpark block size of 9, a batch size of 1, and a temperature of 0. We evaluate them on five benchmark datasets.

All three drafter models deliver noticeable throughput improvements on both the large-scale accelerator (H100) and the edge deployment (M4 Max MacBook).

For LFM2.5-2.6B, speedup on the MacBook is especially noticeable, as it pushes the interactivity level a user can enjoy far beyond the throughput offered by most proprietary cloud models (around ~140 tok/s, depending on the dataset).

Across various multi-tool scenarios, DSpark reduces the latency by 57% on average for LFM2.5-2.6B.

For LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct, we see much more variance in dataset acceptance rates, so speedup varies by as much as 52% depending on the underlying text distribution.

For LFM2.5-8B-A1B, the acceptance rate increases compared to two dense models, yet on-device we get only an 18% improvement on average. This gap is due to the current MoE implementation in llama.cpp's Metal backend, and to the fact that verifying k tokens activates more experts and thus more weight traffic than a single decode step.

Running the DSpark draft models with SGLang requires an SGLang build with DSpark support for LFM2 targets (PR #31041). Launch the target with the draft attached:

Then query the OpenAI-compatible endpoint at http://localhost:30000/v1. The block size is read from the draft's config.json; the baseline is the same command without the three --speculative-* flags.

Running them with llama.cpp requires the respective llama.cpp build (PR#27383).

The block size is read from the sidecar metadata (n-max is clamped to it). Speculative decoding is exact: the target verifies every proposed token, so greedy output equals the target alone; per-response timings report draft_n / draft_n_accepted.

The DSpark draft model checkpoints are available on Hugging Face as Safetensors and in GGUF format:

For citations, please use the following reference or BibTeX:

Liquid AI, "LFM2.5-DSpark: Up to 3.2x Faster Inference from H100 to MacBook", Liquid AI Blog, Aug 2026.

#9922. Smart meters to cost the UK billions: 2G switch-off means replacing 12-13 million

Sunset of legacy cellphone tech means forced upgrade for many millions of smart energy meter users

Between 12 and 13 million UK smart meters could stop working properly when  2G and 3G networks are switched off by 2033, and replacing them all is likely to cost around £4 billion ($5.3 billion).

Smart meters have long been a controversial topic thanks to the British government's botched rollout of the technology; they were supposed to be fitted into 80 percent of households by 2020.

But numerous delays and technical hitches, such as consumers finding their meter stopped being smart if they switched energy supplier, hindered progress.

Now, a report from connectivity biz Wirepas, "The European Connectivity Trilemma," shows that it isn't just Brits who have problems, but that other European countries also have their share of smart meter issues and that no two countries have adopted the same approach.

The UK's issues center on the fact that early meters used 2G or 3G cellular connections to transmit energy usage back to the supplier. These continued to be fitted until 4G versions began arriving at the end of 2024, the report says.

This issue was covered by The Register back in 2023, and again in 2024.

However, the government had already announced measures to phase out 2G and 3G networks by 2033 several years earlier, back in 2021, so it was known that any meters being fitted would have a limited lifespan.

In fact, 3G services have now already been withdrawn by the networks, and they all plan to phase out 2G ahead of the 2033 deadline. BT/EE will begin closing its network from May 2029, VMO2 will start the same summer, and Vodafone aims to switch off in spring 2030.

The report claims the UK now faces two substantial areas of expenditure as a result. The first covers newer, second generation (SMETS2) meters, where only the communications module needs swapping out, but even this is likely to cost £1.3 to £1.4 billion (c $1.7 to $1.9 billion) before the hardware cost of each new hub is even factored in.

The other is for an estimated 7 million older, first-generation (SMETS1) meter installations, which have the cellular comms hard-wired in, so the whole meter typically needs replacing. The report authors estimate this will cost another £2.1 billion to £2.45 billion ($2.8 billion to $3.3 billion), at an indicative replacement cost of £300 to £350 per installation.

This results in the estimated £4 billion in gross replacement costs, which will ultimately feed into household energy bills, adding to the very costs the government is currently trying to reduce.

We asked the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), which oversees smart meters, for comment.

While some of these older meters would naturally have been due for replacement as part of normal asset renewal cycles, the cell network shutdown makes the replacement program unavoidable and dictates when much of the expenditure must occur.

According to the report, the SMETS2 replacement largely applies to central and southern Britain, as second-gen meters in the north use a long-range radio network and are not subject to the 2G/3G cut-off. However, the issue of older SMETS1 meters applies nationwide.

Wirepas' interest in all of this is that it specializes in IoT connectivity and is pushing NR+ as a solution to the issue. Based on the DECT-2020 New Radio standard developed by the European Telecommunication Standards Institute (ETSI), this is designed to be scalable and operates in the license-exempt and globally available 1.9GHz part of the spectrum.

When 4G technology reaches the end of its life, (which isn't likely to happen until the 2040s, and there is no planned date) the UK's smart meters will need to be replaced once again, the report asserts. However, this is sufficiently far in the future that it is unlikely to trouble policymakers anytime soon. ®

#9921. SecurityDataPipeline.com Launches as a New Educational Resource for the AI Era

The ungated resource explains how security data pipelines reduce SIEM ingestion costs, preserve detection coverage, and prepare the data layer for AI-driven security operations.

BOSTON, Nov. 5, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Realm Security today launched SecurityDataPipeline.com, a new educational resource designed to help cybersecurity professionals understand security data pipelines and reduce SIEM costs without weakening detection coverage.

For many security teams, rising data volumes present a difficult choice between cutting data and keeping detections. Security data pipelines offer a way to address this challenge. Because they sit between security data sources and destinations, these platforms collect, process, filter, and route telemetry before it reaches a SIEM, data lake, or other security tool.

"Most security teams are being asked to cut SIEM spend and roll out AI agents at the same time, and both of those decisions come down to the data layer," said Chris O'Brien, VP of Marketing at Realm Security. "We built SecurityDataPipeline.com so practitioners can understand how pipelines work and how to reduce volume without losing detections, before they ever talk to a vendor, including us."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Security data pipelines are becoming essential infrastructure as AI reshapes the SOC. As enterprises deploy AI agents for triage, investigation, and response, the data layer underneath those agents determines whether those agents get clean, normalized context to reason over. SecurityDataPipeline.com is a resource for security leaders trying to understand how to turn raw logs and fragmented cybersecurity data into clean, actionable intelligence for AI SOC agents and other AI cybersecurity initiatives.

The resource also covers how security data pipelines route telemetry to destinations including Splunk, Microsoft Sentinel, and Databricks Delta Lake; how OCSF-normalized data supports AI SOC agents; and how MITRE ATT&CK coverage can be preserved as teams reduce SIEM ingestion volumes.

On SecurityDataPipeline.com, visitors can:

Explore a beginner's guide explaining security data pipelines and their core functions.

Try an ungated interactive pipeline demonstration showing how security events are filtered, transformed, enriched, and routed.

Use a SIEM cost calculator estimating potential reductions in data ingestion costs.

Learn about practical use cases covering SIEM cost reduction, SIEM migration, SOC efficiency, data governance, and AI readiness.

Read technology comparisons explaining the differences between security data pipelines, SIEMs, data lakes, log forwarders, and observability pipelines.

The resource addresses how to reduce the cost of managing security data without weakening detection capabilities by looking at the role of data filtering, normalization, enrichment, routing, and retention. It also shows how teams can identify which information their security detections need and which data can be stored more economically.

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

The website is intended for CISOs, security architects, SOC managers, and cybersecurity professionals evaluating ways to manage growing telemetry volumes.

SecurityDataPipeline.com is available at https://securitydatapipeline.com/.

Realm Security gives security teams independent control over their telemetry before it reaches the SIEM, data lake, or AI agent. The platform understands what each source produces and what each downstream system needs, then guides teams on what to keep, archive, and route. Headquartered in Boston, Realm deploys in about a week and typically cuts SIEM ingestion costs by 50% or more. Learn more at www.realm.security.

#9920. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9919. Ransomware threat blares from Vanderbilt University computers during cyberattack

BYOD claims extensive data theft as campus Wi-Fi returns, most systems remain restricted, and classes carry on

Classes at Vanderbilt University are proceeding as scheduled today, although access to most university systems remains restricted following a cyberattack claimed by ransomware group BYOD.

Vanderbilt announced on Monday morning that it was dealing with "an active cybersecurity incident," and that the fallout may affect university devices, systems, and cloud-based services.

The Nashville-based university initially told students and staff to shut down university devices and disconnect from campus Wi-Fi. It warned them to watch for unexpected prompts, altered files or permissions, unfamiliar applications, and unsolicited authentication requests.

Campus computers reportedly began playing an audio threat attributed to BYOD. Student newspaper The Vanderbilt Hustler cited posts on campus social network Fizz showing the message.

"You have been compromised by BYOD," the recording said. "We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one."

By Monday evening, Vanderbilt had restored access to campus Wi-Fi, but warned that access to most systems remains restricted.

"We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university," it said. "Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation."

Students were told to attend classes as scheduled on Tuesday and contact instructors about flexibility on coursework deadlines. Staff were instructed to report to work normally.

Vanderbilt's Athletics department said that its ticketing system was unavailable, and that students were unable to claim tickets for the college's football game against Alabama on Saturday.

BYOD claimed responsibility for the attack on Vanderbilt on Monday, along with extensive data theft.

"If you could not tell already, your databases are locked [and] we have your entire estate and research data," it said via its leak site.

"Over 1 million SSNs, full names, email addresses, phone numbers, student and employee records, full takeover of your DC, whatever was on your network, we possess."

Vanderbilt has not confirmed BYOD's claims about the extent of its access or the data allegedly stolen.

BYOD may be a familiar name to some. The group previously claimed attacks on the University of New Mexico and Trump Mobile's customer database.

BYOD also claimed responsibility on Monday for an attack on Texas Health and Human Services. The agency has not publicly confirmed an incident and did not immediately respond to our questions. ®

#9918. What's new in Node.js 27

Node.js 27 brings V8 15.6 with Iterator.zip, Iterator.zipKeyed, Math.sumPrecise, net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, and a 4 GB default heap limit.

On October 29, 2026, the Node.js team published v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0. If you have been using Node.js for a few years, that version string alone probably made you do a double take. Where is the usual October v27.0.0 Current release?

Node.js 27 is the first release to follow the new annual schedule. Under the old schedule, October brought a major release that reached end of life six months later without entering Long Term Support (LTS). October now starts a six-month Alpha phase, ahead of the 27.0.0 Current release in April 2027 and LTS promotion in October 2027.

Wait, an odd-numbered Node.js release becoming LTS?

Yes, the odd/even split is gone. Version numbers now match the calendar year (27 in 2027), with one major release per year, and every release becomes LTS. We covered the timeline and the reasons for the change in Node.js is changing its release schedule and version numbers. Because Node.js 27 is currently in its Alpha window, I will keep updating this article as new builds land on the way to April 2027.

In this first Alpha, V8 moves from 14.6 to 15.6, adding Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), and Math.sumPrecise(). There is a promises API for node:net, along with async-iterable TCP servers. The Virtual File System (node:vfs) is now unflagged, the Permission Model gains --allow-env, and HTTP and memory defaults change too.

We’ll start with the JavaScript and Node.js APIs you can use in everyday code, comparing them with the older approaches. Then we’ll cover runtime changes and what to check before upgrading.

Every code block with a file path in its title matches a runnable file in the companion repo lmammino/nodejs-27-examples on GitHub.

For example, we can format a list of products and total their prices:

If you want to experiment locally, check your current Node.js version before running the snippets below.

This is the part of the release I’m most excited about. I love seeing how far we can push streams, iterators, and generators. Our article on JavaScript async iterators should give you an idea of what I mean.

In What’s new in Node.js 26, we used Iterator.concat() to consume multiple iterables one after another. Node.js 27, through V8 15.6, lets us consume them side by side, pairing values at the same position.

Suppose you are checking a weather forecast against the temperatures recorded over the same four days. The predictions come from your model, while the actual values come from observations. To calculate each day’s error, you need to pair the values at the same position. Both sequences must cover the same days in the same order.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, if both sequences were arrays, you would typically use .map() with an index lookup:

That works well for arrays. But what if observations come from a generator, or your model returns an iterator of predictions? Index lookups won’t work on those inputs, and converting them to arrays means loading both sequences into memory first.

In Node.js 27, Iterator.zip() takes an iterable of iterables and returns a lazy iterator of pairs. We can calculate the errors with the same pipeline whether the inputs are arrays or iterators:

Each pair contains a prediction and its corresponding observation. A positive error means the day was warmer than predicted; a negative error means it was cooler. The pairing and mapping happen one item at a time. Only the final .toArray() collects the errors into an array so we can print them together.

Another common use is the dot product of two vectors: multiply matching components, then add the products. This operation appears in graphics, machine learning, and numerical computing:

Here we never collect the pairs or products into an intermediate array. We also use mode: 'strict' because a dot product requires vectors of equal length: silently ignoring extra components would hide an input error.

By default, Iterator.zip() uses { mode: 'shortest' }: it stops when the shortest input finishes and closes the remaining open iterators. For the forecast example, that means comparing only the days available in both sequences. Use { mode: 'strict' } if a missing prediction or observation should instead throw a TypeError. Or pass { mode: 'longest', padding: [null, 0] } to continue until the longest input finishes, using the corresponding padding value when an input runs out.

So far, our inputs have been arrays. But Iterator.zip() also works with iterators that have no end. Imagine a home with two power meters: one measures solar generation, and the other measures household consumption. Each meter gives us its current reading in watts whenever we poll it. Subtracting consumption from generation tells us whether the house has surplus power to export or needs to import power from the grid (assuming there is no battery).

We can wrap each meter in an endless generator. Here we simulate the readings with random values so the example runs without hardware:

Neither generator reads anything until we request a value from netPower. Each request polls both meters once and calculates the difference. Both input iterators can keep producing readings forever, but .take(5) limits this demo to five pairs. Collecting either input with [...solar] or .toArray() would never finish and would eventually exhaust memory.

These are synchronous, on-demand readings: the two meters are polled sequentially, close together, rather than at exactly the same instant. The loop takes five readings immediately; zip() does not add a polling interval. With real hardware, the callbacks would read the meters instead of generating random numbers.

Tuple arrays like [prediction, observation] are easy to read for two or three items, but once you have four or five parallel sources, positional destructuring gets easy to mix up.

Iterator.zipKeyed() accepts an object whose values are iterables. Each step yields an object with the same keys, so you can refer to values by name instead of position:

If an API returns each field as a separate array, like user IDs, names, and roles, Iterator.zipKeyed() lets you process them together as a lazy sequence of row objects. The arrays must describe the same records in the same order.

In Node.js 26, a common way to format a lazy iterator pipeline as a string was to call .toArray().join(', ') at the end. The final .toArray() allocated an array of strings that .join() consumed and discarded.

V8 15.6 adds two terminal helpers directly onto Iterator.prototype:

For join(), let’s return to our sensor readings. This time we only need one temperature sensor, and we want to format five readings as a comma-separated string. As before, we simulate the hardware so you can run the example locally:

.take(5) makes the endless source finite, .map() formats each reading, and .join() builds the string without collecting an intermediate array. These five readings are taken immediately, with no delay between them. Without .take(5), joining this endless iterator would never finish.

For includes(), imagine checking whether a commit message references a particular issue. String.prototype.matchAll() already returns an iterator, so we can extract the complete references and search them directly:

includes() stops as soon as it finds APP-142, without extracting the later reference. Matching complete references also avoids the false positive you would get from message.includes('APP-14'), which matches part of APP-142. The search consumes the iterator, so create a fresh one for another search.

The iterator helpers shown above work with synchronous iterators. Their .next() calls return results directly; these helpers do not await promises from async iterators. You cannot use the same chains on an async function* generator or a Node.js readable stream’s async iterator. Use for await...of or a library with async iterator helpers for those sources. Async iterator helpers are covered by a separate TC39 proposal and are not built into Node.js 27 as of v27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0.

Beyond iterator helpers, V8 15.6 also brings a useful addition for numerical calculations: Math.sumPrecise(). To see why it matters, let’s look at a familiar floating-point surprise.

When you sum numbers with .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0), each addition rounds its intermediate result to the nearest representable 64-bit float. Over dozens or thousands of additions, those tiny rounding errors accumulate. Worse, if you add a small number (0.1) to a huge number (1e20) and later add -1e20, the 0.1 is lost completely during the first addition because a 64-bit float doesn’t have enough mantissa bits to hold both magnitudes at once.

In Node.js 27, V8 15.6 enables Math.sumPrecise() by default. It accepts any iterable of numbers, computes the sum using an internal high-precision accumulator, and rounds only once at the very end:

Math.sumPrecise() accepts any iterable, so it also works with the iterators from the previous section. You can pass the result of .map() directly into Math.sumPrecise() without calling .toArray() first:

When you still need integer cents or decimal libraries

Math.sumPrecise() avoids rounding after each addition. Its result is what you would get by adding the exact mathematical values of the input floating-point numbers, then rounding the total once to the nearest representable 64-bit float. But those inputs may already differ from the decimal values you intended:

As the MDN explanation points out, the literals 0.1 and 0.2 are stored as binary floating-point values slightly greater than their exact decimal counterparts. Adding those stored values and rounding once still produces 0.30000000000000004. The method cannot recover the intended decimal inputs.

For money calculations that require exact decimal arithmetic, use integer minor units (like cents) or a decimal library with explicit rounding rules. Math.sumPrecise() improves summation accuracy; it does not turn JavaScript numbers into decimal numbers.

The core node:net module gets iterator support too.

For years, node:fs, node:dns, node:stream, node:timers, and node:readline have all had .promises sub-modules. Yet node:net remained purely callback- and event-driven. If you wanted to spin up a TCP server on an ephemeral port in a test or connect a client socket using async/await, you had to wrap 'listening', 'connect', and 'error' events by hand.

In Node.js 26 and earlier, setting up a TCP server and client with async/await looked like this:

Node.js 27 introduces the experimental node:net/promises module with two helpers, listen() and connect(), and makes net.Server itself an async iterable.

Let’s try something fun and build a small TCP chat server. Each connected client can send a line of text, and the server forwards it to every other client, prefixed with the sender’s connection ID:

Then open two or three other terminals and run this command in each (with netcat installed):

Each terminal receives its connection ID, for example Connected as 127.0.0.1:54321. Type a message and press Enter. The other terminals receive a line such as 127.0.0.1:54321 > Hello everyone!. The server does not echo messages back to their sender. Press Ctrl+C in a client terminal to disconnect, or in the server terminal to close the chat and all active connections.

With three netcat clients connected, each terminal receives the other clients’ messages:

listen() resolves once the server is listening. The clients map tracks active sockets by their remote address and port, which distinguish connections to this server. These are connection labels, not permanent user identities: reconnecting can give a client a different port.

Inside each handler, readline turns the socket’s byte stream into lines. TCP chunks do not correspond to messages: a line may arrive in several chunks, or one chunk may contain several lines. Each completed line is broadcast to every other active socket. The finally block removes disconnected clients and closes their resources.

The outer connection loop starts each handleConnection(socket) call without awaiting it. That lets it accept the next client while earlier handlers wait for messages. Each handler still awaits its own incoming lines, so clients can remain connected and chat concurrently. The .catch() handles rejected handler promises; socket errors are handled separately, and server.maxConnections = 10 caps open connections for this demo.

The pitfall: awaiting each connection handler

This small change would break the chat’s concurrency:

handleConnection() stays active until its client disconnects. Awaiting it here means only the first client gets a handler and joins the clients map. Later connections can be accepted by the server, but the loop will not dispatch their handlers until that first client leaves. There is nobody else in the map to receive the first client’s messages!

The server iterator documentation warns that a slow consumer can buffer connections without bound. Set server.maxConnections explicitly and choose a limit appropriate to your workload, including when dispatching handlers concurrently.

The iterator yields TCP connections, not individual chat messages or application-level requests. Awaiting a handler can be appropriate for deliberate sequential processing, but a chat server needs overlapping connection handlers.

Testing code that reads configuration files often means mocking node:fs or creating temporary directories and cleaning them up afterward. Bundling assets or templates into an archive poses a related problem: how can your application read them through its usual node:fs calls?

The new node:vfs (Virtual File System) module was originally introduced behind --experimental-vfs, and in Node.js 27 it is unflagged and available out of the box (though still marked Experimental Stability 1 while the API settles).

With node:vfs, you can create an isolated, in-memory file system with vfs.create(), populate it using standard fs-style methods, and mount it so regular node:fs operations (and import / require()) can read from it directly. VirtualFileSystem also supports Explicit Resource Management (using), which unmounts it when execution leaves the block:

The using declaration tells JavaScript to call memoryFs[Symbol.dispose]() when execution leaves the block, including when an error is thrown. VirtualFileSystem implements that method to unmount itself. Declaring it with const would require us to call unmount() explicitly.

memoryFs.mount() mounts the virtual file system under a reserved namespace (path.join(os.devNull, 'vfs'), such as /dev/null/vfs/1 on POSIX), so a virtual mount can never accidentally shadow or overwrite real files on your disk. If you want to compare this with working on real files, check out our guide on reading and writing files in Node.js.

You can also use node:vfs through --vfs-load on the CLI without an experimental flag:

That command mounts the companion repo’s 04-vfs/bundle directory and runs its index.js, which prints Hello from the VFS bundle. You can also pass a ZIP archive; Node.js runs its package.json "main" or index.js entry point from the mounted archive. And if you use Single Executable Applications (SEA), vfsArchive is now mounted at layer 0 and automatically available inside Worker threads too.

There are changes across the standard library too, from temporary files to HTTP server defaults.

Until now, if you needed a temporary file in Node.js, your safest built-in option was fs.mkdtemp() to create a temporary directory, and then opening a file inside it. Creating a random filename yourself and calling fs.open() was error-prone and required a retry loop in case of collisions.

Node.js 27 adds APIs modeled on POSIX mkstemp(3): fs.mkstemp(), fs.mkstempSync(), and fsPromises.mkstemp(). It atomically generates a unique filename (appending six random characters to your prefix) and opens the file in a single step, returning both the path and the open FileHandle (or file descriptor fd):

The built-in fs.glob() (introduced in Node.js 22) was ported from JavaScript to native C++ in Node.js 27. The maintainers’ benchmarks show substantial speedups for some workloads, but gains vary by API and options, and one synchronous exclude-pattern workload regressed. Benchmark your own patterns before assuming a speedup.

As we covered in our guide to environment variables in Node.js, process.env is where most applications keep their most sensitive secrets (API keys, database URLs, signing tokens). It is also the very first place a compromised dependency looks when trying to exfiltrate credentials.

Node.js 27 adds --allow-env to the Permission Model (--permission). When --permission is enabled, every environment variable not explicitly matched by --allow-env is scrubbed at process startup before any JavaScript runs (except runtime variables like PATH, HOME, LANG, and NODE_OPTIONS, plus variables explicitly loaded via --env-file):

Node.js also scrubs disallowed variables from the underlying OS environment block and restricts access to /proc/self/environ on Linux. Native code loaded by Node.js sees the reduced environment too. This reduces accidental exposure; the Permission Model is not a sandbox for malicious code. You can remove a variable after reading it with process.permission.drop('env', 'VARIABLE_NAME'). Keep NODE_ENV explicitly if your application uses it, since it is not preserved by default.

The built-in node:test runner has three updates:

These three HTTP changes affect production web servers:

If you are curious why this change was made: it seems a bit weird on the surface, right? Why would Node.js remove the prototype from an otherwise ordinary object?

req.headers is a dictionary: the keys are header names chosen by whoever sent the request, and the values are whatever they sent. An ordinary JavaScript object is a poor fit for that kind of data, because it inherits properties from Object.prototype that have nothing to do with what you stored in it:

Our empty ordinary object already “has” a constructor, inherited from its prototype. __proto__ is even more surprising: Object.prototype defines an accessor with that name, so reading it returns the prototype, and assigning to it tries to change the prototype instead of storing a value. Both names are already lowercase, which matters here because Node.js lowercases incoming header names. A client can send a constructor or __proto__ header, and it arrives under exactly that key.

Notice that the example uses __proto__ in two different ways. { __proto__: null } is special object-literal syntax that creates the object with no prototype at all (Object.create(null) does the same thing, and the new Node.js code uses the literal form). The later headers['__proto__'] = ... is an ordinary assignment: with no inherited __proto__ setter to intercept it, it simply stores an own property, like any other key.

That’s the motivation in PR #62900, by Matteo Collina. Besides consistency with the *Distinct APIs, its commit message says the change “Fixes prototype pollution concerns where headers like __proto__ could be interpreted as prototype manipulation.” My reading is that the goal is clean dictionary semantics: a key exists in req.headers only if the request sent it.

The March 2026 security releases already included a real bug of this kind. CVE-2026-21710 was a denial-of-service flaw in req.headersDistinct, and it went like this:

Because the exception is thrown synchronously inside a property getter, an 'error' event listener can’t catch it. The fix initialized the headersDistinct and trailersDistinct objects with { __proto__: null }, which is the behavior PR #62900 later extended to headers and trailers. The advisory covers headersDistinct only, so it doesn’t mean req.headers had the same crash. The bug also stopped at crashing the process: a header couldn’t use it to modify Object.prototype globally. And a null-prototype object removes inherited-property hazards only where the headers are created. If you merge headers into an ordinary object, that target still has the inherited __proto__ accessor.

Node.js 27 also updates its engine and bundled dependencies. Most of the V8 details below come from Joyee Cheung’s Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha) on the Node.js blog, which is worth reading in full if you maintain performance-sensitive code or native tooling:

Default Heap Limit up to 4 GB on mid-sized machines: When --max-old-space-size is not specified, V8 now sets the default old-generation heap limit to half of physical memory (or container cgroup memory), clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB. Previously, machines with less than 15 GB of RAM were capped at 2 GB. On an 8 GB container or VM, the default old-generation limit therefore rises from 2 GB to 4 GB (and on a 6 GB machine, from 2 GB to 3 GB). These are old-generation limits, not limits on the process’s total memory use.

Buffer and ArrayBuffer memory affects garbage collection scheduling: Memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances is now included in V8’s global allocation limit. If your app allocates large off-heap buffers (for example, image processing or large file buffers), this affects when garbage collection is scheduled. The global allocation limit is distinct from the old-generation heap limit and does not impose a hard cap on the process’s total memory.

Slightly more memory per worker and per native object: Each V8 isolate (the main thread and every worker thread) uses about 180 KB more for property lookup caches, and every JavaScript object that wraps a native resource (a socket, file handle, stream, hash, or blob) may use about 16 bytes more on the heap and about 50 bytes more outside it. That’s negligible for most apps, but it adds up if you spawn many workers or hold many open sockets.

Fewer hard crashes on fatal errors: More fatal V8 errors now go through Node.js’s fatal error handling before aborting, so --report-on-fatalerror can produce a diagnostic report in cases that previously aborted without one. Some extreme inputs (overly long template literals, classes with too many elements, a regexp too large to compile) now throw a RangeError instead of crashing the process. The V8 post is explicit that this isn’t guaranteed, so don’t build program logic around it.

These numbers come from V8’s own benchmarks, and the impact varies with platform, workload, and build configuration. Measure your application before counting on a speedup.

OpenSSL 4.1.0, Undici 8.12, SQLite 3.54, and npm 12.1.0: Node.js 27 upgrades its bundled cryptography to OpenSSL 4.1.0, strips out all legacy OpenSSL 1.x compatibility shims and engine APIs, bumps npm to 12.1.0, and updates NODE_MODULE_VERSION to 153.

The Alpha window gives you time to check for breaking changes before the stable release. Most applications won’t encounter all of these, but check your code and dependencies for the following changes.

As we saw in the HTTP section, the header dictionaries no longer have a prototype. Normal property access (req.headers['content-type']), destructuring, and Object.keys() work as before. What breaks is calling methods inherited from Object.prototype: req.headers.hasOwnProperty('authorization') now throws a TypeError (and calling a method looked up on a dictionary of external data was never a good idea anyway).

Replace it with Object.hasOwn(req.headers, 'authorization'), which doesn’t rely on the object’s prototype and works on both Node.js 26 and 27. Please don’t “fix” this by restoring Object.prototype on the headers object. The in operator still works on null-prototype objects, but the updated Node.js docs advise against using it here, and Object.hasOwn() expresses the own-property check you actually mean.

This runnable example shows both the failure and the fix. Keep in mind that checking for a header’s presence does not authenticate its value:

If you run multiple Node.js processes on a 6 GB or 8 GB machine and relied on the old implicit 2 GB heap cap to keep them from starving each other, pass --max-old-space-size=2048 explicitly. Similarly, if your application holds hundreds of megabytes of Buffer data in memory alongside a large JS heap, be aware that Buffer allocations now influence V8’s global allocation limit and garbage collection scheduling.

Most V8 changes are invisible, but a few can break code that depends on exact results:

The V8 changes post lists more edge cases, including fractional getTimezoneOffset() values for historical dates and stricter take()/drop() limits on iterators.

When testing your project or library against Node.js 27:

For production, the release date matters. For library authors and local experiments, there is already code to try:

If you want to install the Alpha side by side with your stable LTS runtime without messing up your system setup, check out our guide on 5 ways to install Node.js using version managers like fnm or nvm.

Want to write modern, production-ready Node.js?

Our book Node.js Design Patterns covers streams, iterators, async control flow, modules, and scalable architectures. The runtime changes each year; these patterns help you design applications across releases.

Node.js 27 starts the annual release schedule, with every major version going on to LTS. Its first Alpha includes V8 15.6, node:net/promises, an unflagged node:vfs, fs.mkstemp(), and --allow-env.

I’d start by trying Iterator.zipKeyed() and Iterator.prototype.join() in a data-transformation script. They let you process parallel collections lazily without collecting intermediate arrays.

For the full list of commits and low-level details, check out the official Node.js 27.0.0-alpha.0.0.0 release notes and the companion post on Notable V8 changes from Node.js 26 to 27 (Alpha).

Thanks to the Node.js releasers, V8 maintainers, and contributors who worked on this first Alpha and the new release schedule.

Node.js 27 is the first version under the new Node.js release schedule. Instead of two major releases per year, Node.js now ships one major release every April, preceded by a six-month Alpha testing phase starting in October.

Yes. Under the new release schedule, the old odd/even rule is gone and every yearly major release becomes LTS. Node.js 27 will enter Current in April 2027, move to LTS in October 2027, and be supported until April 2030.

Thanks to V8 15.6, Node.js 27 ships Iterator.zip(), Iterator.zipKeyed(), Iterator.prototype.join(), Iterator.prototype.includes(), Math.sumPrecise(), and Intl.Locale.prototype.variants enabled by default.

When --max-old-space-size is not set, V8 now defaults to half of physical memory clamped between 256 MB and 4 GB (meaning an 8 GB machine gets a 4 GB heap instead of 2 GB). Additionally, memory held by Buffer and ArrayBuffer instances now counts toward V8’s global allocation limit, affecting when garbage collection runs.

If you are reading this before April 2027, keep production workloads on an LTS release. Node.js 27 is still in its Alpha testing phase during that period, intended for library authors, CI pipelines, and experimentation. It is scheduled to enter Current in April 2027 and LTS in October 2027. Once a stable release is available, evaluate it against your application’s support requirements.

InfoQ Homepage News Entire's Git Forge Rethinks Git Collaboration for Coding Agents

Nov 08, 2026 3 min read

Entire is a Git forge designed specifically for collaboration between human developers and AI coding agents. Its premise is that traditional software development infrastructure, particularly the pull request (PR) model, is not well suited to an environment where AI agents generate, review, and iterate on code at high speed.

As Thomas Dohmke, former GitHub CEO and currently CEO of Entire, explains, GitHub and GitLab transformed human-to-human collaboration by centering it around asynchronous code reviews and version control. A multi-agent forge, by contrast, centers around the asynchronous orchestration, versioning, and auditing of AI agents working alongside humans.

Built on top of a fully distributed architecture that enables pushes up to 89 times faster than GitHub, Entire's core component is trails, which addresses the challenges AI coding agents pose to the traditional PR-based development model:

The pull request [timeline] has become an audit log that only the agent reads. It does not provide the information for the developer to decide whether they can merge with confidence.

Trails bring the most relevant information to the top of the page in the form of eval scores that are updated on every push. These scores help developers assess whether a PR has reached a stable state or requires another iteration of agent-driven coding and review:

Only when the confidence is high, risk is low, and all findings are cleared, the merge should happen.

A trail can be initiated from a bug report, a feature request, or manually, and can span multiple repositories. Whenever new code is pushed, a review agent running in a cloud sandbox evaluates the changes and returns a score and a rationale based on code quality, security, slop, and whether human code review is required. For example, if the slop score is orange, developers can ask their coding agent to improve the code and push a new change, thus triggering a new iteration.

The last 5 runs and the current run are shown for each eval. We believe this is crucial as one-shot loops are often missing a critical issue. Repeating the loops and stabilizing the scores is crucial for the success of agentic coding.

Evaluation agents can be configured through Entire's interface or repository-level JSON configuration.

Review agents can suggest fixes or improvements, which remain visible in the trail while it is open. All review findings must be either resolved or closed before a merge is allowed. Developers can also configure repository-level Gates to define the conditions required for approval.

Another foundational concept introduced by Entire is continuous memory, which preserves all accumulated knowledge in the repository so that agents can reuse it across sessions rather than starting from scratch. Continuous memory is implemented by two open-source tools, entire-graph, which builds a precomputed map of the Git repository including ranked code searches, definition and callers, types and routes, and more; and entire-brain, which creates a persistent memory layer by combining the codebase map with previous agent sessions and information recorded in Git history.

This allows agents to always have the right context at the right time, aka the "why" behind the "what changed."

As a final note on Entire, it also supports integrations with CI platforms like Buildkite and Depot.

Commenting on the announcement on Hacker News, user conartist6 expressed the view that engineers have delegated writing code to agents because of programming languages and tools that leave much to be desired. Haimantika, currently at Entire, points out that the problem has never been languages or tools, rather

it' s that the reasoning gets thrown away between the person and the artifact. Commit messages were always bad, docs always rotted, “why is this here” was always answered by whoever remembered. Agents just made that acute, because now there's no one who remembers. That's the bit we're trying to fix. If a better language fixes it too, honestly I'd take that.

Entire is only one of several new players in the source code management arena, which also include Zed DeltaDB, Anthropic Scion, East River Source Control, Cursor Origin, Radicle, and others.
