#9907. Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for a wide range of applications, such as retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, semantic textual similarity, and more. Its v6.0 update introduces a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, alongside a complete training approach for it. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use it to finetune a multi-vector model that outperforms general-purpose retrievers on your data. This method can also train strong new multi-vector models from scratch. Everything below runs on pip install -U "sentence-transformers[train]".

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

Lastly, in the Evaluation section, I'll show you that my finetuned multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical model, trained in 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 alongside this blogpost, easily outperforms every general-purpose retrieval model I could find on my medical retrieval evaluation: dense, sparse, lexical, and multi-vector alike.

If you're interested in finetuning dense embedding models, sparse embedding models, or rerankers instead, then consider reading through my prior Training and Finetuning Embedding Models, Training and Finetuning Sparse Embedding Models, and Training and Finetuning Reranker Models blogposts.

This blogpost is about training multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to use them, from loading and encoding to indexing in vector databases, see the companion Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model compresses a whole text into a single vector, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model) skips that compression. It keeps one small vector per token and scores a query against a document with the MaxSim operator, where every query token finds its best-matching document token and the scores are summed. Token-level matching preserves exactly the fine-grained signals that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval, at the cost of a bigger index.

The companion Multi-Vector Embedding Models blogpost covers the architecture, encoding, scoring, and indexing in detail, so I'll keep this section short and get to the training.

Finetuning multi-vector models significantly improves their retrieval performance on your specific domain: the vocabulary, the query style, and the notion of relevance all differ between web search, legal discovery, code search, and scientific literature review. Because queries and documents are matched token by token, multi-vector models pick up fine-grained domain signals that single-vector models tend to average away, and they respond very well to even modest amounts of in-domain finetuning data.

Beyond that, most released retrieval models were configured for short passages. The classic ColBERT checkpoints truncate documents at 180 or 300 tokens, and many popular dense models at 256 or 512, because their MS MARCO-style training data rarely goes beyond that. If your documents are long, these models silently discard most of every document before scoring it. On my medical evaluation with passages averaging 941 tokens, I measured that this truncation costs up to 0.24 NDCG@10, considerably more than any difference between model architectures. When you train your own model, you configure the document length that your data needs.

LightOn ran into this same dynamic with code retrieval, where general LateOn wasn't enough and they trained LateOn-Code. Your domain, whether that's medical, legal, financial, or your company's internal documents, is not getting an official model. This blogpost shows you how to build it yourself, in a matter of hours, on a single consumer GPU.

Training MultiVectorEncoder models involves the following components:

Let's take a closer look at each component.

Multi-vector training gives you a real choice of starting point, and it matters more than you might expect.

If you want to further finetune an existing multi-vector model, you don't have to worry about the architecture at all:

The checkpoint brings its own recipe along: its query and document marker tokens, its projection head, its scoring skiplist. For finetuning, you generally want to keep all of that and change only what your data demands. The first thing to check is the length configuration, since many released checkpoints cap documents at 180 to 512 tokens (see Why Finetune?), and my medical passages run to 1,400 tokens. The mLateOn family already serves the backbone's full 8192 token context, but if your starting checkpoint carries caps, lift them:

With the per-task caps unset, truncation falls back to the tokenizer's model_max_length, which is why I configure that limit at load time above.

I made one more change, adding a punctuation skiplist that excludes punctuation tokens from document-side scoring and storage. In a 4-way ablation (none, punctuation, stopwords, both) it modestly won on quality, and it shrinks the document index by 9.6% on this data for free:

You can also point MultiVectorEncoder at any base transformer, and a fresh, randomly initialized token-level projection is appended for you:

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them down to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. The projection starts random, so training is required before this model is useful. Interestingly, this works with strong dense embedding backbones too. A fresh projection on Alibaba-NLP/gte-modernbert-base reached within 0.03 of the existing-checkpoint starting points in my experiments, from nothing but the projection and 25k training pairs.

The classic ColBERT tokenization tricks ([MASK] query expansion, [Q] / [D] prefix tokens, a document length cap, a punctuation skiplist) are all off by default and configurable. See Creating Custom Models for the full set. For what it's worth, I tested [MASK] query expansion in four configurations for my domain finetune and none of them made a measurable difference, so don't feel obliged to reach for the classic recipe.

I measured this directly while preparing this blogpost, taking six starting points and training each with the identical recipe on 25k medical question-passage pairs from MIRIAD, then evaluating on 1,000 held-out questions against a 50,000 passage corpus:

The result surprised me, and it replicated across two model families. *The -unsupervised checkpoints adapt to a new domain far better than their finished siblings, overtaking them despite starting lower. These checkpoints sit after large-scale contrastive pretraining but before supervised finetuning on general retrieval, so they carry all the late-interaction structure with none of the general-purpose tuning that domain training then has to undo. The finished checkpoints, by contrast, barely moved or even regressed, at every learning rate I tried.

So, if the model family you like publishes a pre-supervised checkpoint, start there. If not, a fresh projection on a strong retrieval-pretrained backbone is a close runner-up. Continuing from a fully finished checkpoint is the weakest option for domain adaptation, despite being the most natural-feeling one.

The MultiVectorEncoderTrainer uses datasets.Dataset or datasets.DatasetDict instances for training and evaluation. You can load data from the Hugging Face Datasets Hub or use local data in whatever format you prefer (e.g. CSV, JSON, Parquet, Arrow, or SQL).

Note: Lots of public datasets that work out of the box with Sentence Transformers have been tagged with sentence-transformers on the Hugging Face Hub, so you can easily find them on https://huggingface.co/datasets?other=sentence-transformers. Consider browsing through these to find ready-to-go datasets that might be useful for your tasks, domains, or languages.

You can use the load_dataset function to load data from datasets on the Hub:

This is the dataset I'll train on in this blogpost: 4.4 million medical questions from MIRIAD, each paired with the source passage that contains its answer (averaging 941 tokens). Simple (query, relevant passage) pairs like these are the easiest retrieval training data to collect for your own domain, and as you'll see, they're all you need.

You can also use load_dataset for loading local data in common file formats:

And if your local data requires pre-processing, you can use datasets.Dataset.from_dict to initialize your dataset with a dictionary of lists:

It is important that your dataset format matches your loss function (or that you choose a loss function that matches your dataset format). Verifying whether a dataset format works with a loss function involves two steps:

There are two multi-vector specific conventions on top of this:

Loss functions quantify how well a model performs for a given batch of data, allowing an optimizer to update the model weights to produce more favourable (i.e., lower) loss values. The right loss function for your task depends on the data you have and what you're trying to achieve. You can find a full list of options in the Loss Overview.

For the common case of question-answer or question-passage pairs, the workhorse is in-batch negatives training with MultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, where every other document in the batch acts as a negative for each query. Bigger batches mean more negatives and stronger training, so in practice you'll want its GradCache variant, CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss, which decouples the effective batch size from what fits on your GPU:

The mini_batch_size parameter bounds the memory by encoding documents in chunks of this size, while the effective contrastive batch size (128 in my run below, and in my ablations bigger batches bought nothing further) stays a free choice. GradCache guarantees identical results regardless of the chunk size, so lower it for smaller GPUs at only a wall-clock cost. When your document lengths vary a lot, consider its sibling mini_batch_num_tokens, which packs each chunk to a total token budget instead of a document count, so a chunk of unusually long documents can never spike your memory (my mini_batch_size=16 at roughly 940 tokens per document corresponds to mini_batch_num_tokens=15_000).

One multi-vector specific trap is that the contrastive losses default to scale=1.0, unlike the dense embedding equivalent which defaults to scale=20.0. That 20.0 exists because a cosine similarity is a single value in [-1, 1], too narrow a range for a sharp softmax. A MaxSim score instead sums one best-match similarity per query token, so it already spans roughly [0, query_length]: a 32-token query can score up to 32. So don't copy scale=20.0 over from a dense training script, since it would saturate the softmax and kill your gradients.

For distillation from a stronger teacher, which is how the strongest general-purpose late-interaction models are trained, see MultiVectorDistillKLDivLoss and the Knowledge Distillation tab in the Training Overview documentation.

You can customize the training process using the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments class. This class lets you adjust parameters that can impact training speed and help you understand what's happening during training.

For more information on the most useful training arguments, check out the Multi-Vector Encoder > Training Overview > Training Arguments. It's worth reading to get the most out of your training.

Here's an example, using the values from my actual training run:

To track your model's performance during training, you can pass an eval_dataset to the trainer for evaluation loss, but concrete retrieval metrics are much more informative. Sentence Transformers includes the following built-in evaluators for multi-vector models:

For domain finetuning, the MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator built from your own held-out data is the one that matters. One tip on constructing it is that the corpus should be hard enough that models can be told apart. In my case the MIRIAD questions are generated from their own source passages, which makes retrieval unusually easy. Against just the 10k gold passages, nearly every model scored above 0.97 NDCG@10. If your evaluation saturates like that, add distractor passages (I use deduplicated passages from the training split) until the scores spread out:

The MultiVectorEncoderTrainer is where all previous components come together. Here is the complete script that trained multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical, the model from the introduction:

That's the whole recipe: a pre-supervised checkpoint, a million domain pairs, in-batch negatives, full document length, and a higher-than-usual learning rate. The run took 14.5 hours on my single RTX 3090 at a peak of 17.5 GB VRAM, and every one of those choices was the winner of a measured comparison rather than a guess.

For readers on smaller budgets, my scaling experiments put 100k pairs (75 minutes of training) within 0.012 NDCG@10 of the full million-pair run. Most of the gain comes in the first hour.

The MultiVectorEncoder trainer supports various transformers.TrainerCallback subclasses, including:

Enable these via the report_to training argument, e.g. report_to=["wandb", "codecarbon"], with the required dependencies installed. It defaults to "none", and report_to="all" activates every integration whose dependency is installed.

Refer to the Transformers Callbacks documentation for more information on these callbacks and how to create your own.

Typically, top-performing general-purpose models are trained on multiple datasets simultaneously. However, this approach can be challenging due to the varying formats of each dataset. Fortunately, the MultiVectorEncoderTrainer allows you to train on multiple datasets without requiring a uniform format. Additionally, it provides the flexibility to apply different loss functions to each dataset. Here are the steps to train with multiple datasets at once:

Each training/evaluation batch will only contain samples from one of the datasets. The order in which batches are sampled from the multiple datasets is defined by the MultiDatasetBatchSamplers enum, which can be passed to the MultiVectorEncoderTrainingArguments via multi_dataset_batch_sampler. Valid options are:

To find out where the finetuned model stands, I evaluated it against over 50 retrieval model configurations across four architecture families on the MIRIAD evaluation set, built exactly as in the Evaluator section above, with 1,000 held-out medical questions searching 200,000 unique passages (the 10k gold passages hidden among 190k deduplicated distractors from the training split). This corpus is four times the size of the 50,000-passage one from Which starting point should you pick?, so scores are not comparable between the two tables.

The headline results, with the full table in the collapsible below:

The finetuned model tops the table, beating the strongest zero-shot model of any architecture by +0.062 NDCG@10. In other words, the strongest zero-shot model returns the right passage as the very first hit for 75.8% of the queries, while the finetuned model does so for 84.9%, cutting the rank-1 error by more than a third.

The architecture pattern is just as clear, with the top of the table exclusively late interaction. On long documents, one vector per token beats one vector per document, even at matched training and matched backbones. DenseOn and LateOn share training data and architecture except for the head, and the late-interaction sibling wins by +0.12, with the multilingual pair (mDenseOn and mLateOn) replicating this at +0.13. Scale doesn't rescue single vectors either. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest dense model with roughly 33x the active (non-embedding) parameters of mine, still stops 0.13 short, and the 8B version scores lower than the 4B.

BM25 also performs surprisingly well, beating every sparse model, every truncation-capped multi-vector model, and all but three dense models: the multi-billion Qwen3-Embedding-4B and 8B, and voyage-4-nano, which reads its full 32k token context to edge past by just 0.006. Don't expect that to transfer to your own data though. MIRIAD's questions are generated from the passages, so the lexical overlap between a query and its gold passage is far larger than in typical retrieval, and BM25's unlimited context length lets it use every one of those overlapping words while most neural checkpoints truncate. A BM25 baseline is cheap and always worth running, just don't count on this margin.

The full field at a glance, sorted by score and colored by architecture family.

Models marked @N are evaluated with their document length cap lifted to N tokens, since their native caps (180 to 512 tokens) would otherwise truncate the 941-token average passages. For every multi-vector model this lift was worth +0.08 to +0.24 NDCG@10 over the as-served row, and even the dense DenseOn gained +0.03 from the same treatment.

Note that this does not mean that multi-vector-encoder/mLateOn-medical is the strongest model on all domains. It's simply the strongest in my domain. This is totally fine, as I just need this model to work well on my data.

Don't underestimate the power of finetuning multi-vector models on your domain. Fourteen and a half hours on a single consumer GPU produced a model that no general-purpose retriever comes close to on this data, and the recipe is a single script with no teacher model and no mined negatives!

The fair objection to multi-vector retrieval is index size, and this domain is close to the worst case for it. Storing one vector per token, my model needs about 878 vectors per passage, so the 200,000-passage corpus takes roughly 45 GB at fp16, where a dense model needs well under 1 GB. Document length is what makes that gap so wide. The Natural Questions passages in the companion post average about 125 token vectors each, seven times fewer, so a corpus of short passages starts from a far smaller index than this one does. The HierarchicalTokenPooling module compresses exactly this by clustering each document's token embeddings and storing the cluster means, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the vectors:

I measured it post-hoc on the finished model, with no pooling-aware training, and on long documents it is remarkably cheap.

The solid points are uncompressed embeddings, so that every family is counted the same way and scored with exact search. You would not deploy any of them like that, though. Dense indexes routinely use int8 or binary quantization with rescoring, sparse indexes compress their postings, and multi-vector indexes use PLAID-style residual compression. Don't read those points as the disk you need to buy, but as relative storage cost.

Token pooling is the solid line. Halving the vector count costs 0.0033 NDCG@10 and leaves rank-1 accuracy untouched, and keeping only a quarter of them, at 11.2 GB, still scores 0.8991. The curve keeps going (I measured out to a tenth of the vectors, still at 0.8765) but there is little reason to push pooling that far once quantization is on the table, which is what the dashed line below is about.

The dashed line is what a real deployment might look like. I gave Omar Khattab early access to the model and the benchmark, and he measured these configurations with fast-plaid at 1-bit residual quantization, using compact 17-bit centroid ids and 18-bit document ids instead of its ordinary unpacked 64-bit integers, plus document-side pruning:

That first row is 13x smaller than the raw embeddings, for 0.0155 NDCG@10. That is a far better trade than anywhere on the pooling curve. Quantization shrinks each vector while pooling and pruning cut how many you keep, so they compose, and quantization is the one to reach for first. Push further and the last row lands at 1.45 GB, smaller than the fp16 embeddings of Qwen3-Embedding-8B (1.64 GB), while scoring 0.0895 higher. The objection that multi-vector indexes are too big does not survive a properly configured index.

The pruning here is naive, meant only to establish that token reduction works on top of quantization, so read the bottom two rows as a floor rather than the frontier. If you would rather not hand-tune quantization at all, the Indexing section of the companion post covers fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa.

Multi-vector retrieval is only as expensive as its index. The raw embeddings for this corpus are 45 GB, and a properly configured index is at least 7x smaller at nearly the same accuracy. The index deserves as much of your attention as the checkpoint.

Thanks to Omar Khattab for measuring the quantized and pruned index configurations in Optimizing the index, and for the discussions around late-interaction index costs.

For further learning, you may also want to explore the following resources on Sentence Transformers:

And here is an advanced page that might interest you:

And the companion blogpost, covering everything about using these models:

Finetuning multi-vector models involves several components: the model itself, datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. I'll have a look at each of playfy these components, accompanied by practical examples of how they can be used for finetuning strong multi-vector models.

This is a really interesting deep dive into multi-vector embedding models... 🔥 The introduction of MultiVectorEncoder in Sentence Transformers v6.0 looks especially useful for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval, where keeping multiple representations can capture much finer-grained matching than a single dense embedding. The fact that the same framework supports RAG, semantic search, and reranking makes this a very practical direction for modern retrieval systems. 🚀

I also like how the post breaks the finetuning process down into the individual pieces... datasets, loss functions, training arguments, evaluators, and the trainer class. 🧠 Having practical examples around each component makes the approach much easier to understand and reproduce, especially for people who want to move beyond using a general-purpose retriever and actually optimize a model for their own domain.

The medical retrieval results are probably the most impressive part... 💡 Training the mLateOn-medical multi-vector encoder for just 14.5 hours on a single RTX 3090 and getting better results than dense, sparse, lexical, and other multi-vector approaches shows how valuable domain-specific finetuning can be. It’s a great reminder that the biggest gains in retrieval often come from matching the model and training data closely to the actual search task rather than simply choosing the newest general-purpose model. 👏📚

Overall, this is a great practical resource for anyone experimenting with advanced retrieval pipelines... ⚡ The ability to train strong multi-vector models from scratch as well as finetune existing ones opens up plenty of possibilities for specialized search and RAG applications. I especially appreciate that the whole workflow can be set up with sentence-transformers[train]... it makes an otherwise fairly complex retrieval training process feel much more approachable. 👍🤖

InfoQ Homepage News Pinterest Replaces Journey Clustering with 4B Qwen3 LLM, Reports Improved Engagement

Nov 09, 2026 2 min read

Pinterest has moved its user-journey inference system from a multi-stage clustering pipeline to a fine-tuned 4-billion-parameter language model, reporting a 1.1% improvement in email click-through and 1.3% higher push opens.

Rather than clustering keywords into interests, the model examines users' activity histories to identify longer-term goals and feeds those journeys into Pinterest's existing recommendation infrastructure.

Pinterest defines a "journey" as a goal that connects interests, intent, and context across multiple sessions. Someone renovating a kitchen, for example, might search for cabinet designs, save countertop ideas, and later explore backsplash tiles or lighting. These interactions collectively suggest a coherent project rather than several unrelated interests.

The company's previous system extracted keywords from user activity, grouped them using embeddings and hierarchical clustering, named the resulting clusters, and ranked them with additional models and diversity heuristics.

Although effective compared with earlier interest-based notifications, the approach could fragment related activities into separate journeys, produce generic labels, or mistake incidental engagement for sustained intent.

The new system instead treats journey inference as a generation task. A fine-tuned LLM reads a chronological history of up to 150 user actions across a 360-day window, alongside a compact user profile, and generates a ranked set of journey names. Search and save actions carry more weight than incidental clicks, while the prompt instructs the model to consider repeated engagement, recency, and specificity.

("Journey Inference" - Source: Pinterest)

The consolidation moved much of the previous system's ranking and filtering behavior into the prompt. Instructions discourage unrelated interests from being merged, suppress one-off activity and noisy automatically generated tags, and allow an empty result where there is insufficient evidence of a meaningful journey. Pinterest treats changes to these instructions as production launches rather than simple prompt edits.

To build the system without an extensive human-labelled dataset, Pinterest used frontier models to generate synthetic training examples from its user activity histories. These examples were used to fine-tune smaller open-weight Qwen3 models through supervised fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA).

The team tested models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters, selecting the 4B model for its balance of inference quality and serving throughput.

Running the resulting model at Pinterest's scale presented a separate engineering challenge. The company deployed NVIDIA Dynamo in front of vLLM workers running on L40S GPUs, using continuous batching, PagedAttention, and prefix-cache-aware routing to improve inference efficiency.

(Journey Inference Architecture - Source: Pinterest)

However, one of the largest throughput improvements came from avoiding unnecessary inference altogether. The system tracks when each user's journeys were last generated and skips users processed within the preceding couple of days.

Pinterest evaluates journey quality through side-by-side comparisons, a separate LLM judge assessing relevance and support from user activity, and online experiments. Initial A/B testing in the US and Canada produced the reported 1.1% email click-through and 1.3% push-open improvements over the clustering-based system, alongside statistically significant engagement and retention gains.

The approach has parallels with Netflix's work on foundation models for personalised recommendations. Netflix has described learning from long sequences of member interactions to create representations that can be reused by downstream recommendation models.

While Netflix focuses on reusable preference representations and Pinterest generates explicit journey descriptions, both approaches use longer-term behavioural histories to enrich existing personalisation infrastructure rather than replace it entirely.

#9904. APT29's Watering Holes Target Thousands of Mobile Users

After compromising websites, the Russian state-sponsored threat group is fingerprinting victims, then harvesting information from the interesting ones.

It has emerged this week that Russia's APT29 threat group compromised the website of a Ukrainian SEO and website analytics service, and briefly used the access to distribute malicious device-fingerprinting code to potentially thousands of iPhone and Android users.

The weeklong compromise earlier this year was part of a broader watering-hole campaign from APT29 (aka Cozy Bear, Midnight Blizzard, and The Dukes) that also used other legitimate and fake websites to distribute the fingerprinting malware, and later to collect sensitive personal information from selected devices.

Researchers at Sekoia who are tracking the campaign are unsure if the state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) had specific targets in mind, or if it was simply trying to infect as many vulnerable phones as possible.

"Across the directly compromised websites, no single sectoral targeting pattern emerges from our analysis," Sekoia's threat research and intelligence team wrote. "While the victimology shows a focus on Ukraine and the United States, the inclusion of unrelated entities such as an Australian medical clinic complicates a broad strategic interpretation."

Related:Indonesia Hit by Android Banking App-Cloning Campaign

APT29 is a familiar threat actor that the US government has formally tied to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its primary mission is intelligence gathering on behalf of Moscow, with a focus on government agencies, diplomatic organizations, think tanks, technology companies, healthcare, and research institutions.

Among its most prominent campaigns were the breaches at the Democratic National Committee in 2016, efforts to steal COVID-19 vaccine research in 2020, and the SolarWinds supply-chain compromise, which gave it access to numerous US government agencies and private-sector organizations. The group is known for stealthy, long-term intrusions, and in recent years has increasingly targeted cloud environments, email accounts, and technology providers to gain access to downstream victims.

In its latest campaign, APT29 used three separate infection vectors to target iOS and Android devices. One involved compromising legitimate websites and injecting malicious JavaScript that exposed visitors to a device-fingerprinting script. Among the websites the threat actor turned into watering holes were those of a US chemical-industry trade association, a Ukrainian gas producer, and a Bulgarian military-related organization.

When unable to compromise a legitimate website, the group created lookalike domains that impersonated the real sites, and modified their content in real-time to inject the malicious code. Two examples it impersonated were the America250 national celebration website and London's Raffles hotel.

Related:ToxicPanda Banking Trojan Matures Into Enterprise Threat

The third vector involved a supply chain compromise of Ukrainian website analytics firm Plerdy. According to Sekoia, thousands of websites, most of them Ukrainian, use the company's tracking scripts. By injecting malicious code into that script, APT29 potentially exposed visitors to those sites to its device-fingerprinting and exploit-delivery infrastructure, Sekoia said.

The fingerprinting malware collected device and browser data from Android and iOS devices and sent it to an APT29 command-and-control service, which then delivered one of three different exploit chains depending on the mobile platform and browser/OS versions. Each chain targeted specific vulnerabilities in iOS or Android that had remained unpatched on the exposed devices.

Related:Video Call Exploit Chains Two Flaws in Unisoc Modems

Sekoia said it found several indicators linking the campaign to APT29, including remnants of a separate 2025 watering-hole operation that researchers have previously attributed to the group. Sekoia also found signs that the attackers may have obtained their exploits from a third party, possibly a commercial surveillance vendor (CSV). The campaign's victims include organizations in Europe and the US, though most are based in Ukraine, a country that Russian threat groups have incessantly targeted since the beginning of the war in Ukraine.

APT29's latest campaign is another indication of how mobile devices have become attractive intelligence targets for threat groups. Commercial spyware vendors are fueling the trend by making technology available that enables large scale surveillance and data theft via mobile devices. APT29's likely sourcing of the DarkSword exploit kit from a third-party provider suggests that sophisticated mobile intrusion capabilities that were once largely associated with highly targeted espionage operations are finding their way into broader campaigns.

"The adoption of packaged n-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation," Sekoia warned. "Over the long term, we assess that the proliferation and reuse of CSV exploits among state-sponsored intrusion sets will likely become more frequent."

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. #9903. Building a networking switch ASIC chip

I am currently on a quest to build some open source networking equipment with the final boss being a full router.

There are a lot of very valuable and less complex pieces of hardware on the way that also need building, one of them being the common networking switch.

Previously I was building the infrastructure to handle ethernet packets and worked my way up to a simple three-port switch that I had taped it out via Tiny Tapeout. But a few days after that tapeout, as I was still reeling from the adrenaline of rushing to meet the deadline, an unexpected opportunity presented itself: the possibility of taping out my own full chip, free of charge!

But there was one slight problem, I only had four days to design the entire thing, also known as 96 hours ( putting it in hours definitely does not make it sound less terrifying ).

A few months back, I wrote that building a full matrix multiplication accelerator with some in-silicon debug infrastructure in under 2 weeks was too tight of a deadline, all around a terrible idea and should absolutely never be attempted, especially not in a corporate setting. Well since then I have discovered a new circle of hell: designing a full ASIC solo in 4 days.

But now that I have gazed upon these new depths of hell, let me tell you about the journey of building full ASICs!

Fully open-source full chip tapeout of the unmanaged cut-through 100Mbps Ethernet switch and the Heat Death of the Universe beacon. Targeting 0.5x0.5 waffer.space run#2.

But they will talk to wafer.space, and wafer.space will talk to me.

Now I suspect you might be wondering: what is wafer.space again ?

A few months ago, something happened. Tim Ansell, formerly part of the team at Google that got us the SkyWater 130nm and GlobalFoundries 180nm open source PDKs, left Google and started wafer.space where he opened up the possibility for mere mortals to taped out their own chip at GlobalFoundries for an affordable price. They offer the services of getting your chip manufactured on GlobalFoundaries 180nm and optionally get it packaged.

Chips come in all rectangular sizes with the size measured in area.

Area is one of the primary concerns of the design as it is once again a question of cold calculated economics, because, when you go to get a chip manufactured you pay per \( mm^2 \) of area.

Take for example the price quoted bellow by IHP (another fab) for their own multiwafer runs. If you participate in this run you will get back a set number of chips (40 in this case) and your final chip cost will correspond to how big your chip ultimately is.

Yet, more area is not simply more expensive because of the direct manufacturing cost, there is a second more subtle factor inflating the price, and that is yield.

Ultimately broken chips have no value, actually we could argue that we should ascribe negative value to broken chips because identifying which chips are broken costs money, and selling a customer a broken chip costs even more money. So maximizing the ratio of good chips to manufactured chips is of primary importance. This ratio is called the yield.

Chips can be broken for a plethora of reasons, but for simplicity I will put them in two different buckets. Firstly it could be a design issue, in which case all your chips are equally affected. Secondly it could be a manufacturing defect that affects your chips semi-randomly.

Manufacturing defects that occur during semiconductor device fabrication can be modeled as constant defect probability per unit of area, meaning that chips with higher area have a higher probability of having a defect, and thus lower yield, leading to ultimately higher costs.

This doesn’t impact the price which I pay to the chip area per-se, but it affects the average net price that I will pay per functional chip.

This is the double reason why area optimization is such a concern when designing chips.

Now GlobaFoundaries 180nm (gf180) is not a young node, and the polite way of calling something old is “matrue”. With node maturity comes increased expertise of the process by the foundry leading to better yields over time. So gf180 is a node with excellent yields for which area related defects are not a concern especially compared to younger leading edge nodes.

Wafer.space now offers 4 chip sizes, commonly referred to in the community as the “full”, “half”s and “quarter” slots.

For people in need of some perspective, the full slot and its nearly 13mm2 of area is the same size as the entire Tiny Tapeout gf180 shuttle chip. The same chip that is capable of accommodating unto 160 project tiles and all the Tiny Tapeout common infrastructure. For reference, my two systolic arrays (8 bit integer and bfloat16) and the original switch all fit on only 4 tiles and my largest design to date, the blake2s hashing accelerator on 8.

But getting the silicon manufactured is only the first battle of the war.

Once you get your chip onto a wafer, there are two more important steps to clear before it can actually be called a chip.

Semiconductors are manufactured on a substrate called a wafer, this is a solid silicon disk that then needs to be very precisely broken up into individual chips. This step is called dicing.

So once the wafers have exited the fab and the guys at wafer.space take delivery of the full set of wafers, they call to another specialized service to dice them into individual chips along the scrible lines using a very precise diamond saw.

At that point, wafer.space offers two possibilities. The first is to mail you the diced chips directly, the second is to get the chips packaged for you.

Raw semiconductor silicon is beautiful but unless you are also in the habit of collecting expensive crystals to look at, they are not much use as is. After all, how do you communicate with a piece of doped silicon crystal?

In order to both power our chip and be able to communicate with it, we need to package it in the form in which we can connect it to a wider electronic circuit.

That is, unless you just happen to have a micromanipulator and about 56 microprobes lying in your garage that you can use for chip bringup. In which case please do tell me if you ever need some help clearing out your garage, I have nothing planned that day.

Chip packages come in different forms, the most common being some kind of black plastic enclosures used not only to create accessible connections to the silicon but also for protecting the delicate die and the connections from the environmental damage caused by shocks, humidity and extreme temperature fluctuations.

The type of package we chose also affects how we architect the IO and thus what our silicon floorplan will look like. There are two big families of packages:

In the case of flip-chips the IO pin connections will be spread out regularly all over the floorplan leading to shorter logic to pin connections, and supporting a greater pin density and count. But on the flip side (put intended), flip chips packaging requires a lot more precision and is more expensive compared to …

Wire bonding works by conning your silicon to a pad in the package using a very thin fly wire made from gold or aluminium.

This is done by a wire bonding machine that will physically pull a wire from a IO landing pad on the silicon and connect it to a landing pad on the package. The silicon would be placed at the center of the package and would be connected to the pads placed all around it on the package, themselves connected to the larger exterior pads.

In this case the IO pad structures of the silicon would be located towards the exterior of the chip creating two distinct zones, the padring and the core region where most of the logic is located.

There are many sub-flavors of wire bonded packaging, and wafer.space decided to offer something called chip-on-board packaging (CoB), which is a bit different to how mass market chips are classically packaged but also much more cost effective for small scale fabrication.

For CoB the chip is not bonded out to an enclosed package, but rather, the connections are made directly to a PCB.

Once the chip has been bonded onto the PCB, a protective epoxy layer called a globtop is deposited and hardened on top of the silicon and the bonds. Some of you might have already noticed black blobs on commercial PCBs in the past, and without even realizing it you might have been looking at a CoB packaging.

But unlike the dull black glob tops, wafer.space has opted for the rarer beautifully transparent epoxy, allowing you to directly see the chip bonded though the package.

With your silicon bonded you now have what can officially be called a chip! 🥳

What wafer.space is selling : the possibility for anyone to make their own full prototype chip run for the price of an expensive vacation, is honestly revolutionary.

DARPA and google gave us the tools, Tiny Tapeout offered us a chance to sharpen our skills and wafer.space gave us direct access to manufacturing.

Once more, in the spirit of transparency, I was invited onto the shuttle for free, but this sentiment comes from a genuine belief, so much so that as soon as the following manufacturing run sales opened I put my money where my mouth is, and bought my slot outright.

Somehow this is still cheaper than flying back for Christmas.

If you are new here and this is your first time reading this blog, welcome.

For those for whom this isn’t our first rodeo: you might be wondering how full chips differ from what I have been doing so far ?

In previous episodes, I had been taping out my designs through Tiny Tapeout. Tiny Tapeout is a shuttle chip where multiple projects share the same chip, and in doing so share a common infrastructure. That infrastructure includes handling the silicon’s IO, the power and clock distribution as well as manufacturing and sticking the chip onto a functional development boards.

All important parts that I now get the luxury of handling on my own, which also means I also get the luxury of making all the mistakes!

But, after having gotten the chance to perfect my understanding and experience of the tapeout process through 9 prior Tiny Tapeout tapeouts this sounds the natural next step.

With Tiny Tapeout, you don’t control the number of pins, nor do you have a precise idea of the timing of the signals arriving from the chip’s pins to the pins of your macro. Additionally, even though you can buy extra tiles on Tiny Tapeout, the smallest quarter slot chip on wafer.space still gives you more core area than the largest configuration of Tiny Tapeout has to offer. And finally, Tiny Tapeout only gives you one chip per dev board, whereas with wafer.space you get a minimum order lot size of 1000 chips.

For the purposes of the networking chip project, the real game changer is having control over the pin architecture, meaning I can now decide both the number and the type of the pins.

Because I am comunicating with the PHY chip using an RMII interface, I care very much about pins as each Ethernet port interface requires 7 pins. This was also the reason why the initial version of the networking switch had only 3 ports: I only had 24 pins.

You can refer to the previous article Designing an Ethernet Switch ASIC for an explanation on why each port needs 7 pins and each pin is used for.

So now that I have a whopping 46 pins maximum to play with, we can get cooking!

Anatomically pins are analog blocks with a landing pad for the wire bonded wire on one end. These are included as part of the GlobalFoundries open source foundry provided IO cell library, and although all the pins share the same height, width and landing pad sizes, each features different analog layouts according to its functionality.

The most important types of pins for this design are the input pins, the bidirectional pins and the power delivery pins. Have fun playing spot the difference.

Interestingly, the standard library does not offer any pure output pins, so outputs are handled by bidirectional pins statically configured in output mode.

Looking at the floorplans provided above you might notice that these pins have no analog components directly under the landing pad, known as a “circuit under pad” design, making them a little less compact but more structurally resilient.

This is because these pins were originally designed to be compatible with a version of the GlobalFoundary 180nm process with only 3 metalization layers, but multiple levels of a metal structure must be present between the top metal layer where the pad is and the analog circuit beneath in order to help isolate it from the force applied to the pad of wedge bonding. During wedge bonding the bond is physically pressed in place requiring applying a lot of force to the silicon and potentially leading to breakages in the circuits underneath if sufficient structural support pillars aren’t present.

As discussed earlier, there are different families of packaging for chips resulting in different types of I/O design: flip-chips and wire bonding. Wire bonded chips such as mine have their pins facing the exterior of the chip organized in a structure called a pad ring. This is a ring surrounding the core area of the chip, connecting all the different I/O pads together. This ring is used both for noise isolation and to share power between all the different pins. Because the padring is an uninterrupted crown of pins the space between the pins is filled by very simple structures called filler cells used to close the power connections within the ring.

The IO also plays a crucial role in dealing with electrostatic discharge. (To whom many electronics have perished, including my little sister’s laptop that I may or may not have murdered while upgrading her ram when I was 15. 🪦 )

Each pin contains structures that will act as forward biased diodes in the event of an electrostatic discharge steering the charge though the power rails and protecting the sensitive core logic.

So we actually have four types of power delivery pins : two for ground and two for power.

The difference between the two groups is that one is used to provide power to the IO itself and the other is used to power the chip’s core logic.

Thus, it is possible to run the I/O and the internal design at different voltages. The areas for which a different power source is used is called a power domain. For example, the I/O could run at 5V, accepting 5V input signals and driving 5V outputs while internally the chip core runs the logic at 3.3V. In this case, we would have different pins for powering the I/O and for powering the internal core. But, in the case of this networking chip, core power is shorted to IO power and both are in the same power domains.

Such a setup is only made possible because the foundry provided 7 track standard cell library is, to put it mildly: rugged. The cell target operating range is between 1.62 and 5.5V voltage and -40 to 125C.

So shorting the IO and core voltage and deciding to run the entire thing at 5V is just an average Tuesday.

Example of a random timing report from another chip I am working on, with corners ranging from 3 to 5.5V and -40 to 125C. And again, this is still just a subset of all the corners there are: there are even more where this came from!

For reference, this is just a tiny bit unusual.

Most designs have separate power domains as modern nodes have cell libraries designed for much lower operating voltages in order to help reduce the area power density making cooling easier and to help optimize power consumption. In the case of leading edge nodes, internal logic targets operating voltages as low as 0.7 to 0.8 V. This forces having at least separate IO and core power domains, since your IO typically starts at 1.8V and above.

Yet, you sometimes need separate power domains even if they operate at the same voltage, such as cases where you want to isolate a sensitive analog block from the power supply noise caused by a quickly toggling digital part. You might even prolong this separation of an analog and digital power domains to the IO, in which case rather than having a fully connected padring working within the same power domain you would be splitting the padding into analog IO power and digital IO power.

Remember the filler cells I talked about earlier? Well there exists a special type of filler cell called a splitter used specially to split the pad ring in such cases. But, because of ESD concerns this splitter is not as simple as breaking the power line, but that is a discussion for another day.

The clock for this chip is supplied though a Schmitt trigger input pin and is strategically logged in the corner of the chip right next to the reset signal, and isolated from the rest of the pins by two power pins. This is done to limit the clock signal’s impact onto the neighboring pins given its toggle frequency, as well as to prevent the clock signal for the neighboring pins cross talk. The reset signal by comparison is a very stable signal producing little crosstalk of its own.

From this point on the clock signal is pulled into the center of the floorplan and then distributed through a balanced clock tree throughout the chip.

Such “shielding” is even more important in our case since we are doing wire bonding and we can also have cross talk between signals occurring between the fly wires, this would be less of a problem for a flip-chip package.

This is a different challenge compared to what I was doing with Tiny Tapeout as I now have access to two great resources: firstly, a lot more pins to play with, and secondly, a lot more space. Even if I target the smallest possible chip, I am still blessed with more area than I know what to do with.

Even before being invited to contribute I was already eyeing the wafer.space slots, so selecting the switch at the crown project of the ASIC was the easy choice.

The problem is that the switch was initially designed for the constraints of Tiny Tapeout. As such, not only does it have an odd architecture with only three ports, but it was designed to be as space efficient as possible. Here, space is something I am swimming in, but with only 96 hours ahead of me I have no time to redesign an entirely new switch from scratch. So the plan is to re-adapt the existing switch to make the best use of being its own chip.

The first and the most important change was to be able to make use of these abundant pins and have the switch to support more ports.

No longer shall I be constrained by my pin count! 🔥 w 🔥

… (Until I need more than 7 ports that is.)

Most of the verilog code you will see online tends to use hard coded widths like so :

What this code gains in ease of writing it loses in flexibility.

In RTL, we have a concept called parameters, which exist for an instance of a module and allow you to define, at instantiation, certain values. These values can then be used to size up buses or are macro like conditions to define which sections of the code should be included in the final hardware.

These generic values can then be inherited down the design hierarchy allowing dependent modules to be resized accordingly.

The original switch implementation was partially generic : it contained quite a few generic values, but these were mostly added out of habit to help clean up the design and keep things more readable, rather than truly making the design dimensions fully configurable.

The reason for not making the design fully generic was out of a calculated decision to shy away from as much unnecessary complexity as possible. The original design was facing the hard physical constraints of Tiny Tapeout pin count, so making it fully generic to support an arbitrary amount of ports would have been an unnecessary premature optimization, and most importantly cost complexity.

My grief against complexity comes from two calculated trade-offs.

First, I find it is orders of magnitude cheaper to add complexity than to remove it.

Secondly, complexity is especially expensive for hardware design because of the necessity to not have no have any bugs in the hardware. The only way of reaching this bug free state is through thought verification of operation under all possible scenarios. As we add complexity, we add hardware states such that the size of the space of states we need to explore grows exponentially.

Now I know exponential growth might sound like an exaggeration, after all exponential growth is so fast that it is hard for our brains to conceive, but I assure you I am not.

This problem is more formally called the “state explosion problem”.

So the biggest change in the switch was to move the number of supported ports from a static three to a generic number.

Even if the RTL scales, and I could theoretically run a simulation with 48 ports, the logic itself still has scaling limits. After all, behind the abstraction of the code we are designing hardware logic for which physical constraints still apply.

As the structures get wider, the number of logic elements on a path increases, the paths get physically longer and the timing degrades. And so, with \(1.73mm^2\) of core area available, timing is the wall I hit first.

Given the switch was already quite tight on timing, scaling it too far would push it beyond the limits of the current design requiring a rethink of the architecture. Rethink that I cannot afford to execute in so little time.

Lastly, I said I was scaling the number of ports, but because of how tight the timings are on the switch lookup table already was, it is not getting scaled up. And because it still only has four entries, and scaling beyond four ports would result in too much contention on the table and not enough hits, it would not make any sense to go beyond 4 ports for now.

Thus, I settled on four ports for the switch.

Given I now control the full ASICs layout I can also control exactly which signal maps to which pin on the padring.

Since the switch was intended to work with a specific Microchip family of external physical-layer chips, and that these chips had a known pinout, I decided to choose the pin order based on how directly I could draw the connecting wire onto the PCB.

One of the best drawbacks of the switch scaling limit was that I was left with a few pins and lots of area to play with.

And unlike with Tiny Tapeout where multiple projects share that same common infrastructure allowing only one project to be enabled at a time, this time I could have multiple designs working in parallel. And I had just the perfect project to include in parallel.

A few months back I did the two things the entire Internet knows not to do: firstly I asked Reddit for advice, secondly I followed it.

This project is called “Until Heat Death Do Us Part" and is a very serious implementation of an ethernet connected beacon that broadcasts its current time over 100 Mbit Ethernet with the ability to do so without overflow for the next \(10^{100}\) years. Also believed to be roughly the estimated heat death of the universe, give or take a few powers of 10 years.

Counting until the heat death of the universe, and broadcasting the counter every second over 100Mbps ethernet.

I have a full write-up about this ASIC’s here for those interested in getting the full story: Until Heat Death Do Us Part.

Putting it all together: this chip features two designs, the 4 port 100Mbps networking switch and the ethernet broadcast beacon. The networking switch is the denser design on the right hand side of the floorplan with the beacon being the on the left side, each designed placed next to there respective port pins.

It’s already been a few months since the chip has been sent to the fab. Since then the first batch of produced wafers have exited the fab and been received by the wafer.space.

Andrew Wingate shared with us some absolutely gorgeous pictures of the diced wafers, and there is my little chip in the flesh sitting on the top right corner of the reticle:

The dies are then picked off the diced wafer using a custom built robot and sorted per chip type into a tape reel. From there the chips will be either sent to the bond house for packaging or directly sent to the customer.

Your browser cannot play this video. Download video.

And now I am like a child waiting for Christmas, impaciently awaiting a package, inside the first batch of my own full custom ASIC chips.

Now, the chip doesn’t make a full networking equipment on its own, which is why I am also prototyping a PCB for the switch. Hopefully someday I can plug the chip in to get a fully functional switch.

Here is to hoping the first iteration of the silicon just works !

.. which anyone working in the industry can attest to, A0s are rare enough to be legendary.

Manufacturing revisions of a chip are identified by a letter followed by a number.

A0 is the first iteration, minor revision such as changing some of the higher metalization layers will increment the number and major revisions requiring a new mask set for the bottom layers, where the transistors are built, increment the letter and reset the number. So revisions might go: A0, A1, A2, B0, B1, B2, B3, C0, etc…

Meanwhile the networking equipment project continues, chasing after building increasingly complex systems. Without going too deep into which next networking features I want to add, it is becoming quickly apparent that I will need to integrate some form of a CPU.

This is because as I target more advanced networking applications the tasks my silicon needs to accomplish become increasingly varied and start featuring a large array of tasks that occur rarely enough, and have sufficiently lax performance requirements to be better suited for software than hardware.

As for the matter of which CPU architecture to choose, although RISC-V is in vogue I find that, as a result of RISC-V’s architectural choices, it is just too expensive to implement in terms of area for systems like mine.

My needs when selecting witch CPU architecture to use are:

If only gcc were to maintain something like the “Status of Supported Architectures from Maintainers’ Point of View” at https://gcc.gnu.org/backends.html then maybe I could know what my options where.

Behold: so many beautiful options supported that most people have never even heard of!

And within this list there is one 16 bit architecture that caught my eye, at the heart of one of the longest produced systems and deeply intertwined with computer history as it saw the first version of Unix written in C.

A year ago, I started on a journey to go from being solely a hardware designer to building an entire ASIC from scratch without any institutional backing.

It’s been a long road, passing though multiple smaller macro tapeouts, each allowing me to delve deeper into what it takes to make ASICs. This chip is my 10th solo tapeout, a fitting number to finally graduate into building full chips.

Standing upon this mountain I can tell you the road ahead is still very long.

And with my first batch of full custom ASICs landing into my mailbox in a few weeks a new risk has emergeded, leading me to proclaim a new goal: not starting a fabless semiconductor company.

Thanks again to wafer.space for giving me this opportunity to join the shuttle, Tiny Tapeout for making the 9 previous tapeouts possible and the open source silicon community for building the tools making all of this possible.

If you enjoyed this, I will be sipping coffee at a Silicon Valley neighborhood cafe between the 10th and 12th of November, so if you feel like nerding out over caffeine shoot me an email.

#9902. Critical security vulnerability affects OpenSSH on Alpine Linux systems

Version 10.6p2 of OpenSSH has been released with a workaround for a critical vulnerability that affects Linux systems that use musl libc with PAM disabled, such as Alpine Linux. OpenSSH developer Damien Miller said:

If you operate a Linux system that uses musl libc without PAM (Alpine Linux is one example) then stop reading and set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY.

This vulnerability does not exist on non-Linux systems, Linux/glibc systems and Linux systems that use PAM for password authentication.

We consider the root cause of this bug to be outside OpenSSH itself, but we're in a good position to deliver a mitigation quickly.

The Alpine Linux project has announced that it will be backporting the OpenSSH fix "all the way back to Alpine 3.16", which was released in May 2022.

It's starting to feel near impossible to keep up with all the urgent patching requirements these days though... (I mean in general, not Alpine specific.)

The name is *sshole. The vulnerability is so named because it relies on a string comparison between a "*" in /etc/shadow on one side and a "*" returned by a hashing function on the other side comparing equal, even though they should not compare equal. Additionally, the vulnerability is related to ssh, and it is a security hole. Hence, it is an *sshole. I agree with you: that was very well done.

Posted Nov 5, 2026 19:30 UTC (Thu) by Cyberax (✭ supporter ✭, #52523) [Link]

There are also a wide variety of intrusion detection systems that monitor ssh logs and lock out IP addresses and/or accounts that have too many consecutive login failures. Realistically, unless the password is particularly weak ("4") or has been leaked/compromised via some other mechanism, there's nothing inherently wrong with using ssh password authentication.

Realistically, unless the password is particularly weak ("4") or has been leaked/compromised via some other mechanism, there's nothing inherently wrong with using ssh password authentication.

There are certain scenarios that public key authentication protects against that password authentication doesn't. You have to decide for yourself whether those are relevant for you. Password authentication requires the user to transmit the password in a form that the server can decrypt. The server will know the cleartext password (even though it was encrypted in transit) and must know that to be able to verify it. (Even though in the server's user database it's stored in a hashed + salted form.) This means that if someone manages to successfully impersonate the server (e.g. via a compromise of the private key of the server, maybe because a system backup was available on a public S3 bucket, for example), they will obtain all the cleartext passwords from password authentication. With public key encryption this is not possible, even if the server is compromised it will not be able to learn the secret key. Now granted, that DOESN'T mean that password authentication is completely broken or something - it's NOT an automatic red flag to me - but we should acknowledge that it has some real drawbacks compared to e.g. public key authentication.

What are the drawbacks, other than it being less easily understood by non-technical users?

Posted Nov 7, 2026 2:35 UTC (Sat) by Cyberax (✭ supporter ✭, #52523) [Link]

Just off the top of my head, major problems include: a) Can't log into the system locally (be it text console or GUI environment) using a public+private key b) Restricts what systems you can log in _from_ -- any such systems need access to a copy of your private key c) In practice, most SSH keys are passphrase-less, used for *convenience* [1] rather than "passwords bad".
