#9892. What We Missed: Knicks Phishing Test Goes Out of Bounds

In this video conversation, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from an ill-conceived phishing simulation to a hacktivist attack on a US government agency.

Phishing tests can be an important part of cybersecurity awareness training. But as the NBA champion New York Knicks recently showed, they can also go awry.

According to a recent report in The Athletic, Madison Square Garden (MSG) Sports, which owns the Knicks, deployed a poorly timed and ill-conceived phishing simulation ahead of its banner-raising ceremony on Oct. 20. MSG Sports sent out emails to employees with offers of free championship rings commemorating the team's historic NBA Finals victory in June.

Team employees often receive championship rings at the start of the following season. However, the emails in this case were part of a phishing simulation, and when employees clicked on the links to select their rings, they were informed they failed the test and had to attend mandatory cybersecurity training. And they didn't get the rings, either.

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: a hacktivist group breached the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and published personnel records for more than 40,000 employees, and it's unclear how the agency was compromised; and a New York Times report claims a NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset.

Related:AI Gave Your Incident Archive a Second Job

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and, sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Rob Wright: Hi, I'm Rob Wright with Dark Reading.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

DR's Rob Wright: And this is "What We Missed." This is a discussion about some of the news stories that we didn't get a chance to cover in the pages, pods, and videos of Dark Reading. And Alex, first up, we've got a doozy.

DR's Rob Wright: So this one was pretty interesting, and in the spirit of Cybersecurity Awareness Month, I think it's extremely relevant. The story came out from The Athletic about a week and a half ago, two weeks now almost, that the NBA champion New York Knicks — credit to them, I'm a Celtics fan, I hate the Knicks but, you know, good for them, they won the championship last year — that employees from the team apparently got a phishing test email saying your employee championship ring is here and that they could choose, you know, from different types of championship rings no cost to the employees, and when the employees clicked on the link they were informed that they had failed a phishing test and that they would have to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

I just want to point out, before we discuss this, that the employees traditionally do get championship rings. And this story is made worse by the fact that apparently the owner, James Dolan, did not give out rings to a lot of employees. So that makes it extra worse. But Alex, what'd you think of this story?

DR's Alex Culafi: From just your description alone, I have two opinions. The first is, phishing tests should be appealing to click on, right? That's one thing.

DR's Alex Culafi: My other opinion is it shouldn't lean on the desperation of your employees or the economic or rewarding of your employees —

DR's Alex Culafi: Right, don't do a security test that highlights the idea that you might not be taking good care of your employees as well as you should.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, that they're not getting rings. Sad. All right. What else we got this week?

It contains records for roughly 41,000 DHS employees and contractors across agencies, including ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement], CBP [US Customs and Border Protection], USCIS [United States Citizenship and Immigration Services]. The attackers claim the data came from a DHS Okta-based identity system, which Okta currently denies or kind of denies; they said Okta is secure and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised. What is also interesting is that rather than denying that a breach occurred, the DHS said that it's looking into and doing incident response for what it calls a potential breach, which is — it's a little short of a full confirmation. NVIDIA, obviously huge right now, huge part of the AI industry, AI growth in the United States. And this story, this Times exclusive, basically charts how the US government found out that this executive, Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, but that this person was a Chinese asset. Pretty interesting, Alex, pretty interesting. And apparently Jensen Huang did not know this was happening at the time, that she was being surveilled. So it's a very thorny story. DR's Alex Culafi: This AI stuff is crazy.

These reports about OpenAI teaching employees not to be seduced, like humanly seduced in order to give up trade secrets.

DR's Rob Wright: Well, yeah, to your point about Google or OpenAI or — this was OpenAI, right?

DR's Alex Culafi: This was OpenAI, the Saudi stuff.

DR's Rob Wright: So there's that. There's physical security concerns here with infiltration of foreign agents, foreign assets trying to get in, steal trade secrets, steal intelligence, steal policy, developing policy moves and get ahead of them, etc.

I think the thing that's interesting here is that I know NVIDIA came out and said, this is normal. Like, he meets with a lot of CEOs and stuff like that. And there's nothing salacious in this story. It doesn't say that they had a romantic relationship or like intimate relationship of any kind. It just says close relationship.

But to me, if I were them — if I were NVIDIA, and if I were the US government — I would try to come out with a little bit more information about this to qualify, you know, what steps were taken to warn him, what steps were taken to, if any, to get ahead of this, to mitigate the threat, and to move away from this person who's been identified as a Chinese asset. #9890. Give Your Coding Agents a Memory You Own

I work across several machines, and I switch coding agents depending on the task. Every one of them meets my projects as a stranger. The reasoning from “last Tuesday” disappears when the session ends. Each new agent, on each new host, starts from zero.

Earlier this year, Software Forgets: Agent Traces Are the Memory made the case that coding agents already produce the record we keep losing. As they search a codebase, try approaches, hit errors, read documentation, and change direction, they leave behind a dense account of not just what changed, but why.

While the diagnosis is correct, traces are only potential memory. The session logs of an agent are still just an archive. You cannot grep your way to “why did we move off the streaming parser?” across ten thousand turns. For an agent to use those traces while it works, they need indexing, retrieval, ranking, and exact provenance.

That is what funes provides. It is a durable memory layer for your agents (Claude Code, Codex, pi, and Hermes). It is built from the sessions already on your machine. It works locally and becomes part of your agent's normal workflow with one command. When you want it to, it can also travel to a Hugging Face dataset you own, private by default.

funes is a single binary. Its default inference backend has no ML runtime dependency, and embedding and reranking happen on your machine. Install it:

That one add command builds the first index, gives the agent recall and get tools, and installs the automation that indexes each completed turn. Indexing is incremental, with new runs adding new turns rather than embedding the whole history again. The older and deeper content can backfill in bounded steps.

From there, you just work. When a task touches a past decision, rationale, or finding, the agent can reach for recall itself. You do not need to remember the old session or paste its context into the new one.

With funes added, recall happens inside the conversation. The agent reaches for its memory on its own and names the session behind its answer.

recall returns the original text, not a summary, and shows exactly where it came from (the agent, timestamp, session, and turn). Each result includes a get command that opens the full turn and its surrounding context.

Underneath, one deterministic pipeline parses every supported trace into the same turn-and-block shape, chunks it, embeds it with a pinned local model, and writes it to a local Lance dataset. A query combines vector and BM25 search, fuses their rankings, reranks the candidates with a cross-encoder, reweights them by recency, and attaches neighboring chunks.

That design gives funes three important properties:

The agent as a stranger problem is already solved on one machine. But memory gets more useful when the next agent is running somewhere else.

To make a memory follow your work, bind one when you add funes to an agent:

The bind publishes your current memory there. funes then keeps it current, indexing each turn locally and publishing at session boundaries. The agent recalls from it throughout. Run the same command on another machine and the memory follows you there.

Underneath, the local memory is a Lance dataset, and the shared memory is a Hugging Face dataset (private by default) you own.

Before anything reaches the Hub, credentials have already been redacted during indexing. Publishing then scans every chunk again and withholds anything that still looks like a secret. The scanner behind this is documented in SECURITY.md, including what it does and doesn't cover.

When an agent reads a remote memory, funes caches the dataset files locally, so warm queries return to local speed. The Hub supplies the ownership, access control, versioning, and distribution it already supplies for other datasets. Your memory does not become an account in a separate memory service, and you do not rent it back through an API.

recall is shaped for agents. When you want to put a question to a memory yourself, use ask. It reads your local memory by default:

Or point it at a shared memory. We published a memory of funes development, so you can ask why funes works the way it does without creating a memory of your own:

funes ask is the read-only, one-question sibling of funes add. It recalls the passages, hands them to a coding agent, and returns a grounded answer that names its sources. It does not install an integration or change the agent's persistent setup.

A retrieval miss is not papered over. If the passages do not support an answer, the agent says so. You can rephrase the question or add funes to the agent so it can search the memory iteratively during normal work.

A shared memory is not tied to the agent or model that created it. Start a task in Claude Code, continue it in Codex next week, and the second agent can recall the first agent's reasoning. Use pi with a local model or one served through the Hugging Face router, then return to Claude.

Claude makes a decision; a hook indexes it; Codex recalls it in another session. The older hits in the demo are earlier recordings of the same experiment: an append-only memory remembered the rehearsals too.

Published memories carry a dataset card and the funes tag, making them recognizable and discoverable on the Hub. The Hub already hosts open weights and datasets. funes adds open working memory. It holds the decisions, failed approaches, and rationale behind a project, queryable by another agent and traceable to the sessions that produced them.

A long investigation bloats a session until each turn costs more to carry the context than to do the work. The usual answers are to let the agent compact and carry on, or to write a handoff and start fresh. Recall is a third, so we measured them against each other on the handoff-vs-recall benchmark: two tasks whose answer cannot be reconstructed without the session prior knowledge.

Compaction is what most agents do by default, and it was the only one of the three whose result divided: it arrived on one task and never arrived on the other. Where it failed, its summary had flattened the findings that mattered. Recall returns the passages themselves, so a finding does not have to survive summarization.

Recall was the cheapest of the three on both tasks, 8x cheaper than a written handoff on one and 4x on the other.

The lighter segment of each bar is the one-time charge for preparing the channel, the handoff or the compaction, paid before the first question is asked and counted once. A cross marks a channel that never arrives, and so has no cost per success.

“To think is to forget differences, generalize, make abstractions.” — Jorge Luis Borges, Funes the Memorious

Your agents already wrote the record. funes lives at github.com/huggingface/funes, one command away from turning that record into a memory the next agent can read, on whichever machine you happen to be on.

funes invents little of this. It leans on open-source embedding models good enough to run locally, on Lance's append-only datasets with cheap incremental writes, and on the Hub's caching and content-dedup for datasets. The work is in fitting them into a memory an agent can actually use.

funes is open source too. Open an issue for anything from an install snag to a recall that missed, or an agent you'd like supported.

Ran funes 1.3.0 on a machine with 19,195 coding-agent sessions already on disk (LongMemEval laid down in the real ~/.claude and ~/.codex layouts), 100 questions whose answer sits in exactly one session, scored by whether that session comes back. Disclosure: I maintain deja-vu, one of the tools in the same table.

Full index: 2h03m on an M4 pro laptop (308k chunks), 6.3s per query. With defaults: hit@1 9/100, hit@5 39, found@50 71. With --half-life 0: 19/46/71 — the 30-day recency half-life halves rank-1 on history older than a month, which is most of what's on a real disk; worth a mention in the docs. Once recency is off, the vector+rerank stack is clearly the best ranker in the table at rank five. The documented one-minute first pass leaves 218 of the 19k sessions indexed (0/100 answered), so the "about a minute" framing is really "about a minute until the embedding job starts".

For comparison on the same corpus, deja-vu (plain BM25 over 24 agents' files) indexes in 29s and answers in 24ms at hit@1 18/100, hit@5 35. Corpus, drivers and every row: vshulcz.github.io/deja-vu/guide/day-zero.html - happy to be corrected if a setting I missed changes the numbers.

longmemeval does not really need semantic search: BM25 already gives the same ratio you mentioned IIRC, so for this use case this is pretty much expected that it is not worth paying the cost of evaluating the embeddings (this extra cost you see at indexing and recall time). funes shines when the information is actually difficult to find.

#9889. How Much Energy Does Building Distro Packages Use

When I set up the infrastructure for Casuarina Linux I repurposed an AMD AM4 system with RyzenÂ 9Â 5950X 16-Core CPU (105W TDP) and 32Gb of DDR4 RAM as the build server. I set it up in our laundry, connected it via a smart plug, and reset its counters. Over the course of the project I would regularly pull package updates from Chimera Linux, build and install them locally, and then push them to the repo, which would trigger Buildbot to build and publish them.

You can select a different currency, which will use exchange rates from the time of writing.

The project ran from 30 March 2026 to 8 November 2026 (a bit over 7 months) the total energy used was 98.4 kWh. My electricity plan is a 100% renewable plan (meaning they offset the non-renewable parts) and costs AU$0.33 kWh. Ignoring the daily service fee the cost of that electricity is AU$32.47 .

Since it turned out I was the only one doing package updates I kept the builder off when idle. When there were packages to build Iâd hit the power button (on the machine, not the smart plug) and some time later when it was done Iâd press it again to shut it down. This was pretty beneficial as the idle draw was about 55W.

The number of package builds was around 5000. SELECT COUNT(name) FROM logs WHERE name LIKE 'pkg:%'; from the Buildbot state.sqlite yields 5201, however thatâs probably slightly inflated due to rebuilds/packages that failed to build on the first try.

The actual usage is likely more than double the 98kWh figure as all packages were built on my desktop machine first, before pushing to the repository for the builder to pick up. That machine is an AM5 system with AMD Ryzen 9 9950X3D 16-Core CPU (170W TDP), 64Gb DDR5 RAM. Additionally our house has rooftop solar, and where possible I would kick off builds during the day so there was a better chance of using the solar. That would have reduced the actual cost, but I have no way to measure the specific amount.

The slowest package by far to build was Chromium, taking just shy of 4 hours to complete. For comparison Firefox takes about 50 minutes. Power draw measured by the smart plug when the builder was fully loaded is about 193W. So 4 hours at 193W is 0.77kWh, which means a Chromium build costs about 25 cents.

Overall it cost a bit under AU$5 a month (ignoring solar, and my workstation) to build all the packages for a Linux distribution. Thatâs not too bad I think.

I also publish new posts as emails in my newsletter.

#9888. Seven stable kernels with fixes for three Xen vulnerabilities

Hot on the heels of the previous two stable kernels, Greg Kroah-Hartman has announced the release of the 7.3.3, 6.18.62, 6.12.116, 6.6.162, 6.1.192, 5.15.225, and 5.10.274 stable kernels. Each one only contains fixes for three use-after-free vulnerabilities announced today by the Xen security team.

Two of the vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to cause a denial of service (DoS) for the entire Xen host machine with possible information leakage (CVE-2026-100080, CVE-2026-100082), and one may allow privilege escalation as well as a DoS of the host machine (CVE-2026-100081). Users should, of course, upgrade if they are using Xen.

InfoQ Homepage Podcasts Distributed LLM Inference on Kubernetes with llm-d, Wasm, & TornadoVM

In this episode, Edoardo Vacchi discusses the evolving landscape of WebAssembly on the backend, running Java workloads on GPUs using TornadoVM, and optimizing distributed AI inference using llm-d and vLLM on Kubernetes. Edoardo explains how llm-d manages cache locality (KV and prefix caches), request routing, and batch inference across Kubernetes clusters to maximize expensive GPU utilization.

December 15–16, 2026. Examine how senior practitioners run agents, evals, model serving, and AI-assisted engineering in production, including what failed and what changed. Register Now.

The other one is Andrea Peruffo. Eduardo worked for a long period of time in the WebAssembly ecosystem, he did some spotting around other types of VMs, and today he's back at Red Hat and he's trying to make things easier in terms of Kubernetes and inference. Edoardo Vacchi: Right. So, for the benefit of our audience, I don't know how much all of them are familiar with it, but you will know that Wasm was born for web browsers, but more recently, and by recently now it means a few years, people were also interested in running it outside the browser, and for the backend specifically. So, running software on Wasm. And in that sense, it could be seen as a sort of a similar thing to the JVM in spirit. And that's why I guess some of us that were working on the JVM were interested in working on Wasm as well. So, Wasm has changed fast in some senses, it evolved quickly in some senses, it evolved just slowly in others. So, there's been a lot of discussion around the component model, which is this new modular system that's built around WebAssembly. That is probably where a lot of the development happens these days, I'd say.

But I'd say that the space for WebAssembly on the backend has changed a lot in the last few years. I think that all of our development landscape has changed. So, things have shifted a little bit. I think it's very meaningful and relevant today, even more possibly than it was when there was much more hype, because it has a lot to do with sandboxing. And as you know, sandboxing is all the rage these days.

Olimpiu Pop: One good scoring point for WebAssembly was earlier this year I was talking to the local first community, and what was interesting was that they were mentioning that one of the libraries they built, the name is eluding me now, but what they said is that rather than just thinking about providing implementation in different programming languages, they built it in Rust, and that meant that they can just compile it to WebAssembly and then use it via WebAssembly to different programming languages. And that was the nice part from their side, and they were quite happy with the result. And I think that's where the power of WebAssembly comes. Or I think the previous year I spoke to a couple of guys that used to work on infrastructure and they spoke about Firecracker. And what was nice, is that they said that most often than not, the harder that you have in the server acts is idle.

So, what they did on top of those idle space, they just had very small WebAssembly machines... Well, containers, I think it's a better wording for that. That was doing very small things that were quite useful for other people. So, I feel that there are all those different scenarios where people are using WebAssembly.

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. I think one interesting aspect that connects to what you were saying right now is even migrating workloads somehow, like running stuff in the browser, but then you also have these WebAssembly run times that can run, even on devices or in general outside the browser, and you have the same workload that runs on your browser, and we have demos of things that are migrated, even live migrated, from the browser to an end user device without breakage. That's really fascinating. And I think these days when we talk about agentic workloads, that's an interesting space. That's where I think Wasm is still relevant. I mean, Wasm is still relevant, especially for browser related work, and many other, but these scenarios for the word that's changing a lot these days for developers, those are the use cases with really good shine.

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. As you mentioned, isolation is important and is getting more and more important these days. So, I think that's quite useful. What is bugging me for at least one week now, and probably I'll try it the following week, let's see what you are going to say to that, I'm just thinking to run a small language model inside the WebAssembly in a browser, is that feasible? Is not feasible?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes, I mean it is feasible, there are examples of that. The thing is, I've been on the receiving end of this question a few times now, so it depends is the short answer.

Edoardo Vacchi: WebAssembly is meant to run on the CPU first. And as we know, we can do inference on the CPU, but generally it works much better. And for the way LLMs, modern LLMs, I mean, the modern architectures for LLMs are designed, they are meant to be run with highly parallel architectures. And the CPU is parallel, but not as parallel as a GPU. So, long story short, smaller models, which basically make sense to run in a browser, for instance, do make sense to run in WebAssembly, much bigger workloads... Well, those in general, we probably want to run on a GPU anyway. However, there are experiments that I'm aware of to translate WebAssembly into GPU kernels.

So, yes, possibly. But the short version of it is for all those workloads that are meaningful to run on a CPU, so relatively small language models, Wasm can be used, and there are many versions of these workloads that exist. I think that Hugging Face for some of the smallest models will run them on your browser, I think. And there are a few examples, on the Wasm I/O conference, there were quite a few talks of people showing this, running these workloads in the browser especially to do inference. So, yes, it does work, it depends on your workload. TornadoVM: Translating Java Code to GPU Kernels [08:26]

Olimpiu Pop: Yes. Well, I'm going to say it anyway, it's simple, it's more about just trying and seeing how things evolved, and fingers crossed that something will happen and not just smoke. But in order to work and consolidate the point that I stated about an expert into putting boxes into boxes, you had the posts, I think last year or the previous year, about TornadoVM. I know that you just had a small exposure to it, so maybe just have a short summary what's TornadoVM and when should we use it?

Edoardo Vacchi: Yes. So, TornadoVM is, we could say a flavor of the JVM or an add-on, a plug into the JVM, depends on how you see it. TornadoVM allows you to run Java code essentially on the GPU. This is the bottom line, the selling point, the very short version of it. It's a little bit more nuanced than that. But yes, basically you can, speaking of boxes inside boxes, yes. It's called the VM because it allows you to translate on the fly your Java code, and compile it on the fly into GPU-specific kernels. So, PTX for NVIDIA, SPEAR-V, whatever. And it handles for you this translation. So, you can basically write Java code and then it will translate for GPU backend. Now, the code that you write there, it is Java code, but you have to write the code in a specific way. You might have to use some libraries that TornadoVM provides you.

You cannot run basically any code... You won't be able to run Spring on TornadoVM. I mean, yes, but it will run in Java mode. You won't run Spring on the GPU, that's the point. But yes, you can write GPU kernels using Java, and that's the beauty of it. And the blog post you were referring to, I think it was last year's, I'm walking through the reader... One of the examples in the code, I think there is an example of writing a simple kernel and running on the GPU, that's one thing that we show in the blog. But then we run GPU Llama 3, which is an implementation of the Llama 3 model that runs on GPU. And this implementation is completely written in Java. So, that's fascinating. The blog post walks you through how this works.

In the latest DevOps Belgium, if people want to catch up a little bit, they had demonstrated, I think there was definitely a talk about TornadoVM, there were talks from the GraalVM team of the similar projects to run Llama and other language models using GraalVM that will do the acceleration for you, and then there was also former GraalVM team member that spun off his own startup. I think his name is Alfonso Alfonso, I remember it because his nickname is Alfonso Squared. And he started his own startup branching off some work that he did originally in GraalVM, again to run Java code, I think, on the GPU and LLM.

So, yes, fascinating stuff. And so, bottom line, the reason why I started to look into this is fan of boxes inside boxes, fan of languages and compilers, so it felt like a natural evolution of the things that I did in the past, including compilation to WebAssembly to learn about compilation to the GPU.

Olimpiu Pop: That sounds quite interesting, and it definitely makes sense these days. For instance, I saw that a lot of the big companies are just using Java for inference, and that makes perfect sense to just have this closing the loop. Today, you are part of the team at Red Hat, back again at Red Hat, that is working on llm-d. And in my understanding, what llm-d is, taking a step back, if VLLM is making sure that everything runs perfectly on one box, llm-d is trying to make sure that everything is efficient if you have a Kubernetes cluster. Is that a correct affirmation or did I understand wrong?

Edoardo Vacchi: No, no, it is correct on a high level. More specifically, so VLLM is our inference engine. So, you can think of it, if you will, as the JVM of language models. So, it has support for several language models, there's an interesting aside here, it is a platform to run LLMs. The interesting aside here is you would expect that this is a general sort of VM, and the LLMs are sort of software that you load on top of it. But unfortunately every LLM architecture is slightly different. So, VLLM has to basically include the implementation of every LLM that gets released. So, when people release LLMs, they do not release the software to run them, they release the weights. So, all of these inference engines, such as VLLM, what they do is implementing basically the software, the kernels, the components that actually load the weights and then actually do the inference.

So, VLLM is our platform to run the core and effectively VLLM is able to serve, it's a server... I mean, it's an inference engine, it's also server that exposes endpoints that you can call to do inference, and it does so efficiently. It was originally VLLM, I think the V in VLLM originally stands for virtual, as in virtual memory allocation. Because it was the first engine to implement page detention, basically a mechanism inspired by good old systems programming to do paging of memory, memory pages, but for memory that gets allocated on GPU, this is in a very high level way. So, VLLM is able to do high throughput inference. So, you can do several requests at once and VLLM will pack them and try to serve them together, and do inference in one pass for several requests at one time, this is called continuous batching. But this gets you to a point.

Essentially, at some point you have your GPUs on your machine, and your inference engine and that's it. You will not be able to scale further than the resources that you have on that machine. So, how do you scale further? Well, you can scale by having more VLLM instances, right? So, you have several VLLM instances and you want to serve your inference requests using these few VLLM, these few VLLM instances that you have. Now, you have another problem. How do you route requests across your VLLM instances? So, if you are on Kubernetes, what you will do... And most people are on Kubernetes these days, it's the standard for platforms for serving services in an efficient way. So, you can scale your VLLM instances and have several VLLM instances that serve the possible the same request... I mean that gets selected by the scheduler, by the VLLM scheduler.

If you do it the traditional way and let the Kubernetes normal router to pick across the VLLM instances that you have replicated, you won't get necessarily good performance. The reason is inference does not behave like a traditional service, a traditional HTP service. Basically, if you send a request to one specific VLLM instance, especially if you are doing conversation, if you're doing a chat and if you're doing agentic coding, it's still a chat basically. There's a lot of exchanges back and forth between you and your server, between your agent and your server. You want to stick for as much time as possible to the same VLLM instance. This might be counterintuitive in a way because for microservices, we know we don't want to hammer the same service on and on because otherwise it will get overloaded. We want to do sort of round robbing or random robbing across the replicas.

But the thing is microservices or service in general, these are usually in a way stateless. The state is usually stored somewhere else and it's not part of your request. I mean, the request can be served independently by any instance. Unfortunately for LLMs, in order for LLMs to do their inference in an efficient way, you want to stick for as much time as possible to the same instance. But at the same time, you cannot stick forever to the same instance because at some point you will reach some limit. You are not the only user of that VLLM instance. You want to serve and distribute the load across your VLLM instances. So there's a balance that you have to strike between staying with the same instance and benefit of the caches, the KV caches, the prefix caches that are in place, the systems that allow you to do inference in an efficient way and lower costs.

But at the same time, you don't want to overload the same instance too much. So you also have to keep this into account. This is not the job for a traditional Kubernetes schedule. And that's where llm-d comes into place. That's what llm-d does. llm-d is not just a router or a scheduler. It's actually a family of projects and they are all meant to give you a set of tools to do distributed inference so that you can leverage all of the GPUs that you have and use it at their maximum as much as possible so you get the best value, the best bang for your bucks because these hardware is expensive whether you loan it or you own it. So you want to use it 100% as much as possible. And that's why we provide scheduler. We have something that we're going to release. I mean, in the open source ecosystem, it's already been released.

We're going to release also as part of product of Red Hat. This is called batch inference. Batch inference is using your cluster even when it's under load. #9886. Fine-tuning a 350M Model for Better Structured Outputs in 100 GRPO Steps

This guide is a fully public, inexpensive recipe for making a small model substantially better at structured-output compliance. We fine-tune LFM2.5-350M with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) using the TRL library and evaluate it on the IFStruct benchmark. The full run takes around 500 samples and 100 training steps, small enough for a free-tier Colab or Kaggle GPU, and is available on GitHub. The results show that even a light fine-tuning procedure improves performance from 22.6% to 29.7% on the IFStruct benchmark.

Structured output is one of the most common real-world tasks for LLMs, yet most benchmarks fold it into broader reasoning or extraction scores rather than measuring it on its own. Whether a model reliably returns valid, parseable output in the requested format and shape — schema compliance — is often what decides whether it can be wired into a downstream system at all.

Note that the training pipeline described here is not the one used to train the RL model described in the IFStruct blog. This notebook doesn't aim to recreate the IFStruct benchmark score, but to show how task-specific fine-tuning of smaller models can improve performance and match that of far larger models.

This guide has two halves that run in different places:

We will need uv for the Python tooling and llama.cpp for serving. Following the Liquid AI llama.cpp deployment docs, install llama.cpp with Homebrew and verify that llama-server is available:

Before we begin, let's evaluate LFM2.5-350M on the IFStruct benchmark and see whether we can reproduce the reported score of 21.1%.

IFStruct is a benchmark for testing the validity of LLM outputs and schema adherence. The benchmark is open-source in Liquid4All/ifstruct, with the public benchmark dataset available on Hugging Face at LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0.

For the eval comparison, we serve the model locally on the MacBook with llama.cpp. We will use the BF16 GGUF (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M-GGUF).

Then we start the base-model server with the following command:

Once the server is running, we can run the full benchmark with 2000 samples:

The IFStruct release blog reports 21.1% for LFM2.5-350M. Our local llama.cpp/BF16 setup measures 22.6%, close to the 21.1% reported in the IFStruct blog. We use this local result as the baseline for the same serving stack comparison.

The full, runnable pipeline lives in the accompanying notebook. We will cover only the relevant pieces in this section.

We use nvidia/Nemotron-RL-instruction_following-structured_outputs, which pairs each prompt with a target JSON Schema and an expected field count. We use about 500 samples for training.

Because the Nemotron data distribution differs from the IFStruct evaluation, we augment the prompts to close two gaps between them:

We load LiquidAI/LFM2.5-350M and attach a LoRA adapter. Because LFM2.5 uses a hybrid attention/convolution architecture, we target the LFM-specific module names:

This trains ~6M parameters, about 1.66% of the model.

Then we define three reward functions, each on a [0, 1] scale, which score every completion on whether the extracted structure is correct:

We combine the three as a weighted sum with reward_weights=[1.0, 0.5, 2.0].

We train for 100 steps with 8 generations per prompt group, sized for a free-tier 16 GB GPU:

As you can see in the notebook, over the run, all three reward components climb, the KL from the reference model lifts off zero after warmup, and the truncated-completion fraction stays near zero.

Finally, we merge the LoRA adapter back into the base weights and save it as a single self-contained checkpoint, ready to convert to GGUF for serving:

After GRPO fine-tuning, we rerun the IFStruct evaluation. For this, we need to convert the merged model checkpoint into a BF16 GGUF. The converter script ships with the llama.cpp source, so we clone the repo once and install the converter's gguf package.

Then we serve the merged model with the following command:

Then, we will run the full IFStruct evaluation again with the fine-tuned model:

Comparing the two runs on the identical serving stack:

The gains land exactly where the training aimed: the JSON pass rate rises by nearly 14 points (18.0% → 31.9%), while YAML stays mostly the same. While this is still below the Qwen3.5-2B score of 33.15%, it shows that even light task-specific fine-tuning can bring a small model close to a larger one.

A short GRPO run with about 500 samples and 100 steps can lift a small 350M parameter model from 22.6% to 29.7% on IFStruct. The takeaway is that a cheap, task-specific reward signal can make a small model substantially more reliable about form, closing much of the gap to models several times its size.

To reproduce or extend this work, see the original IFStruct v1.0 blog post, the Liquid4All/ifstruct benchmark repo, and the LiquidAI/ifstruct-v1.0 dataset.

#9885. [$] Locking down hibernation for the winter

When a computer hibernates, the kernel writes the contents of memory to disk and then shuts the system down. Resuming from hibernation involves reading that data back into memory, and then having the kernel pick up where it left off. Unfortunately, the kernel does not have any way to know that the data it is reading back has not been tampered with, which is why lockdown, an optional kernel feature that attempts to prevent modifications to the running kernel, disables hibernation. Matthew Garrett, who has been working on lockdown for many years, has shared a patch set that aims to fix this problem. His solution must also protect against downgrade attacks (where an attacker reboots the computer with an older kernel version to bypass new protections), which complicates the implementation.

#9884. NeoMME: an efficient Multimodal-native and Multilingual Encoder

We introduce NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M multilingual multimodal encoders. Unlike many generative visual language models, NeoMME does not use a separate pretrained vision tower or a causal language model. A single bidirectional Transformer processes both text tokens and raw image patches, and we train the entire model from scratch with a masked discrete-diffusion objective.

We fine-tuned NeoMME for visual document retrieval using ColPali's page-image approach. NeoMME-Retriever returns dense and late-interaction embeddings in one forward pass. Both model sizes lie on the ViDoRe v3 Pareto frontier for nDCG@10 and model size. At a matched 2048×2048 image input size on an NVIDIA L40S GPU, the 260M model encodes about 51 pages per second, or about twice ColModernVBERT's throughput. Hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization reduce late-interaction index storage from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page (255× smaller) while retaining more than 95% of baseline nDCG@10.

NeoMME is available in Hugging Face Transformers. We release all model checkpoints under the Apache 2.0 license.

Many recent visual document retrievers are adapted from pretrained generative visual language models. A separately pretrained vision encoder produces visual features, which a projector maps into the language model's input space. A causal decoder then processes the combined image and text representations. Retrieval, classification, and token labeling do not generate text autoregressively, so they do not require a causal decoder or the parameter and compute overhead of this architecture.

ModernBERT brought efficient architecture and training improvements to bidirectional encoders. For visual document retrieval, ModernVBERT applied a bidirectional ModernBERT-style text encoder while retaining a separate pretrained SigLIP2 vision tower. We wanted to push this even further by designing and training a multimodal encoder without having to carry over the parameter and compute overhead of a VLM.

NeoMME (pronounced "nee-oh-me", IPA /ˈniː.oʊ.mi/) is a multilingual, multimodal foundation encoder that generates vector representations for input text and/or images using a single Transformer encoder. It is not based on an existing pretrained vision tower, text encoder, or text decoder.

Images and text use the same computational path, so NeoMME can more easily support pretraining, fine-tuning, parallelization, and serving across both modalities.

NeoMME comes in two sizes, 260M and 800M. Both variants share the same architecture:

We pretrain NeoMME from scratch as a discrete masked-diffusion text denoiser. For each text-only example, we sample a corruption rate uniformly between 0 and 1. Each eligible text token is then independently masked at that rate.

Multimodal examples use corruption rates between 0.3 and 1. The image patches remain visible while NeoMME reconstructs masked text. With light masking, the model can often recover a missing word from the surrounding text alone. For example, "cat" is a plausible completion of "The [MASK] sat on the mat," even without an image. But high masking forces the model to learn image-grounded descriptions with little to no signal from the non-masked input text tokens.

Pretraining mixes multilingual text, code, mathematics, natural images, and document images. Each model processes about 524 billion packed input tokens, including 290 billion tokens from text-only examples. This text budget is relatively small compared with ModernBERT's 2 trillion training token budget. Hence, we chose the NorMuon optimizer to improve data efficiency during training.

To get a meaningful downstream evaluation of the backbone, we fine-tune NeoMME for visual document retrieval using the page-image methodology introduced by ColPali. While traditional text-based retrieval consists of retrieving text chunks, NeoMME-Retriever ranks document page screenshots and bypasses all the preprocessing OCR steps necessary to extract text from PDFs. Treating the pages as images preserves layout, charts, tables, font type and size, and other visual clues that cannot be captured even by a perfect OCR model.

NeoMME-Retriever reuses the NeoMME backbone but adds two jointly trained heads on top of it for retrieval:

Omar Khattab, who introduced late-interaction in ColBERT, explains why the term is more precise than "multi-vector." It describes the granularity and learnability of the scoring function, not simply the number of stored vectors.

To learn more about late-interaction, we recommend reading this crash course by Amélie Chatelain.

One NeoMME-Retriever forward pass returns both representations, which gives you flexibility no matter your use case and infrastructure. We recommend using late-interaction embeddings in general since they are more powerful and can be used easily with open-source libraries like NextPlaid. However, if you have a very large corpora, you can run a single forward pass with NeoMME-Retriever to get the dense embedding, retrieve a small number of documents through an ANN index, and then use late-interaction to rerank the retrieved candidates.

We report nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3. NeoMME-Retriever-260M reaches 0.523, the highest score among evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters. It is within 0.002 nDCG@10 of ColQwen2.5 while using about 14× fewer parameters. NeoMME-Retriever-800M reaches 0.556, within 0.009 nDCG@10 of the similarly sized Vultron Retriever Flash (0.8B). Both NeoMME-Retriever models lie on the model-size Pareto frontier.

ViDoRe v1 and v2 use nDCG@5. On both benchmarks, NeoMME-Retriever-260M outperforms ColModernVBERT and the twice-larger ColSmol-500M. NeoMME-Retriever-800M outperforms ColPali v1.3 while using 3.6 times fewer parameters.

† Scores from MTEB. ‡ Results from our own evaluations.

Late-interaction storage scales linearly with the number of vectors in the output embedding. Higher-resolution images contain more patches, so they produce larger embeddings. For example, a 2048×2048 square page produces embeddings containing 4,200 vectors with NeoMME-Retriever, or about 2.1 MB in float32. Across the ViDoRe v3 benchmark, the measured average is about 1.5 MB per document.

To reduce the storage footprint of the late-interaction index, we combine two complementary compression methods:

We tested this setup on ViDoRe v3. With a pooling factor 10 and int8 queries and documents, storage decreased from about 1.5 MB to 39 kB per page, a 39× reduction, while keeping more than 99% of the baseline nDCG@10. A more aggressive configuration uses pooling factor 8, int8 queries, and binary documents. That version uses 6 kB per page (255× smaller) and keeps more than 95% of the original retrieval quality.

Users can pick a compression setting from that frontier based on storage budget and required retrieval quality.

Before you can search a corpus, a retriever model must turn your documents into embeddings, which will be stored in a vector store like Qdrant, Weaviate, or Milvus. Faster encoding makes building and adding new documents to the index faster, thus reducing the GPU uptime and compute cost required.

So we measured image encoding speeds for NeoMME-Retriever against other multimodal document retrievers. We used preprocessed image tensors and calibrated the batch size separately for each model and image size. At a matched 2048×2048 input size on one NVIDIA L40S, NeoMME-Retriever-260M encodes about 51 pages per second, nearly twice ColModernVBERT's 26 pages per second. Both 260M and 800M NeoMME-Retriever models are also faster than the other models we compared on smaller input images.

NeoMME-Retriever (260M and 800M) returns dense and multi-vector embeddings together. The example below scores two text queries against two document-page images with MeanMaxSim late interaction and dense cosine similarity.

We provide separate dense and late-interaction checkpoints for fine-tuning with Sentence Transformers v6. Following the same pattern as text encoders such as ModernBERT, Sentence Transformers loads the backbone through NeoMMEModel rather than the dual-head NeoMMEForRetrieval class. Sentence Transformers currently supports one retrieval head per model, so each checkpoint lets you fine-tune the dense or late-interaction head independently. To train both heads together, use NeoMMEForRetrieval with a custom Trainer.

Visual document retrieval can be used as the first stage of a visual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system. Unlike text RAG, which retrieves extracted text chunks, visual RAG retrieves the original page images and sends them to a visual language model. The model can then use tables, plots, diagrams, and page layout that text extraction may flatten or omit. Here is how visual RAG works:

You can test visual RAG directly with NeoMME-Retriever in our HF Space: 🤗 tonywu71/neomme-retriever-demo.

NeoMME replaces separate pretrained image and text encoders with one long-context bidirectional Transformer. We train it from scratch to process both multilingual text tokens and raw 32×32 image patches.

NeoMME-Retriever is a fine-tuned version of NeoMME for visual document retrieval. One forward pass produces both dense and late-interaction representations. The 260M model outperforms all evaluated models strictly below 800M parameters and, at a matched 2048×2048 input size, encodes pages at about 2× ColModernVBERT's throughput. To reduce the large storage footprint of late-interaction embeddings for high-resolution documents, we experimented with hierarchical token pooling and asymmetric quantization and managed to reduce the late-interaction embeddings from roughly 1.5 MB to 6 kB per page, a 255× compression, while retaining more than 95% of the baseline nDCG@10.

We release all NeoMME model checkpoints and a day-zero Hugging Face Transformers implementation to allow practitioners to build efficient multimodal and multilingual representation models on top of our work.

NeoMME began as a side quest between two good friends. We worked with limited time and compute, and we decided to share the results so the community can build on them. We thank H Company for supporting the work and providing the compute used to train NeoMME.

Posted Nov 7, 2026 9:43 UTC (Sat) by alspnost (guest, #2763) [Link] (18 responses)

Quoting from the article: > Package-based OSes generally provide the user with a large number of regularly updated software packages (many thousands) with complex dependencies, which are composed into a working OS on the final machine it is deployed on. Installations in this style tend to vary greatly from system to system. Even with an identical selection of packages for the target system, the installation/update order, the stateful update logic and the file system data structures generally mean that the bytes that hit the disk on each machine are always different. This is called drift. > Systems put together this way are hence not reproducible, not predictable, and hard to compare and analyze which is essential for tracking down security issues. The second paragraph does not logically follow from the first paragraph. It is just a complete non-sequitur, but the word "hence" suggests otherwise. Systems put together this way can be reproducible, predictable, easy to compare and analyze. Side note: with ASLR, in-memory layout is not predictable, but only very few people complain about that and image-based OS don't make ASLR predictable either. There also is little conceptual difference between a flattened view of layered file system images for an image-based OS or a pre-flattened file system image for a package-based OS, just the time of flattening differs. One could even make a case that creating a flattened view of multiple file system layers at runtime is less reproducible than having a pre-flattened file system which is identical on every boot (at least in the read-only case). OTOH, maybe the Amutable people really have a hard time comparing and analyzing systems with package-based OSes. In that case, maybe their own solution is the only one they can easily work with, and hey... it is valid to create a system they can understand. That's the beauty of FOSS. I just wish they wouldn't bash choices different from their own.

By the time you start an upgrade and by the time it's actually done globally, there very well could have been a package update that came in at the end which the beginning ones did not receive. Many times, it's immaterial, yes -- distributions have done a great job at versioning and keeping non-breaking changes out of versioned releases, but it's a variance nonetheless. Not only packages, but even config changes within a fleets config management system can flow changes into it that the first round didn't, as changes get picked up. Often we don't have the convenience of downtime when managing baremetal systems, which something like Kubernetes abstracted away, but something still has to run baremetal. Amutable's core idea itself is not new, image-based and immutable cores have been around for a long time. What I find most interesting about their approach is the comprehensive approach they are taking with it, from offering a control plane and verification across the entire stack. I've seen these ideas employed in production individually, but am interested to see where they take it when it's coming entirely from the ground up.

Amutable's core idea itself is not new, image-based and immutable cores have been around for a long time. What I find most interesting about their approach is the comprehensive approach they are taking with it, from offering a control plane and verification across the entire stack. I've seen these ideas employed in production individually, but am interested to see where they take it when it's coming entirely from the ground up.

That said, if you have a configuration and package management which is idempotent, the suffering is not too bad. Debian with Saltstack is one such combination, but others exist as well. It helps to think of an image as a giant package where you have to update everything at once. Suddenly, the magic of images disappears. Additionally, there is no difference between a file system image and an archive. Case in point: The original Microsoft Word .doc files are more or less FAT file systems in a file. Another case in point: initramfs is a file system image which happens to use the cpio archive format as file system.

Now, of course, image-based solutions themselves aren't without their caveats either. You can't easily just pick any host in the fleet and then hand-modify it for the purposes of testing "just this one thing" while facing production traffic in a production environment. Which yes is a bad practice, but sometimes in an outage all-hands-on-deck scenario, having that flexibility is what saves hours of downtime. Image-based solutions, you have to run a whole CI to spit out a new image with your bumped version, then deploy it. Compared with SaltStack, you can run the state everywhere or even cmd.run it if the urgency calls for it and the change is small enough. But I think those are solvable problems and I think there's a middle-ground to be achieved there. For now, we remain primarily a SaltStack + package management fleet, but I am interested to see more ideas in this field when it comes to addressing systems management at this scale.

I suppose that's why Amutable has these sysext/confext overlays. Just build an image with the package(s) you want to replace and boot the node with it on top.

Debuggability requirements tell me that there should be a way to do this without rebooting. I need a way to actually interact with a misbehaving system.

There are ways around this. For example, /etc can be made read-write, it's just not persistent across reboots. It's more of a pain if you want to install new packages, but in our case we have docker installed so plugins can be added. In that case you can build a docker image with the software you want, and then run the image with sufficient permissions to use the software in the way you want. Image based distributions mostly offer: (a) reboot goes back to known state each time, (b) updates cost fixed amount of time no matter the changes (reboot), (c) you know every system is running the same bits as you tested in your test environment. Amutable appears to offer this plus a whole signing mechanism to prove it's not tampered with, but that's not relevant in our case.

So hosts have to be updated at different times and subsequently inevitably see different package repositories during time-of-update. This in turn means that different hosts go through different upgrade paths now; and even if this is mostly not relevant for a well-managed stable distro, it is not really reproducible anymore. With image-based approaches you don’t have this problem; there are only two possible system states now: image X before update, and image Y after update – no matter if you have five or five hundreds of hosts, no matter if some hosts have been setup yesterday or last year. This is just tremendously more well-defined. I mean, for most operators this is not super relevant, because usually nothing happens; and most deployments are in such a bad shape that this is really not a concern for them. On the other hand, drift like this can be relevant IRL. I know, for example, that my previous employee got bitten by that once: Quite some years ago, something in some default configuration changed on Ubuntu – hosts that were older than X retained an old config, whereas newer setups had another default variant (no dist-upgrade mind you!), which caused some subtle but annoying reliability issues. For them, the solution also was to go image based – they already had a canary system in place to test updates and stuff; so instead of going apt on each system, they just took a snapshot from the canary and redeployed it everywhere every time. (There was an exception for critical security patches; those were installed immediately – any potential drift would be eliminated during the next regular snapshot deployment anyways.)

That's only because most classic distro update mechanisms lack version locking and instead always go to the latest package versions available in the repo. There is no need to go full image based, if you want to avoid that. The easiest and practical way to avoid this is to mirror the repository and not update it until all machines have received the update. I know that this doesn't make it fully reproducible, but it solves the "inevitably see different package repositories" part.

That is quite obviously not true. Of course you can have multiple lock lists floating around at the same time in your corporate network. Lock lists = client side built "images".

This is a valid approach, especially given that it also has other advantages (clear audit trail of what packages changed when for example), but it is also tremendous maintenance overhead and only solves parts of the problem (e.g. this would not have helped against the problem of old installations vs new installations). And you can probably find a workaround for this problem too. Then you will discover another problem, and you can certainly find some bandaid for that as well. But... you could also just choose the architecturally sound approach here and go image-based. Whether it has to be OCI images, or disk images, or virtual machine images, or tar archives, or reference-based images via SHA2-manifests, or... that's a totally different question. But taking a seed and replicating that is always better and simpler than having a fleet of distinct systems, and then trying to come up with lots of bandaids to maybe hopefully eliminate all potential mutations to maybe hopefully ensure all the systems maybe hopefully are guaranteed to maybe hopefully evolve in exactly the same way. I mean, if people don't wanna go image-based for whatever reason that's fine – there are hundreds of different setups for hundreds of different use-cases; but if you want to have a fleet of identical systems, some approaches are more robust and easier to manage than others.

We have used this with (old) Redhat, Fedora Core, Ubuntu, Debian, Devuan, and back to Debian. Our Slackware days predate the controlled local mirror but I seem to recall we were using physical CDs to keep boxes in sync back then. We roll out updates from the local mirror to regression test nodes before deploying them to the live nodes.

We roll out updates from the local mirror to regression test nodes before deploying them to the live nodes.

Concur. Even with base image + app overlay based fleet management, you will never have uniform systems. Fleet diversity will scale at least logarithmically with size of fleet. You need to be able to live with diversity, because you're never going to have just 1 image deployed.

You need to be able to live with diversity, because you're never going to have just 1 image deployed.

Indeed, if you have constraints on not being allowed to reboot or nodes which will be temporarily offline, the state of your fleet will differ widely.

We "push" the content of the root filesystem from a single "distmaster" to ~250 nodes overnight. "push" means to compare the destination filesystem to an index generated on the master and to fix it up as needed, possibly requesting the required file data. A few files and folders are excluded (e.g. /etc/hostname).

So the installations don't drift as far as userspace is concerned. Yes, running processes might run old code. This is seldom a problem and if it is, we can distribute a restart recipe together with the new code. Biggest problem areas here are "plugins" (shared objects loaded at runtime). Looking at you, pam, nss, systemd, httpd...

Test installations, mistakes etc. are automagically reverted the next day.

As a sysadmin who manages fleets, I don't agree that reproducible system installation and update in package based systems is impossible. I have been doing it via xCAT (install) and SaltStack (update/manage) for a long time. You don't need these exact tools, but they are useful to us due to size of our fleets here. If you want extremely strict, SaltStack even has CF-Engine like drift-protection features yet I don't use them, because a system you don't touch doesn't drift.

Given a fixed state, any update set applied by apt and rpm are always deterministic. This is why they are so complex. Even so, this state can be the beginning and you can be bootstrapping a new image for yourself (I also did some distro development for some time).

Image based systems may have their advantages, but smearing other alternative to just strengthen one's position leaves a bad taste in my mouth, to be honest.

I've always wondered how much one can trust a factory reset. Let's put a real case: I had my phone hacked by a nation state some weeks ago. Their spies held it physically for several hours, and they had the PIN. Of course, after that, I don't trust that phone at all. Why would I trust the "factory reset" that comes with Android? I expect they could also tamper the image with which it is reset. At this point, the whole phone is a brick, IMO, and so I bought a new one.

Posted Nov 7, 2026 12:40 UTC (Sat) by NekkoDroid (guest, #176638) [Link] (5 responses)

I am unsure if AOS does it like this, but what Lennart has always been working towards is that the UEFI verifies the kernel (UKI) using the public key, which then verifies the /usr/ partition (which is read-only), which then loads the rest. "the rest" here would be the factory reset part, which is the only really modifiable part (also EFI variables get reset).

So say the nation state enrolled some kinda public key into the mutable part of the system (/var/ or possibly /etc/ but it sounds like it is also read-only) so that the system now also loads some of their system extensions or so, a factory reset would basically wipe those keys (and the extensions). /usr/ can't be enrolled, since that is pinned by the verity root hash and changes in the data would cause errors during reading by the kernel and the UKI is "pinned" by you (or I guess in the case of Amutable them) signing new UKIs. This is assuming you can prevent the nation state from enrolling their keys in your UEFI. But even if they did enroll their own keys in the UEFI the PCR values would be different, resulting in the mutable LUKS partitions not being automatically unlocked, so your mutable data is still inaccessible.

So as long as the cryptography implementations are sound and not bypassed by some 0-days it should be sound for the most part. Unless they are able to get below the bootloader it should be fine (but at that point they don't even need your PIN).

Do tell me if I maybe missed some attack vector which could possibly still exploit something.

Signed bootloaders won't save you if they control that.

#9881. US Government Email Systems Open to Abuse Thanks to Typos

Erroneous or outdated DNS records can give attackers surprising powers over organizations' email systems.

Simple oversights in domain name system (DNS) records are exposing government organizations to all kinds of potential impersonation, spying, and more.

In a new study of more than 25,000 government-related domains, SH Consulting founder Alex Shakhov found dozens whose DNS records referenced either mistyped, expired, or otherwise repurposed domains. Though few in number, those vulnerable included all sorts of agencies representing US towns, cities, counties, regulatory boards, and more.

Many of the erroneous records pointed to domains that were either available to, or already snapped up by, attackers. Depending on the nature of the error, they could allow attackers to send or receive email on behalf of vulnerable government agencies, reconfigure their DNS records, read their security records, and more.

"Typos in DNS are very dangerous, because technically the organization is being hacked without anyone breaking into its systems," Shakhov tells Dark Reading. "You already have a domain with a reputation established over years. You put whatever IPs you want into DNS, spin up an email server, and send emails out, exploiting that reputation and users' trust. And these attacks are very difficult to detect, because the attackers didn't break anything. They just registered a domain sitting in the DNS that nobody knew existed."

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Little matters more to a website's security than its DNS records, which include instructions about where the website lives in IP space (A/AAAA), its domain (CNAME), how its email is handled (MX, TXT), and who decides these details in the first place (NS). At the end of the day, though, it's a totally public set of information in plaintext. A simple typo in any of these instructions can have surprisingly significant impacts.

Take Livingston County, Mich., and the city of Pikeville, Ky. These two government bodies seem to have authorized Amazon's Simple Email Service (SES) for its day-to-day email needs and, as such, their TXT records specify it as a trusted third-party provider. The domains they list, however, contain typos: "amzonses[.]com" and "amasonses[.]com." Thanks to these mistakes, these bodies have been allowing a non-Amazon entity to send emails on their behalf.

To what end? When Shakhov checked the two organizations' Sender Policy Framework (SPF) allowlists, he found that Pikeville's listed 75 IP addresses, and Livingston's listed more than 32,000 different IP addresses, all authorized to send mail on behalf of their official domains. As a result, Pikeville's official government domain is now listed on the URI blacklist website "URIBL," and Shakhov assessed that "it's reasonable to assume the domain is still being used for abuse."

Related:PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

In the Livingston County case, the "included" SPF list was rotated every three to eight days since 2021. This suggested that an attacker was performing a "snowshoe" operation: switching to new sending IPs, sending unwanted or malicious emails, and once those IPs attained bad reputations, cycling in new ones.

This information alone doesn't necessarily prove that attackers were abusing Livingston County's email domain, or prove how much they might have. But it does prove that they could have. Shakhov connected the actor behind this compromise to a previously documented group that was seen abusing websites from major corporations such as Oracle and CNN Money as well as universities — like the Universities of California in Los Angeles, Davis, San Diego, and Santa Cruz (UCLA, UC Davis, UC San Diego, and UC Santa Cruz) — and the Connecticut state government, thanks to expired CNAME records.

Just about any DNS record can be abused if it contains a typo or refers to an otherwise incorrect domain for some other reason. The nature of the abuse depends, however, on the record in question. Once they register a so-called "dangling" (purchasable) domain, attackers can intercept mail (if the issue lies with an MX record), serve spam content (if it's in CNAME or NS), send phishing that appears to come from a legitimate sender (SPF), or collect security intel through Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC).

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

For example, the website for the City of Rupert, Idaho, currently refers to its neighbor Heyburn's old domain name, heyburnidaho[.]org. That domain was purchased by a malicious actor, which reworked its name server (NS) records to point to its shady gambling website. The actor also arranged to be able to send and receive emails from addresses with an @heyburnidaho.org suffix.

A less serious exposure could occur if attackers grab hold of a DMARC reporting domain. DMARC is an email security protocol, and its part of a TXT record can tell a mail server where to send reports. Those reports can contain sensitive information about an organization's email infrastructure. Shakhov found 11 local government institutions at risk of this sort of information theft, including four county and law enforcement agencies from Jennings County, Ind.

Taking advantage of these situations is one of the easiest jobs hackers can choose for themselves. "Attackers constantly scan DNS records for vulnerabilities and mistyped domains, because it's one of the easiest and cheapest ways to get into someone's infrastructure," Shakhov explains.

"Records at the root domain, like MX, NS, SPF, DMARC, CAA, etc., can be looked up by anyone," he continues. "Subdomains are harder to find, but Certificate Transparency logs reveal most of them. So attackers just scan DNS in bulk and get whatever they want. It's even easier for government domains, because it’s only about 26,000 domains to scan, and attackers can do it multiple times a day at almost no cost. CISA even publishes the full list of .gov domains, so attackers don't have to find them."

Shakhov laments that while DNS has been around for nearly half a century, "There's typically no one at an organization responsible for DNS management. As a result, over time it often turns into a graveyard of expired domains from previous vendors, former corporate domains forgotten after acquisitions and mergers, or just typos, when someone typed a record by hand instead of copying and pasting it."

Proper DNS hygiene, he says, requires that organizations follow at least a few core processes. First of all, he argues, "Admins and IT teams must stop typing DNS records by hand. Across millions of domains we scanned this year, 47% of the unregistered domains we found in SPF and DMARC records were typos, either of the organization's own domain or of a provider's."

Second, organizations must have a map of their DNS infrastructure and know where every DNS record came from. Depending on the circumstances, this can be easier said than done. "At universities, it's quite common for students to put a project on GitHub and ask the IT team to add a CNAME so it lives under the university domain," Shakhov explains. "The student graduates, but the CNAME stays. The GitHub account gets abandoned and removed, so whoever creates an account with the same name already has a CNAME sitting under the university's DNS."

Organizations should also consider registering misspelled versions of their own domains to prevent attackers from snapping them up later.

And, finally, "Regular DNS audits are a must," Shakhov says. "In most cases, it's just a simple script that scans your DNS for invalid domains or destinations and flags them. It's never been that difficult to do a quarterly DNS review to make sure everything is up to date."
