#9824. The Economics of AI Infrastructure: Compute Costs, Cloud Lock-In, and Competition

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

Tech writer sharing insights in a fun and informative way.

We are all watching the AI industry race from one frontier to another. Every few weeks, there's a new model creating hype, a new benchmark that becomes the industry standard, a new agent that promises to do the work of an entire team, or a new approach that makes yesterday's breakthrough look ancient.

I enjoy following these developments as much as anyone here, but there’s a question that is often ignored by us:

What happens when everyone can build with AI, but the infrastructure required to run it remains expensive, scarce, and controlled by a relatively small number of players?

That last part interests me most. We spend a great deal of time asking which model will win. I want to understand what happens when thousands of companies build useful products with AI, then discover that running those products at scale is an expensive business in its own right.

Let us have a look at it through a practical scenario.

A founder has built an AI assistant for accountants. The prototype works fine, and a few early access customers love it, which makes the founder envision a business that could actually run. Everything goes well with the first few customers. Then the usage grows. Customers anticipate quick responses; the service has to stay available, and with that the monthly compute bill begins to look rather different from the one generated by a handful of testers.

A successful start was just the beginning; the founder now has a new set of problems at hand. He needs to rent more computing capacity to keep the business running, hoping that suitable hardware is available at a workable price. To buy new equipment, he needs more capital and the expertise that are necessary to operate it. Luckily, if he finds a new provider with less cost, the migration could consume engineering time the company needs elsewhere.

All this decision-making, along with the founder juggling between hiring more staff, finding new customers, and convincing the current ones to pay more for the products, is a hefty task. And it makes founders wonder if having an excellent business model is enough.

I think the AI conversation needs to get more interesting. Building a capable product is becoming possible for more people. Delivering it reliably, at a competitive price, introduces another set of constraints. To understand those constraints, I started following the money and the hardware.

The first surprise is how many things have to go right before an advanced AI chip reaches a data centre.

Many of us know processor efficiency as something that just needs to perform calculations quickly, but calculations are only part of the job. The machine running on these processors must move enormous amounts of data between its processor and memory. Usually, High-bandwidth memory, shortened to HBM, helps feed data to the processor at the speeds workloads demand. Advanced packaging brings multiple components together so they can operate as one system.

I know these terms are hard for most of the people to understand. Here, let me break them down this way:

Think of a busy restaurant. Hiring a brilliant chef does little for the service if ingredients keep arriving slowly or the kitchen cannot get the equipment it needs. In an AI accelerator, the processor is only one part of the kitchen.

The supply chain behind these components is highly specialized. A shortage in one stage can hold up the finished product, even when another stage has room to expand.

Research from Epoch AI illustrates the scale of this problem. In its March 2026 analysis, the organization estimated that four leading AI chip designers collectively consumed around 90% of global HBM supply and advanced CoWoS packaging capacity in 2025. Its estimate for their share of advanced logic-die production was about 12%.

The contrast in the figures is revealing. Your company can have all the money ready, but if the manufacturing process isn’t up to speed, your orders will remain on a waiting list. Expanding chip production takes investment, equipment, skilled workers, and time. While a software team can deploy an update in days, Semiconductor capacity follows a different clock.

That manufacturing clock becomes more relevant when the entire industry is trying to expand at once. And it goes in favour of those with ample investments in their hands. Making companies with the strongest financing and the earliest access to suppliers have more options and leaving smaller buyers have to work around the capacity that remains available to them.

Even with this race, getting hold of a chip is only the beginning. The way companies buy access to computing power can shape their competitive position long after the initial purchase.

FTC’s staff report from January 2025 raised concerns about potential effects on competition, including increased switching costs and unequal access to important inputs. It identified risks for regulators to examine rather than declaring every partnership anticompetitive.

The commercial logic behind these arrangements is easy to understand. An AI developer who needs computing capacity can get it supplied by the cloud provider, perhaps alongside financing or other support. It looks like a win-win for both parties. The developer gets resources to build its business, while the provider secures revenue and strengthens a commercial relationship.

The complication appears when that relationship becomes demanding to leave.

Think of our accounting-assistant startup that has built its service around a particular cloud environment. Its deployment tools, monitoring systems, security controls, and model-serving software have all been configured to work together. But they found a competitor who is offering a lower price, tempting the founder to consider moving. But even though the new provider may have the right hardware, the transition still requires testing, engineering work, and careful handling of live customer service.

The migration bill and operational risks associated with the transition force the founder to stay with the current provider.

Cloud customers have faced versions of this problem for years. The UK's Competition and Markets Authority has highlighted that AI workloads add their own technical complications, especially when performance depends on particular accelerators and software configurations.

This is the distinction that keeps haunting me: access to compute and freedom to choose compute are two different things.

Yes, I tend to be more optimistic, but this is reality. A provider that offers a startup the capacity it needs today with some commitments. But these technical and contractual commitments narrow the startup’s choices tomorrow. The initial arrangement may be entirely reasonable for both parties. The bigger concern is when many businesses make similar commitments and a small group of suppliers becomes difficult to avoid. What happens then?

The same pressure appears on the other side of the market. Companies that own or rent large fleets of accelerators must turn that expensive equipment into useful work customers will pay for. A warehouse full of GPUs sounds impressive. The economics depend on what those GPUs actually deliver.

I found this particularly interesting while reading a 2025 research from the IEEE CLOUD conference. Researchers affiliated with IBM Research and other institutions investigated GPU bottlenecks in large-batch language-model inference. Their findings showed that memory bandwidth can limit performance even when much of a GPU's computational capacity remains underused. They also explored ways to improve memory allocation and serve additional workloads on the same hardware.

Let’s look at the practical implications of these findings through an example. A provider serving thousands of requests might combine them into batches to improve throughput. Processing more requests together can make better use of the hardware. But waiting for a larger batch increases delay, and customers expect quick responses. The operator has to juggle between efficient hardware use and the service its customers expect.

On top of that, model architecture and workload scheduling add further issues. Two AI services running on similar hardware can produce very different economics. One may use the available resources efficiently; another might spend more time moving data or waiting for work to arrive.

This is why instead of judging the strength of an AI infrastructure business by its installed GPU count alone, the best way is to analyze how effectively it converts expensive equipment into reliable computing services at a price customers will pay.

By having better software and scheduling, those economics can improve. It gives skilled operators an advantage without requiring them to buy another fleet of machines.

But efficiency isn’t the only factor. The money used to build the fleet in the first place is the actual issue.

You all know building an AI infrastructure requires large, long-lived investments. Data centres need buildings, electrical connections, cooling systems, networking, and specialized hardware. Many operators use financing structures that spread these costs across investors, lenders, landlords, and customers.

In his September 2026 working paper, Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh examined how the AI infrastructure boom is being financed. He describes a shift toward arrangements that include leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, and other financing structures.

These can help fund expansion while spreading financial exposure across multiple parties. But at the same time, they also introduce risks around customer concentration, construction delays, technological obsolescence, and the future value of specialized assets.

Consider an operator that borrows money to build a data centre and signs a long-term agreement with a major customer. The contract gives the operator a revenue stream that helps justify the investment. The lender has a clearer basis for assessing repayment, and the customer secures access to capacity.

Everyone has a reason to like the arrangement. The risks still differ.

The customer may have committed to more capacity than it eventually needs. The operator must keep paying its obligations while finding enough demand to use its equipment. The lender depends on the borrower meeting its commitments and the underlying assets retaining value.

I find this part of the AI boom especially worth watching. Even with a booming industry, individual investors can still lose money. Those outcomes are perfectly compatible.

There is, however, a strong counterargument to the idea that infrastructure will remain a durable barrier. But even with discussions like:

Today's shortages and prices tell us little on their own about the market several years from now.

I would be making a mistake if I treated every current constraint as permanent.

The more interesting question is how quickly those improvements spread, who can take advantage of them, and whether they give smaller businesses enough room to compete.

Imagine our founder returns six months later. The product has improved with inference costs fallen, and the team has found a more efficient way to serve customers. Those changes could transform the business. Yet the founder still needs dependable capacity, commercially sensible terms, and enough financial room to survive a period of slower growth.

That is the part of the AI story I want to follow. Yes, we all know that Intelligence is becoming easier to access, and there are real opportunities here. The ability to turn that intelligence into a sustainable business still depends on

The next AI winners may well build better models. Others may win by serving those models more efficiently or finding customers the larger players have overlooked. Some will build the infrastructure that everyone else depends on.

As I watch the next wave of releases arrive, I keep returning to one question:

When more companies can build with AI, who will have the economic freedom to keep building?

I would love to have people from industry share their insights on this matter and share their perspective; we can publish our conversation here on Hackernoon. Don’t hesitate to reach out if you have insights to share.

#9822. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

<|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason,

self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response.Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template:

You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID:

The repository containing quants is here. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever.Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task.We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model).

llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K.

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server:

The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers.

The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content.

The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs.

After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server:

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Send a request using the same Hub model ID:

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9819. Comparing Top ElevenLabs Alternatives for Production AI Voice Agents

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

AssemblyAI builds advanced speech language models that power next-generation voice AI applications.

OpenAI is removing tts-1, tts-1-hd and gpt-4o-mini-tts from its API on January 6, 2027. Inworld retired its first-generation models in June. If your voice agent hard-codes one vendor's model IDs, voices and audio format, every announcement like that is an unplanned migration.

So when a team asks us, "We're on ElevenLabs. Should we be?", the answer is often yes. This post is about the cases where it isn't, and how to test a switch in an afternoon.

The current flagship is Eleven v4, with a real-time variant, Eleven v4 Turbo (eleven_v4_turbo). ElevenLabs lists v4 Turbo at a median inference latency of about 100 ms, excluding application and network latency, with 90+ languages and the same voice cloning as v4. On the API pricing page, v4 Turbo is $0.04 per 1,000 characters ($40 per 1M), and v4 is $0.08. Flash v2.5 is also $0.04, and the docs quote about 75 ms for it, 32 languages, and a smaller model.

For voice agents, three details in the docs matter more than the headline numbers.

ElevenLabs' pronunciation tooling is deep. Eleven v4 reads IPA inline, and pronunciation dictionaries with phoneme tags work on v4 and v4 Turbo. If your agent says drug names or brand names all day, that's a real reason to stay.

From what we see, teams evaluate alternatives for one of six reasons. If none of these apply to you, stop reading and keep shipping:

AssemblyAI comes first because it targets the two most common reasons above: session caps and cost at volume. The rest are ordered by language coverage, widest first, because the first thing you're likely to lose when leaving ElevenLabs is its 90+ languages. Prices are pay-as-you-go list prices from each vendor's pricing page on October 28, 2026.

AssemblyAI-TTS-1 launched on October 27, 2026, and it's built for conversational voice agents, not narration. It was trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data. There are thousands of voices and instant voice cloning in the dashboard. The interfaces are a WebSocket (one session per conversation, one request per turn), an HTTP endpoint, and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Telephony output is pcm_mulaw or pcm_alaw at 8 kHz. You get per-word boundaries for barge-in, US and EU data zones, and LiveKit and Pipecat plugins. The Pipecat service is on Pipecat's main branch now and ships in a release after 1.14.0. The price is $15 per 1M characters.

The concurrency model is the part that matters for this comparison. There's no limit on sessions open at once. What the limits doc does rate-limit is new sessions per minute, starting at your streaming speech-to-text limit.

Where it breaks: six languages (English, Spanish, French, German, Italian, Portuguese). If you need Japanese or Hindi, stop here. There's no language detection, so you set it per session. Sessions cap at an hour and close after two minutes idle without a keep-alive. And it's brand new, without the production history of anything else on this list.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you run high-volume calls in those six languages and the bill and session caps are the problem.

Inworld's current models are TTS-2 and TTS-2 Flash. Both cover 200+ languages and locales and support instant voice cloning. Inworld quotes a P90 time to first byte of 100 ms and 20 ms respectively, measured server-side without the network. Output includes μ-law and A-law at 8 kHz, and there's an OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Pricing is per million characters and falls with commitment. On the pricing page, TTS-2 Flash is $15 per 1M on pay-as-you-go and $7 per 1M on the $1,500-a-month Growth plan. Concurrency is published plainly: 5, 10, 50, 150, and 500 concurrent generations across the self-serve plans. A WebSocket context only counts while audio is being exchanged, and you can hold ten times that many connections open.

Where it breaks: Inworld has already retired its first-generation models, so plan for churn. Language support is tiered by how thoroughly Inworld has evaluated each language, which means "200+" should be read as "test your languages."

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you need many languages at a lower price, and you can commit to a plan tier.

Sonic 3.6 went GA with a dated snapshot, sonic-3.6-2026-08-27, and it speaks 44 languages. That snapshot detail is the most underrated feature on this list. You can pin a version that will never change, run your evals, then move when you choose to. Given the deprecation news above, that's worth something.

The output format docs are written with telephony in mind. They cover pcm_mulaw at 8000 for Twilio and pcm_alaw for European networks. Pronunciation dictionaries take IPA or sounds-like spellings.

Where it breaks: pricing is in credits, about one per character, bundled into monthly plans (Scale is $299 for 8M credits). That's easy to start but harder to project than a flat per-character rate. On the pricing page, "high concurrency limits" are a Scale feature, and custom limits are Enterprise.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you want strict version control over the voice your customers hear.

Deepgram's Flux TTS is on a new endpoint, /v2/speak. Aura-2 voices stay on /v1/speak, so this is a migration even for current Deepgram customers. The design is built around turns. When a caller barges in, you send Interrupt, and the server tells you text_spoken and text_remaining. That answers the hardest bookkeeping question in an agent: what did the caller actually hear before they cut in?

The streaming socket emits linear16, mulaw or alaw, with μ-law at 8 or 16 kHz. Sessions last up to an hour. Deepgram has an EU endpoint, dedicated endpoints, and self-hosting, which is one of the stronger residency stories on this list.

Where it breaks: list price is $0.045 per 1K characters, more than ElevenLabs v4 Turbo. Published concurrency is up to 45 on pay-as-you-go and 60 on Growth. Ten languages are GA, and about thirty more are early access. There's a launch promo that matches Flux TTS spend with credits up to $500, ending December 31, 2026.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: you already run Deepgram speech-to-text, or barge-in correctness is your top bug.

Rime's flagship is Coda, released May 2026. Rime describes it as an LLM backbone with a speech engine trained on full-duplex conversational data. It speaks 10 languages. Mist v3 is the low-latency sibling, with four languages. Arcana has been retired from the cloud API.

Two features stand out for agents. spell() forces letter-by-letter reading of codes and IDs. Coda also accepts a custom X-SAMPA lexicon in six languages. Rime's WebSocket outputs audio/pcmu at samplingRate: 8000, and you can run the same models in your VPC or on-prem.

Where it breaks: pricing is per minute of generated audio ($0.050 for Coda, $0.030 for Mist v3, 20% off on Scale). Rime estimates about 1K characters per minute, but a per-minute price doesn't line up with per-character quotes until you measure your own speaking rate. Requests that omit modelId silently get Mist v3, so set it on every call. Unlimited TTS concurrency is listed as an Enterprise feature.

Better pick than ElevenLabs if: audio can't leave your network, or your agent reads a lot of alphanumeric codes.

gpt-4o-mini-tts is simple and well documented, but the guide now carries a deprecation banner, and the shutdown is January 6, 2027. The endpoint also doesn't list μ-law among its output formats. Starting a new telephony integration on it today means scheduling a second migration before you've finished the first.

Pick two candidates, not five. Then run two tests on each. Neither takes more than an afternoon.

Write the 30–50 sentences your agent actually says that contain something a caller must not mishear: confirmation codes, phone numbers, prices, dates, and surnames from your real customer base. Synthesize each one with every candidate at 8 kHz μ-law, the format the caller hears. Run all the audio through the same speech-to-text model, and check whether each entity survives.

STT is a proxy for a listener, not a perfect one. But a TTS output that a strong STT model can't recover is very likely one a caller on a speakerphone can't either. Holding the STT constant means the TTS is the only variable.

synthesize() and transcribe() are yours to fill in with each vendor's SDK. Listen to every failure yourself: some will be STT formatting quirks, and some will be the TTS reading "K7Q" as a word. Only the second kind counts against the TTS.

Put each candidate behind a real phone number through your actual carrier. Request μ-law at 8 kHz from the vendor (the table above lists each one's parameter) rather than transcoding it yourself. Then measure three things:

Every latency figure in this post comes from a vendor, measured on that vendor's terms. ElevenLabs excludes application and network latency. Inworld measures server-side at P90. None of these numbers can be compared directly, and none were measured over your trunk, from your region, at 9am on a Monday.

Benchmarks also can't hear your content. A model that reads a news paragraph beautifully can still say "K-seven-Q" as "kuh-sev-en-kew." Price comparisons fall apart at the unit level, too. Per-character, per-credit, and per-minute pricing only convert once you know how many characters a minute your agent speaks.

The TTS market converged faster than anyone expected. On clean prose, the voices on this list are close enough that most callers won't pick a winner. What hasn't converged is everything around the voice: how sessions are counted, what a model ID promises about next quarter, which audio formats come back without a resampler, and what the bill looks like at 50,000 hours.

That's why it's worth asking whether you should leave ElevenLabs. But the better question is whether you could leave in a week if you had to. Wrap the TTS call behind your own interface, keep the entity test in CI, and treat the vendor as a part you can replace. The vendor that wins on your test today may not be the right one in a year, and you should be able to switch either way.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Batch Intelligence at Scale: Cost-Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows with Built-In Resilience

Aditya Mulik explains how Walmart Global Tech deployed multi-agent LLM workflows across 4,700 stores for nightly batch inventory forecasting. He discusses tackling production hurdles - schema violations, cross-department data mismatches, and network drops - via MCP grounding and loop agents, while slashing cloud inference costs from $100k+ to $10k per month shifting from PTUs to pay-as-you-go.

Aditya Mulik is a Senior Software Engineer at Walmart Global Tech specializing in large-scale distributed systems and platform engineering, with deep expertise in deploying scalable and resilient solutions. He has led the development of microservices architectures and production LLM systems, enabling high-throughput applications serving millions of requests. He also contributes to open source.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

How much of this whole solution is going to cost to run, is what was the next question. The thing over here is the PTU problem. When the solution went to production, we had humongous amount of input and output tokens being used. Since it was a foundational model, we decided to secure 400 PTUs for that amount of scale that we need to run.

For 400 PTUs, we were almost being charged around 100k to 120k per month, and the solution was not that, because we are trying to also make sure that the inventory is accurate, also save cost. There should not be wastage happening in a particular department. Running at this position, it doesn't make sense, if these much PTUs are going to be used. PTUs is like reserved capacity, and we have to reserve it for the entire day. Any of these vendors who are providing the PTUs, we have to take it for the entire 24 hours, and it's a monthly or yearly subscription that we have to take in. Now the problem is, this is a batch intelligence application, it's only going to run overnight. It's not going to run the entire day. We are not serving any live traffic. For us, we were being charged 400 PTUs for 24 hours, and PTUs reserve capacity for the entire day.

Our workload was nightly batch run, which was not 24 by 7. We were paying for the round the clock capacity which was being used. This was our most critical problem that we were trying to solve in a particular defined set of time, which didn't make sense because of the cost involved. We started exploring options, what are the options? Because this is a foundational model, the best part about foundational model is they are well trained, they are good for such enterprise scale applications. The next thing that came to us was, what AI model should I choose? Here as you can see, we had cheaper models where we can go with open-source models or any other models, which might introduce some latency, or they could be cheaper compared to the one which we already had, whether it's a GPT-4.1 or Gemini, and so on. Or we can just reduce the PTUs, that was another option. Or we could go with pay-as-you-go. We were debating between quality versus cost, and both were not a good option, because we needed high quality but lower cost. That was the main problem that we had to solve.

How did we do that? The decision that we made was, we went with pay-as-you-go. Now just to go with some background, the problem with PTU versus pay-as-you-go, is pay-as-you-go will come with latency issues, as I've mentioned over here, and there will be rate limiting happening. We did observe a lot of rate limit issues, but now the thing is, as I mentioned in my failures as well, we had added a retry logic. This retry logic enabled us, even if there is a rate limit, if there are any 4xx or 5xx errors, I'm just going to retry again. If I do retry again, the output will be generated again. Now, if it's a pay-as-you-go, it's still a foundational model and it still gives very accurate responses, and there was no reserved capacity as well over here. We were not paying round the clock, we were just using as much compute as we require.

The payoff, so what happened over here is, we were supposed to pay around 100k per month, now we are paying just 10k as the final usage, because even with the retries, the cost is just very low. It's just going to happen in that specific 30 minutes, or maybe the time might increase. We don't mind because the stores are already closed, this is going to be a nightly job. Then, eventually, whatever compute is being taken is going to just happen at night, even if there are retries and everything, the cost will be minimal, output will be still matching the quality that we have set, because there is schema enforcement, and all the data engineering pipelines were fixed. This was our biggest win. As I mentioned, same tokens, same model, just a pricing tier switch from PTU to pay-as-you-go, and for a drastic drop in cost. That was the big win that I wanted to mention over here.

Every failure and every fix left us with a lesson worth carrying forward. Here's what we learned, building at scale. These are some of the learnings that I'm going to mention once again. Basically, schema enforcement. Since we are retrying, everything is all planned out, but schema enforcement is not just the one thing that happens over here, basic JSON validation. There has to be semantic validation, because data, what is coming from various sources, like in the AI domain, what I've learned very well is context has to be very accurate. With the data pipelines that we have, whatever context we get, if there is even a slight mismatch, it can just return vague output. We have to make sure semantic validation is in place. Data usability, making data easy to understand and use. We need to have some observability as well. Whatever the data that is coming in, we need to see how the pipelines are running.

All those things have to be taken into consideration. Then comes the data integrity. Maintaining accuracy and consistency of data is very important, is what I've learned from this entire perspective. That's one of the key features. Second thing is data engineering limits AI quality. As I mentioned over here, data quality over here is reliable AI results, accurate and trustworthy outcomes, data rectification, fixing upstream data issues, data engineering, ensuring data quality, and flawed data. What do we mean by all of this? The entire context over here, since it was a nightly job that was being run, this had a huge emphasis on the data engineering aspects itself. Because we were getting data from various sources, there was a lot of focus that was added into this perspective, where data coming from various sources has to be verified. The amount of scripts that we created were validated with the business and the data team, with the engineering team.

We ensured that once the data is very accurate, then that context will be fed properly to the agents with a proper particular prompt, and that will generate the exact output that we are looking for. Because it's a multi-agent workflow, we have to ensure that the data that is coming from various sources has to be very accurate. That was our main goal that we learned from this entire workflow. Also, like flawed data, as I mentioned, unreliable input is also like, once the input is not proper, all the agents will react in a weird output, because it might either not match to the schema, or it might just match to the schema also, but just generate vague outputs, and that's how it would return. Building retry logic, this was one of the most important aspects that I went through. We have been very much emphasizing on this.

Retries can be a very bad loop as well, where if you don't plan it properly, it can just keep retrying, and that would just increase a lot of costs. Just because there are tokens involved over here, you have to plan it very accurately. As I mentioned in the initial flow, we used to retry it at the base, like root level, where all the agents are, like where the workflow runs. Ideally, the agentic retry should be in such a pattern where it is actually needed, whether we are getting the context from the proper data source, so that the further agents don't have to hallucinate, or there could be something that can go wrong. Retry over here, implemented from the outset, reduced unexpected failures. There's proactive system enhancement, cost saving and efficiency. It results into better user satisfaction.

The next learning perspective is observability. This is one of the key things from the entire workflow, that everyone is focused on. Traceability is important, structured logging is important, and enhanced system understanding. Because once you have tracing enabled, for us, initially, when we were having this entire workflow running, we were not able to determine, ok, what's going wrong, just because there are no proper traces set up. If you're not able to identify if the LLM is hallucinating, or if the model is just getting rate limited, all that has to be clearly available. There are tools which help us add those visibility, and then having that in place, make sure that your application is very robust, and can survive any failures to make it very resilient. That's a very important aspect that I'll mention over here. The next thing is matching infrastructure to requirements. This is the key thing that we realized, which is the infrastructure should be used for a nightly batch job.

Here, we can see that the real-time infrastructure, like if you have a real-time infrastructure where users are having conversations with the LLM, in that case, you can have an accurate set of PTUs set up, and so on. In cost effective infrastructures, you need to ensure that you don't need to actually have PTUs only allocated. Here, in our case, we were opting either for like pay-as-you-go, or you can even go with open-source models. As long as it's giving you the proper performance, the correct output, that's the ideal approach that you should be going with. The next one is, I've reached the end, which is, tomorrow at 6 a.m., a store manager will confidently adjust the inventory. They don't know about our schema validation, our loop retries, our nightly API optimizations. They don't have to as well. It's just the ultimate metric, which is the resilient engineering. That's what the perspective is.

Just to recap over here, schema is our table stakes, semantics is the real work. Focus on validation checks that go beyond basic JSON structure. Data engineering limits AI quality, so garbage in results into garbage out as well. Having retry logic is very important. If there are network timeouts, hallucinations, retry can ensure that your output is always accurate. Observability is mandatory. Tracing, logging is very important. Then match infrastructure to the regular requirements. If it's a nightly non-latency sensitive batch job, then you have to ensure that you don't need to actually rely on PTUs, because that would just cost you even more than what's expected. That's the main goal.

Then it went out as a POC, POC to the entire production, like 4700 stores. Then it was foolproof as a concept that got deployed. We iteratively kept adding more and more recommendations. Our initial plan was to do it for a specific department itself. Then that's how we scaled it up.

#9816. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9815. NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

New guidance provides a basic framework for less-technical solo business owners, but it may miss the mark on how to secure technology that requires no human oversight.

Threat actors always target the path of least resistance, and for years that's been small-to-medium sized businesses (SMBs). Now, new guidance from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) aims to help companies with possibly even fewer resources: "solopreneurs."

For solo business owners, incidents can be a dealbreaker, with some shuttering completely following an attack. But risks also extend through the supply chain, as threat actors exploit vulnerabilities as a backdoor to hit larger enterprises.

NIST has published the Cybersecurity White Paper 50 (CSWP), a series of recommendations on how to curb cyber risks for a population that makes up 81.9% of all U.S. businesses.

The agency is trying to offset challenges with guidance for password hygiene, ransomware threats, and adhering to regulations requirements— areas where solopreneurs typically lack the time, money, or people to build out a security program on their own.

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

NIST said the guide translates its Cybersecurity Framework into lay language for non-employer firms. But with 33 pages to work through, is it worth the investment?

Most of the practical core is within reach for solopreneurs, says Martin Zugec, technical solutions director at Bitdefender. People just need to scroll to the short list on Page Two which calls for phishing-resistant multifactor authentication (MFA), a password manager, a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, automatic updates, and tested backups with one copy kept offline.

"None of that needs a security background, and you can do it in an afternoon," Zugec tells Dark Reading.

Compared to other NIST technical publications, Zugec says the CSWP is much easier to digest. Like NIST advertised, the language is plain and every action comes with a reason, a first step, and a note on what changes as businesses grow, he adds.

NIST outlined how businesses can respond to growing contractual agreements and an increasing number of suppliers and third parties as they expand operations and it becomes even more crucial to know third-parties’ cyber postures. That means staying current with regulations and establishing a formal process to manage risks that relationships could introduce.

While Bryson Byrd, cybersecurity advisor at Huntress, applauded NIST for the guidance, he says it still reads like it was written for practitioners. Terms like “least privilege,” “risk register,” and “data sensitivity classification” aren't the language of someone running a bakery or a consulting practice, he adds.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

"For too long, solopreneurs have been an afterthought in cybersecurity guidance," Byrd tells Dark Reading. "The intent is right, but the closer guidance like this gets to the language of everyday business owners, the more likely it is to actually get implemented."

But it's not just the language, Byrd says. It also assumes the owner knows how to turn on logging, review account sessions, and work though a separate spreadsheet of worksheets. And he points to a recommendation on obtaining legal counsel's input before notifying customers following an incident as an extra cost that often is not in the budget.

The guidance doesn’t appear to take into consideration that "nobody goes into business to build the most secure company that exists," he adds, but to build something over time. Every hour a solopreneur spends on asset inventories, backup testing, tabletop exercises, and compliance tracking is an hour taken away from running the business, which is the priority.

"Asking a single person to do all of this is extraordinarily cumbersome and, quite frankly, unrealistic," Byrd explains.

Byrd observes gaps in the guidance in places "we see hurt small businesses in the real world." The first is domain registrar, which is important to address, since attackers regularly go after small business domains to launch impersonation attacks and siphon money from customers and partners. Control of the domain means threat actors assume control over email and the business's website too.

Related:Why CTF Competitions May Be More Important Than Ever

"Locking down the registrar account with multi-factor authentication, enabling registrar lock, and turning on auto-renewal should be part of any baseline for a solopreneur," Byrd recommends.

The second gap he addresses is email authentication. The three core protocols — Sender Policy Framework, DomainKeys Identified Mail, and Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance — are becoming more important to protect a business from being impersonated and to ensure its legitimate email is delivered, adds Byrd.

The third and perhaps most impactful for a business of one is what happens when the owner is unavailable for an extended period of time due to an illness, family matter, or simply to take a well-deserved vacation.

Ransomware groups target businesses during off-hours, weekends, and holidays. If something does happen that demands an immediate response, it's essential for someone to be there. It could mean the difference between an incident and a breach.

"A break-glass plan that gives a trusted person or partner emergency access to critical accounts is still needed, and it belongs in any cybersecurity plan for a solopreneur," he advises.

Previously, SMBs and self-employers adopted the mindset that they were too small to be considered a target. That has since been disproven tenfold and is only growing worse.

Advancements in autonomous tools and artificial intelligence (AI) have lowered the barrier to entry and the cost of attacks, letting threat actors target that population at scale. They realized they had a choice: go after large enterprises with strong defenses for one big payout, or target thousands of small shops with weak security that are far more likely to pay up.

As the struggles evolved, so must the guidance. Daniel Eliot, lead for small business engagement at NIST, says this paper comes nearly 10 years after its predecessor, NISTIR 7621 rev.1.

A lot has changed in 10 years and after the initial call for comments, "that feedback was instrumental in moving the project forward."

AI is forcing a lot of security guidance to be updated and making that guidance easier to write, Zugec notes. He noticed new additions in CSWP included a section on AI and a warning that AI makes phishing more convincing.

NIST urged businesses to take a second or third look at any message that asks people to click a link, download a file, transfer funds, or log into an account.

But contrary to popular belief, AI hasn't brought any new or novel attacks, observes Zugec. It is changing who runs businesses and what they rely on to operate.

Solopreneurs are using AI assistants to read their mailboxes, run commands, write code, and use accounts under the owner's identity, he explains. While it enables one person to do the work of a small team, it also expands the attack surface.

"Many solopreneurs will use agentic AI to grow faster than their security does," he says. "The guide gives no advice on what these agents should be allowed to reach, or on securing the code they write."

The biggest gap Zugec found in the guide is "AI that acts." NIST treats AI as something passive that businesses need to inventory and review outputs for, but agentic AI has increasingly removed humans from the equation.

As agentic AI enables more people to run a business alone, the security of those businesses matters more than ever, Zugec warns. That will warrant outside help, as people increasingly turn to vibe coding to build applications on their own. He urges solopreneurs to have their code reviewed by someone with coding and security experience before anything ships.

If anything is public-facing, that means an attacker can reach it and it needs to be protected.

"AI is good at producing software that works, but not necessarily software with a small attack surface," he says. "The guide doesn't cover this, yet it's often the first risk solopreneurs run into."

Zugec spotted other weaknesses too. For example, NIST pushed for continuous updates, but a solopreneur can’t realistically track every legal and contractual security requirement, negotiate security terms with a cloud provider, or monitor their systems around the clock.

Secondly, it never ranks tasks, which makes prioritization difficult for a one-person team. For example, it opens with governance, the least actionable task, while MFA and backup advice only starts on Page 14. It also fails to cover two common attack routes: ClickFix, which tricks people into pasting a command themselves, and a malware that steals their logged-in session, which bypasses MF

"It lists around 25 actions and says outright that it isn't a checklist, so a busy owner has to decide what comes first," Zugec says. The guide also sets its scope by headcount, which is problematic. Technically the headcount would be one, but risk follows what information businesses hold and who targets them.

It's not just about size, it's about what's exposed. Risk heavily varies between someone who sells candles on Etsy as a side gig versus someone in the finance industry trading billions in cryptocurrency.

"A solo crypto operator or a consultant with client secrets needs far more than the guide’s baseline," Zugec says.

She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.
