#9814. Local vs. Cloud AI Coding Agents: Benchmark Results, Hardware Costs, and Performance

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

Senior Software Engineer and Tech Lead with 15+ years of experience across banking, government, B2B/B2C products, enterprises, and startups. Interested in software architecture, AI-assisted development, and engineering practices.

I’ve written about one of my projects before—open-daimon (a group AI chat for Telegram and a platform for extensions). On top of it, I built my own harness that runs other harnesses in different roles. The public open-daimon repo is not updated because, for now, I develop only locally; it is faster that way.

At some point I wanted to get into local models, and the reason is simple: in the cloud, the rules belong to someone else, and they change without asking.

In October, it came up again that Anthropic's consumer terms say it plainly for residents of the EEA and Switzerland: do not use the services "for any commercial or business purposes". These terms cover Claude.ai and the Pro and Max plans. So a developer in Europe who writes work code in Claude Code on a Max subscription is formally breaking them. For work, you need the API, Team, or Enterprise, and that is a very different amount of money.

The second story is about what you are allowed to do with your own hardware. A Decrypt writer asked Claude Opus 5.5 to help him get root back on his own LG TV. The model's safeguards cut the request off and suggested switching to Opus 4.8. And the researcher known for finding the always-on microphone in Samsung TVs says OpenAI banned his account for "Cyber Abuse" after he analyzed firmware with ChatGPT. About $500 of API balance went with the account. OpenAI has not commented, so for now it is only his word.

The direction is clear: poking around in someone else's software will be forbidden more and more often, and the vendor decides what counts as abuse. Napster was shut down by rights holders. They can come for Claude and Codex too, and there is plenty to ban there.

The models themselves are not safe either. In October, "uncensored" versions started disappearing from Hugging Face. One was taken down for violating the content policy. Another, the abliterated build of Kimi K2.7 Code by huihui-ai (the same huihui-ai whose Qwen3.6 shows up later in this test), just returns an error, and nobody has explained why (write-up). There is no mass purge yet. But in 2020, GitHub took down youtube-dl over a single RIAA complaint and only put it back a month later. As long as everything sits in one place, that place can be shut down.

Since April, Anthropic has been verifying the identity of some users: passport and selfie through Persona. One of the triggers is logging in from an unsupported country, and those accounts get blocked. Money is no longer enough to get the best model: it also matters where you live and what passport you hold.

So I wanted a backup in advance: download the weights while they are still there, and check that they work locally at least somehow. The cloud is unlikely to close tomorrow. But if it does, I want a doomsday agent system at hand: one that runs without a subscription, without someone else's rules and without anyone's permission.

A gaming laptop with an RTX 5080 already had LM Studio with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. LM Studio runs models right on your computer and serves them through the same API as the cloud. I connected it to OpenCode, an open-source terminal agent, like Claude Code but with any model. It was slow, and models on the MacBook were even slower, really slow.

The usual advice here is to give a local agent a very light harness. For example pi, whose system prompt is about 2k tokens.

I decided to test everything on the same task: the cloud, a MacBook, a gaming laptop, an NVIDIA DGX Spark, and cheap, mostly Chinese, models through OpenRouter.

I built the task for my "canary", a script that checks whether Opus and Codex have gotten dumber today. I made it after Opus was noticeably dumb for me for a while. Maybe I was in an A/B test, maybe there were technical problems, but I figured it would be useful.

The agent gets the minibank repo: ~700 lines of Python, a multi-currency banking ledger. Accounts in different currencies, transfers with conversion, fees, monthly statements, a CSV export for accounting. Next to it sits DECISIONS.md with the team's decisions, like in any living project.

And a request, as if from a real manager:

Customers are complaining: the monthly statement total doesn't match the account balance, especially when there were transfers between currencies. Figure it out and fix it. And check whether the same thing breaks anywhere else.

Not a word about tests. Not a word about DECISIONS.md either.

The main bug: the statement does not take the amount that actually landed on the account during a transfer. It recomputes it through the old converter at the current rate. The rate changed during the month, and the statement total drifted away from the balance.

The agent does not see what it is graded with. After the run I take whatever is left in the repo and run:

Some hidden tests and rules check that what worked still works. So an agent that did nothing at all would get 0.31. That is awkward to read, so below every score is rescaled from zero: 0 means nothing changed, 1 is perfect, and below zero means the agent broke more than it fixed.

The limit is 20 minutes from the request. Cloud models finish in 1.5–11 minutes, so there is headroom. If an agent runs out of time, I grade what it managed to do. I picked 20 minutes knowing that the dense model on the Spark needs 16.5. I did not go higher: who wants to wait longer than that for a fix to a small task?

One task, in Python, and mostly one or two runs per setup. On the MacBook I ran more, and there you can see that the same model with the same settings can score 0.21 or go below zero. So this test cannot tell similar local models apart. But the gap between the best cloud models and the fast local ones came out so big that no noise covers it.

Codex does not report its cost, so I calculated it from the run's tokens (280k input, 243k of them from cache, and 4k output) and GPT-6.1 Sol API prices: 2 dollars per million input tokens, 10 cents for cached ones and 10 dollars for output.

All three read DECISIONS.md, did not fall for the bait converter, found the export, updated the traitor test and wrote their own tests that catch almost all the wrong fixes. Opus did it in a minute and a half with 7 tool calls.

Opus and Codex fixed the code the same way. The only difference is in the tests each wrote on its own. If you merge the fee back into the transfer line in the statement, Codex's tests catch it and Opus's tests don't. Opus itself made the fee a separate line, it just did not pin that with a test. Fable has one hole too, but a different one: its tests won't notice if the export starts recomputing the transfer at the new rate again. One missed wrong fix out of nine is the whole difference between 1.00 and 0.96. In a second run, both Opus and Fable missed both of these and got 0.92. In a third run Opus scored 0.96 again, but missed a different wrong fix, the one with the month boundary. The holes are mostly the same; what changes is how many of them get closed this time. I ran Codex only once, so its 9 out of 9 may be luck too. My personal take, as of October 2026: in everyday work I still prefer Opus, even though on this task Codex came out both cheaper and slightly better.

I also ran Opus and Fable in my working setup: with my settings, hooks, MCP servers, and separately also with 178k tokens of someone else's long session before the task, like on a normal working day. Everywhere the same 20/20 and all subtle conditions. The only thing that moves is how many wrong fixes their own tests catch: from 7 to 9 out of 9. In the clean setup it moves too, from 7 to 8, so it is noise. The long context only affected the price: a run costs 2–6 times more.

So the bar is: one and a half to five minutes and an almost perfect solution.

This is the computer many developers already have, and the first thing you want to try.

First, raw speed, without the task. Generation is how many tokens per second the model writes. Prefill is how many it reads: before writing a single word, the model reads the whole context: the system prompt, tool descriptions, open files and the history of steps. An agent's context grows with every step, so slow prefill hurts it more than slow generation.

In a MoE model, out of 30 billion parameters only about 3 work on each token. Each layer has many experts (separate blocks with their own weights: as if the model kept dozens of narrow specialists and called a few suitable ones for each token). The other experts sit idle meanwhile. That is why it is fast. Hence the names: 30B A3B means 30 billion total, 3 active. The dense 27B honestly runs all 27 and gives five tokens per second on a laptop. "4-bit" is quantization: each parameter is stored in 4 bits instead of 16. The model becomes four times smaller and fits in the laptop's memory, but loses a bit of quality.

LM Studio loads some models with an 8192-token context. And OpenCode sends about 15k tokens of system prompt and tool descriptions on every step. The task does not fit in that context. There is no error, the agent just works badly.

So the first thing to do is set Context Length in LM Studio for each model separately. I set 65536 for all of them.

Qwen3 Coder turned out to be the fastest and the most useless. 50 tool calls, a cheerful final report about a "minimal and precise fix". And exactly that trap: it swapped the old converter for the new one but kept recomputing the transfer. By the hidden tests, it was as if it had done nothing. It also left its own test_debug.py in the repo root.

Qwen3.8 27B read DECISIONS.md, the only local model on the laptop that did. And in 20 minutes it did not make a single edit, neither in pi nor in OpenCode.

On the laptop, Gemma 4 12B won. It found the main thing: it took the posted amount instead of recomputing, in both the statement and the export. It missed UTC, ISO time and the fee, wrote no tests and did not read DECISIONS.md. But it fixed the customer's basic bug.

The smallest of the three turned out to be the most useful. It finished in under 10 minutes and did not wander off like Qwen3 Coder. It got this result in only three of its ten runs.

I also played with sampling (the randomness settings for picking the next token) on Gemma and Qwen3 Coder. I tried LM Studio defaults (temperature 0.8, top_k 40, top_p 0.95, min_p 0.05, repetition penalty 1.1), the values recommended by the model authors (temperature 1.0 and top_k 64 for Gemma; temperature 0.7, top_k 20 and top_p 0.8 for Qwen3 Coder), and a temperature of 0.3. It did not help. With the same settings, Gemma scored 0.21 and −0.17 in two runs, so the spread from chance is bigger than from any settings. And the mistakes are the same: no run managed UTC, ISO time or the traitor test.

The gaming laptop: an RTX 5080 Laptop with 16 GB of VRAM and 32 GB of RAM. LM Studio serves the model over the network. It runs Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, also MoE, but bigger.

Generation speed before and after retuning LM Studio:

The drop from 54 to 9.5 tok/s on a long context looked suspicious, and I started digging. The model weighs 21.7 GB and there are 16 GB of VRAM, so part of the model lives in RAM either way. Almost all the weight of a MoE model is in the experts, the same blocks of which only a few switch on for each token. Attention (the part of every layer that, on each new token, looks through the whole context again to decide what matters in it) and the shared layers take little. It pays best to keep some of the experts in RAM: only a few of them switch on per token, about 3 billion parameters out of 35, and the CPU copes with them. But attention has to stay on the GPU: the longer the context, the more it has to look through. Parallel requests and context size turned out to be irrelevant: with one slot instead of four and a 32k context instead of 64k, the speed did not change. What decided everything was how LM Studio splits the model between the GPU and the CPU. The model had no saved layout, and LM Studio decided on its own how many layers to put on the GPU. I set three parameters:

Together with the KV cache, about 14.5 GB of VRAM is in use. Without these settings, judging by the speed, LM Studio moved whole layers to the CPU, attention included. The longer the context, the longer the CPU took to process it, hence the 9.5 tok/s. If you send the experts of all layers to the CPU, only 4 GB of VRAM is used, the GPU sits almost idle, and you get about 40 tok/s. It is fastest when VRAM is filled almost to the top.

I installed pi and compared it with OpenCode on the same model. On the first step OpenCode sends the model about 15k tokens, and pi about 2,200. A local model reads about 1000 tokens per second, so OpenCode's extra 13k tokens cost it about 13 seconds. A cloud model reads that much almost instantly.

Pi finished twice as fast and ran the tests four times, and its tests caught two wrong edits. But both solved the same thing and missed the same conditions: UTC months, ISO time and the fee. With a 10-minute limit it was the same.

Pi became twice as fast: under five minutes instead of ten. The same solution with the same misses, only this time pi updated the traitor test. OpenCode, already updated to version 2.2, still did not fit in the limit: the model reasoned out 55k tokens in it versus 11k in pi, ran the tests ten times, never got to the end, and on top of that broke the corrected rate in the export. So the model got faster, but not smarter.

Separately, about speculative decoding, which this laptop also uses: an extra layer of the model itself (MTP, multi-token prediction) quickly guesses several tokens ahead, the main model checks them in one pass, and where the guess is right, it comes out faster. It is turned on by a separate flag when the model is loaded. If you forget the flag, the model quietly runs twice as slow.

The Lenovo ThinkStation PGX is built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark: a desktop box with a GB10 chip and 128 GB of unified memory. Models run in vLLM, a model server built for many requests at once. The task went to it as an archive (without the hidden tests, only the repo, the request and the scripts) and was run through OpenCode. I graded it with the same script.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, an Opus distill (that is, a model fine-tuned on Opus's answers), in 4-bit NVFP4. This is NVIDIA's quantization format that the Spark's chip computes in hardware. 35–50 tok/s.

340 seconds, finished on its own, 0.25. 12/20, 3/7.

It missed UTC months, ISO time and the fee. Exactly the same conditions as on the RTX 5080 laptop in OpenCode and in pi. Five runs, two different computers, two different servers, two different harnesses, and all five missed UTC months, ISO time and the fee.

ThinkingCap-Qwen3.8-27B is dense and a reasoning model, in NVFP4 with speculative decoding of 3 tokens. 20–25 tok/s.

With a 10-minute limit: an empty diff, not a single change to the code, 0.

According to the log, for the first 5.5 minutes, OpenCode's scout subagent was looking over the project. Until minute 8 the main agent read all the files and correctly named the main bug in its reasoning. At minute 8 it started one long generation, and the limit cut it off. Not a single edit.

The same run without a limit: 987 seconds, 0.92: all subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, its own tests catch 7 fixes out of 9. An Opus-level result.

Another model on the Spark is Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. It is an ablated version, MoE, but of a completely different size: 125 billion parameters, with about 6 working per token. NVFP4 quantization mixed with MXFP8, speculative decoding of 3 tokens, 22–32 tok/s. Its limit was 10 minutes, not 20.

The limit did cut it off, but during a final re-check, all the edits were already made by then, and it says it ran the visible tests in four time zones. I graded what was left in the repo.

0.96. 20 out of 20 hidden tests, all 7 subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, nothing forbidden touched. Seven of its own tests that catch 8 out of 9 wrong fixes. They missed only one: an export that recomputes the transfer at the new rate.

That is Opus level in a clean setup. Six to seven times slower than Opus, and it used up the whole ten minutes.

The price is memory. The driver holds about 96 GiB for the model, about 106 together with the vLLM processes, and the Spark is almost completely full:

Total held by the NVIDIA driver (measured)

PLE table (26.8 GiB on disk, read via mmap)

13–16 in the page cache, the system can evict it

One run. After Gemma gave me both 0.21 and −0.17 with the same settings, I would not draw conclusions from a single run. But 20 out of 20 with all seven subtle conditions does not happen by accident either.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super is another big MoE: 120 billion parameters, 12 active, NVFP4, a draft model guessing 7 tokens ahead. 24–42 tok/s. The driver holds about as much for it, ~96 GiB.

The same 10-minute limit, and it finished on its own within it: 533 seconds.

0.68. 18 out of 20 hidden tests, 6 out of 7 subtle conditions. It fixed the transfer, UTC months and the CSV format. But it left the fee inside the transfer line in the statement, although DECISIONS.md has exactly that as a separate rule. It did not update the traitor test. It wrote its own tests, but they catch only 4 wrong fixes out of 9.

So on the Spark: of the two big MoEs, Flash-Next leads, it found everything. Nemotron is weaker, but finished within the limit on its own. The driver holds about 96 GiB for each.

Between local hardware and Opus at $0.30 per run there is a whole market of cheaper models. Through OpenRouter, I took one or two fresh models from each of eight major Chinese vendors, added Devstral for comparison, and ran them with OpenCode and the same limit. These are the regular versions, not abliterated.

The eight Chinese vendors: DeepSeek, Zhipu (GLM), Alibaba (Qwen), Moonshot (Kimi), MiniMax, Tencent, StepFun and Xiaomi. Devstral is French, from Mistral.

Four models solved the task like Codex: all hidden tests, all subtle conditions, the traitor test updated, and their own tests catch all 9 wrong fixes. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash did it in two minutes for under a cent, 36 times cheaper than Opus, which scored 0.96 on the same task. The September version of the same Flash scored 0.88: its tests caught 6 fixes out of 9. The October snapshot seems to have closed the holes, although that run was still on the old version of OpenCode.

GLM-5.3 is right there: it lost 0.02 only on the traitor test, which it did not update. Three times cheaper than Opus.

MiniMax M3.1 Flash: 20 out of 20, all subtle conditions, 18 of its own tests that catch 7 fixes out of 9. And the same habit as the previous M3: it added a paragraph to DECISIONS.md, which must not be touched. Three cents a run.

Step-5 from StepFun also got 20 out of 20, in under three minutes, but its tests catch neither the swapped converter nor the recompute at the new rate.

Kimi disappointed. K3.1 Pro, the flagship priced at 2 dollars per million input tokens, passed all hidden tests but wrote only three tests of its own, and they catch 4 fixes out of 9. K3 missed the fee and did not update the traitor test. The previous Kimi K2.7 Code (the one whose uncensored build was removed from Hugging Face) scored the same 0.72. K2.7 and K3 have the same holes: the fee and the traitor test. K3.1 Pro closed them, but hardly writes tests, and $0.27 a run is almost the price of Opus.

DeepSeek V4 Pro is a strange case: a bigger and more expensive model than Flash, and half the result, with time zones and the fee missed. Maybe it is the dates: DeepSeek's Pro is from August, its Flash from October.

Devstral missed time zones, ISO time and the fee and did not write a single test of its own.

The cloud Qwen3.8 Max and the local 30–35B Qwens are one family, and their results sit at opposite ends of the table. Max passed every hidden test and every subtle condition and updated the traitor test; the only holes are in its own tests, 7 out of 9. It did think for 11 minutes, though, longer than Flash-Next on the Spark, and cost $0.36, more than Opus. Max has 2.4 trillion parameters, the local MoEs 35 billion. Max found almost everything, and they fixed only the obvious. Then again, the dense local 27B on the Spark scored the same 0.92, it just thought for sixteen minutes.

Qwen also has Max Prime, a faster and more expensive variant of the same Max. It solved the task perfectly, 1.00 in six minutes, but cost $0.73 a run, 2.4 times more than Opus.

One run per model is not enough, we have already seen the spread. But the gap between the top half of this table and the fast local models is too big.

0 means nothing changed, below zero means the model broke more than it fixed.

On this task, you can. On a real project, it is unknown.

A smart local model already exists, but the hardware is expensive and the speed is slow. The dense 27B solved the task at Opus level, it just worked sixteen minutes instead of a minute and a half. The 125B MoE did it in ten, but took almost all 128 GB of the DGX Spark. Small models that fit on a laptop fix only the obvious. Speed is limited by hardware, quants and speculative decoding, and all of that gets cheaper. The smarts, it seems, are already there, at least on 700 lines.

The Chinese cloud is still cheaper and more practical: four models solved the task like Codex, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for under a cent.

A local model is dumb sometimes too, and its spread, as you saw above, is big. But it is always the same model, and nobody can swap it without asking.

And separately about safety. Several of the local models in this test, including Qwen3.6 from huihui-ai and Flash-Next, are abliterated, meaning their refusals were cut out. Pi runs commands without confirmation by default, and its documentation says plainly that watching the transcript does not protect you. A model that can't refuse and an agent that doesn't ask: on a work computer, that pair is better run in a container.

Manual Coding is Becoming the Exception, Not the Default

#9813. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Show interactive benchmark results with downloadable data

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

#9812. PwC's CISO on AI, Robots & What's Next for Security

As AI accelerates change across the enterprise, PwC's James Shira explains why security teams must rethink their approach to risk and adapt their strategies.

James Shira, global CISO and CIO of PwC, has spent more than two decades navigating the evolution of cybersecurity, from its early days as a largely technical function to its continuously growing role in corporate agendas and spending. Shira's path into the industry was, as he puts it, as "consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow." Originally considering a career in law, Shira decided to pivot, more seriously considering pursuing cybersecurity through independent study, and then formal education. Today, he oversees both technology and security at one of the world's largest professional services firms, giving him a broad perspective on the challenges facing security leaders.

In this episode of Heard It From a CISO with Dark Reading associate editor Kristina Beek, Shira discusses the skills and experience needed to build a career in cybersecurity, including the value of industry certifications, higher education, and on-the-job experience. He also examines the qualities that distinguish effective security teams, the challenges of balancing the CISO and CIO roles, and how security leaders can establish credibility with corporate boards. For Shira, successful leadership comes down to more than technical expertise. It involves building trust, communicating complex issues clearly, and creating an environment where employees can develop.

Related:Black Hat India 2026 Makes a Landmark Debut in Bengaluru, Bringing the Global Cybersecurity Community to India

Shira also shares his thoughts on the topic on everyone's minds: artificial intelligence. He warns that rapid adoption is expanding attack surfaces, adding pressure on security teams, but also notes that AI technology will add opportunities for professionals seeking roles in the field. As for what's ahead, Shira expects significant societal and industry change and shares that this rate of change is likely to be the new standard — it’s best if everyone is prepared to go along for the ride.

This is part of Dark Reading's ongoing Heard It From a CISO video series, which features frank, exclusive conversations with cybersecurity leaders in the trenches. Check out the entire series here.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

James Shira: I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times. But I think that makes for better decisions.

Related:NIST: Solo Shouldn't Mean Less Secure

Dark Reading's Kristina Beek: Hi, everyone. My name is Kristina Beek. I'm an associate editor at Dark Reading, and I'm here for another episode of Heard It From a CISO. Today, I'm joined by James Shira. Thank you so much for joining us. I would love it if you could introduce yourself and talk about your background and your current role as CISO at PwC.

James Shira: Sure. It's great to be with you today. My name is James. I am the global CISO and CIO for PwC. I've been involved in what we used to call IT security since 1999. I became a CISO in the early 2000s, I think 2000 or 2001, really based on an opportunity and happenstance. I've been involved in the community since that time, now 25 or 26 years. For the last eight years, I've also been operating as our global CIO.

DR's Kristina Beek: Love to hear that. How did you first get involved specifically in cybersecurity, technology, or security in general? I know there are a lot of different ways people get involved. Some people study computer science, and some come from very alternative backgrounds. What does your path look like?

James Shira: I think my path is probably as consistent and inconsistent as the paths people follow. I was planning on getting a degree to become a lawyer, actually. Then, being a blue-collar kid, I realized I couldn't afford law school. After two years, I needed to make a change, so I redirected toward business and information systems. That was my undergraduate background.

Related:UK Wades Into Tech Sovereignty Amid AI Policy Changes

When I graduated in 1998, there was a bit of a mini-recession, what we often refer to as the dot-com crash. At the time, I used to read the physical Wall Street Journal pretty religiously, and there was a lot of discussion about security. We didn't call it cyber then. I figured this was a space that needed leaders and leadership. I was very interested in working toward and building an executive career path, and I wasn't sure — probably like a lot of college graduates — how to go from having no experience to having an opportunity to be in a role like the ones I'm privileged to have today.

I really started by researching, reading, learning, and studying, a lot of self-directed study, including some computer science-based material. I also did a program at Columbia that's now a master's program, which was very helpful to me. I was one of the first students when we started. The idea was like an MBA for technologists, and I'm proud to say it's now a Master of Science degree. I had the opportunity to be a student mentor there for a long time. It was really on a whim that I thought this space was going to be incredibly interesting, and it's proven to be.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to my next question: What would you recommend to somebody who wants to go into cybersecurity today? In general, what would your advice be? What insights could you provide in terms of what would be best to study? Should they prioritize certifications or a four-year education? There are a lot of different ways to go into cybersecurity today.

James Shira: For sure. I think the four-year education discussion we're all having right now is really relevant. I have younger kids, so I've got some time before they get there. I think it's a really relevant conversation because of the cost. Having worked my way through college and taken out loans at the time, those loan amounts look really small compared with what people are confronted with today. I think it's a very fair question and debate that people should have.

I'm a big proponent of certification on our security team. We really encourage people to do it, and we sponsor some of them. I'm not going to name them because we'd be here for a long time, but I think it's a very smart strategy.

The way I describe it to our folks is that I talk about the concepts of internal equity and external equity. Your internal equity when you come out of college is zero. You're new; you're coming into the industry. You build that up over time with your employer. Obviously, you want to pick the right place to work, as best you can. In the early days, experience in and of itself is the value you're pursuing.

The second piece, external equity, is something you can drive as hard as you want. As a young person without a lot of experience, you can pursue certifications. Some require years of work, but there's a lot out there. The most successful people I've had the privilege to mentor start out with a high degree of emphasis on certifications. Then, after five to seven years of experience, they make a choice about whether they're going to pursue a management track or a higher-end technical director or subject-matter-expert track.

On your question about a four-year education versus certifications, my personal view is that if you want to be in a role similar to mine, or the same as mine, you're going to want that four-year degree. You may even want a master's eventually. If that's your intended path, I would encourage you, notwithstanding the loans, to complete your undergraduate degree. There are a lot of great schools with programs that can be helpful. If you look at that and say to yourself, "That's a significant debt burden, and I don't think it makes sense. I'm not sure I want to pursue being an executive," then I think you should do the certifications and work on getting as much experience as you can.

DR's Kristina Beek: That's a great insight. You talked about building equity and how, when you're fresh out of college, that really depends on your employer and the company you choose to work for. Moving back to PwC, what interested you in the company? Why did you choose to work there, and what has it been like being CISO?

James Shira: When I was coming out of Zurich Financial Services, now Zurich Insurance Group — which was also a great time in my career — I was interested in finding the right CISO challenge at a similar or bigger scale. What interested me about PwC at that time was that it was a 160-plus-year-old institution. I had never worked in professional services; I had only worked in financial services. So a different industry interested me.

I think the organization's values here at PwC were very consistent with mine, and it's been a privilege to be here. It sounds clichéd, but it's really a great place. The quality of people, on average, in my experience, has been really high. People have a desire to do the right thing, and as a CISO, that's incredibly helpful. A lot of our security strategy is culturally centered on employee behavior and training, so those things were very consistent and have been very helpful.

I know some CISOs drive programs through cultures that are less amenable. This culture was incredibly amenable to moving its security program to the next level. Nobody's program is perfect, but that was helpful. Lastly, I had the opportunity to bring a lot of my colleagues with me. I have the privilege of sitting in these roles, but it's not something I did on my own. It's something we've done collectively as a team. Given the scale of the mission here, I had the opportunity to bring some colleagues from my previous employer over, and it's been awesome to see their careers flourish here as well. In short, it's a great place to work.

DR's Kristina Beek: That brings me to a follow-up question. When it comes to a team, whether it's business-oriented or security-focused, what makes a great team? What kinds of people are you looking for, whether in terms of personality or skills?

James Shira: I'm going to answer your question in reverse order. The people I like to work with don't come in a common package. I think there's a lot of strength in diversity of experience and perspective, and so we try to embrace that. I like people who are self-confident and have their own point of view. It makes for mutual learning and some intense debates at times, but I think that makes for better decisions.

The people I'm looking for don't have to have gone to a specific school. They don't necessarily need a traditional profile, but they definitely need to be self-confident and self-directed. I talk to the team a lot about emotional resiliency. I think it's a really important concept in the security industry because, when I got started, security was past the mailroom, past the bathrooms, in the basement somewhere, and rarely in the boardroom. Now, people coming into the field wouldn't even recognize that, because security is such a central, strategically critical issue for companies. I need that confidence in our employees so that, when they become the leaders they can be, they can flourish based on that confidence. It's hard to build a great team without that.

The second piece I think is incredibly important is transparency. It's something I work diligently to practice when I'm speaking in front of the thousands of colleagues I have the privilege of leading: being as brutally transparent as possible about whatever we're trying to do. It's uncomfortable at times, and it can be challenging to answer the questions you get, but I think it provokes the kind of cultural engagement that makes for a great team.

The one thing I'll say lastly is that I don't think mediocrity, as a rule, fits in high-performing teams. You have to embrace your high performers, try to elevate and promote them, and create an environment where they can be as self-directed and successful as they can be.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. When you were answering that, one of the things you talked about was how the CISO role and cybersecurity in general are now in the boardroom. I see a lot of articles about how to communicate with C-suite members as a CISO, how to deal with friction, and how to get your board to believe you. What would you say about communicating your needs as a CISO to the rest of the board? Do you encounter friction in your experience, and how do you deal with that?

James Shira: I think it's a great question. I'm going to offer a point of view. I'll start by saying I've gotten it wrong. I don't have all the answers, but I've learned through mistakes and by having great mentors.

I think credibility with a board starts, frankly, through delivery. The first thing you have to do is build a track record as best you can. That might sound counterintuitive: Don't I need the board's buy-in before I deliver? Somewhat, but I think conversations with our various boards here, and the conversations I've had previously, show that over time, through delivery of the program and driving the change you're advocating for, you can build a lot of credibility.

The second of my three points is that you have to find your own authentic voice. Personally, I'm not a natural. I kind of joke with the team at times that I'm a radio guy, not a TV guy, and I've had to work at being a TV guy. You have to find your own authenticity through your own style. A lot of times, those of us who get the privilege of being in these C-level jobs receive a lot of advice and pressure about how to present and who to be. I would encourage people listening to find their own style and approach that works best for them. Obviously, measure it against how effective it is, but embrace the style that's authentic to you. For me, I just try to be myself with our board.

The last thing I'd say, and I think it's maybe the most important point, is that you have to bring the expertise to the board, not try to drag the board to your expertise. In our domain, don't underestimate how intimidating it can be for the people listening. It's security. They see the headlines. Maybe an issue has occurred in that business. As board members, they feel responsible for providing oversight over management, and they're under tremendous pressure to do so. Don't underestimate that.

If you come at them with a high degree of expertise, terms, acronyms, and things they don't understand, I've found that doesn't work. That would be one of the mistakes I've made in the past. What's worked well for me is not to dumb it down, but to simplify it. If you have enough mastery of a topic, you can describe it in a way that doesn't make the other person feel intimidated and helps them say, "OK, I get that." One suggestion I would offer is to use storytelling. That's what I've done, and it has worked well for me.

DR's Kristina Beek: While you're obviously CISO, you're also CIO, so you have two perspectives. What is it like balancing the responsibilities of both roles?

James Shira: The good news is that, over the last eight years I've had the privilege of being in these roles, there's been a tremendous amount of harmonization between the technology transformation of large enterprises and the need to get the cyber piece right. Therefore, unlike when I started, when security was past the mailroom and in the basement, it's now such a primary issue for organizations that it's really on the CIO's agenda. I think having both of those skill sets is a very critical thing in this day and age.

The one difference I'd acknowledge for the audience, because otherwise anybody watching would think I missed it, is that at times the CIO role can be inherently more political than the CISO role. Let me explain briefly. As a CISO, you objectively know what good looks like: Don't have a breach, don't have an incident, improve your audit posture, drive good risk management, and so on. What good looks like in the CIO world can sometimes be less black and white and more gray. It can change in a way that a traditional CISO might find challenging to navigate.

I, for one, never anticipated the amount of passion and energy that debating different HR or finance platforms might bring. I've learned how to spend a lot of time with CFOs and COOs in our businesses. That's made me not only better professionally, but also more sympathetic to the issues they have, especially in some of the smaller businesses where a decision we might make from a CIO perspective has a significant material impact on their cost basis. There are differences, but in summary, it's a very complementary experience for me. The biggest challenge is time management and moving time between the different things.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. AI is, of course, always part of the conversation. It's changing how attackers work, and it's also changing how organizations operate. What do you see as the biggest cybersecurity opportunity or risk associated with AI right now?

James Shira: I think the most important issue with AI, straight down the middle, is how it changes, evolves, and increases an organization's attack surface. The second issue is the rate of change it brings: how fast it moves and how fast systems have to move. Those are the two dynamics.

What happens to the size of your attack surface? AI can really explode it. At the same time, AI puts pressure on the pace of change across the whole security function. For us specifically, that means dealing with the amount of patching, vulnerability management, inbound requests, and client requests. You have to manage those two dynamics.

On the technology front, in my career — which some people in this audience might think is long, while others might think it's not that long yet — I've never seen anything move as fast. In a short period of time, we've gone from a nascent technology that we're all excited about to actually operationalizing it. At least in my career, I haven't seen anything cross that divide so quickly. Therefore, I think it's ultimately the biggest change-management exercise, maybe ever. That's really where leaders need to center and focus their time.

DR's Kristina Beek: A lot of people are coming out of college or going into college with the expectation of going into cybersecurity or computer science. AI is changing the field very rapidly. A lot of people are scared that they may not even have a job or that there may not be a place for them in this field. What would you say to that, with the rise of AI?

James Shira: I understand where people get that. I understand how people get that. I think it's understandable, but I think it's wrong. The amount of change across society and industries is significant. It's very difficult for me to chart a course in my head for what isn't going to change. Therefore, I think the opportunity for young professionals is to be the change agents — to deliver the change.

I think one thing we don't always do well for our young professionals, but need to, is tell them the truth about the adversity of change management. It's hard. It's hard, and it's going to be hard for them. Do I think AI is a job-elimination technology? I don't. But I understand and respect how people might reach that conclusion.

If you're doing highly repetitive, data-centric activities, that's not, frankly, what you go to college for. Some of us had to do that coming out of college, earning our stripes, but that's not generally what you go to college for. That probably gets changed a lot by AI. Of course. I don't think it's a displacement strategy.

DR's Kristina Beek: Going back to what you said about how AI is changing things so rapidly, what do you think cybersecurity leaders will spend the most time thinking about three to five years from now? I know that's hard because things are changing so quickly, but what do you see for the future?

James Shira: I think the constants I would expect not to go away are the rate of change, the pace, and the pressure. Therefore, I think you have to find consistency in process and strategic principles, meaning how you manage your strategy shouldn't change. You should find the things in executing the strategy and operationalizing it that don't need to change, because so much around you will be changing.

In our history, and in at least my part of the 20-year history of IT security and cybersecurity, when there's been a technical change — think cloud, client-server, mobile, or whatever — we've effectively changed every aspect of how we implemented security controls. I'm hoping and working diligently to avoid repeating that pattern in the AI space because I think it just adds too much volume to an already high-intensity, high-volume situation.

Three to five years from now, I'm hoping AI can be a much more consistent enabler of delivering secure outcomes, but we're still learning how to fully operationalize it. Then there's the issue of token costs, which we're not going to get into today, but that has a high degree of relationship to driving the overall security budget, which we're figuring out as we go.

Secondly, I don't think most companies will have enough money to build a security program the way we've historically done it, at the size and scale that AI could imply would be required. Third, I think organizations are going to have to shrink their digital footprint as they transform. The good news is that — obviously, hope is not a strategy — AI will hopefully allow us to interact with our systems of state much more efficiently than building applications as the recurring front door to all of our systems, as we've done for the last 10 or 20 years. That ought to have a great benefit in reducing the attack surface, too. I think that's what companies need to do, and I think that's what will look so different in three to five years.

Lastly, I'd say I'm expecting significant societal and industry change, especially in a five-year window. I'm not sure I'm going to have a robot at home, but maybe some of us will. I think physical AI is going to place a significant premium on investment capacity, both on the hardware side and on the adoption and implementation side.

There are Orwellian views of that, where you could see the doom and gloom. I think there's also a tremendous opportunity. Some countries are not having the birth rates we need. Frankly, there isn't enough reproduction to maintain the number of people in society. So robots in some places in the world are going to be incredibly helpful in allowing us to deliver the things people need in society.

But I'm excited by it. I'll summarize by saying I think the big fundamental choice you have to make every morning when you wake up is to embrace the change, both in yourself and in how you do the job, because the change is almost — I joked with a colleague the other day, and she's a really capable runner while I am not, that this is kind of like being on the treadmill at the speed Annie would go at, not the speed James would go at. Some days I feel like I'm hanging in there, and other days I feel like I'm about to fall off the back of the treadmill. I think everybody just needs to say that's part of this.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. That's great to hear. Normally, I end these interviews by asking what the future of cybersecurity looks like to you, but we've already touched on that. So I'd rather end with a different question: You've spent a lot of time in tech and security and have seen how it's evolved. What has been the most rewarding part of that work, and what do you think will continue to challenge or motivate you, especially in a field where the risks are sometimes really high?

James Shira: Sure. It's an easy answer for me: It's the people part. It's the team. Every success I've had the privilege of being part of is not a James thing. I had a role, sure, but it's a team thing.

When you see someone — we have a number of people in our organization who started as interns at my previous employer. One colleague started as an intern and is now an executive. Another colleague, Annie, whom I mentioned, is now a partner. Those are the things that lift me back up when I have a bad day, which happens. It's when we see people building and shining in their own way, self-actualizing. That's pretty cool, and I think that's the right way things should work.

Look, it doesn't always work that way. There are probably people on the team who don't feel they got a fair chance, or who feel something didn't go perfectly. That's the challenge of working in teams of people, because people — me, you, all of us — are not perfect.

But the best days for me are when I see colleagues rise, shine, and do great things, and even leave the organization and go do great things somewhere else. That's pretty awesome. I think that's our opportunity with AI and security. We have to embrace it, try to see the positive in it, and grow through it.

DR's Kristina Beek: Absolutely. I so enjoyed this conversation. Thank you so much for joining me today.

James Shira: Me too. Thanks for your time.

#9811. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support
